Robot calibration estimates the parameters that make a robot's measurements and commands agree on the physical world. Classical kinematic calibration has four steps: modeling, measurement, identification and correction <Cite id="roth-mooring-ravani-1987" />.

<Image id="leica-laser-tracker-ats600" />

<SelfCheck
  prompt="On many objects, a grasp misses by a small offset in one direction that grows with distance from the wrist camera. What should you inspect first?"
  options={[
    {
      value: 'hand-eye',
      label: 'Check the hand-eye rotation and its residual',
      why: 'A small angular transform error creates lateral position error that grows with working distance. The consistent direction is a calibration signature.'
    },
    {
      value: 'more-data',
      label: 'Collect more demonstrations at longer distances',
      why: 'More data can teach a stable bias, but the distance-dependent systematic direction points to geometry. Fixing the transform removes the error for every policy and dataset.'
    },
    {
      value: 'larger-model',
      label: 'Fine-tune a larger vision encoder',
      why: 'Capacity does not make the camera and robot frames agree. A larger model may conceal the bias on familiar poses and retain the same physical defect.'
    }
  ]}
  answer="hand-eye"
  takeaway="Systematic, geometry-dependent misses are calibration evidence; measure the transform before changing the learner."
/>

## The calibration chain

A manipulation system chains <Term id="camera-intrinsics">camera intrinsics</Term>, depth alignment, extrinsics, joint zeroes, link and tool parameters, payload, timing and actuator response. FoundationPose tracks novel-object poses with or without a model <Cite id="foundationpose-2024" />, but a wrong hand-eye transform still misplaces the grasp.

<CalibrationChain className="my-6" />

## Camera intrinsics

Intrinsics map pixels to rays through focal lengths, principal point and lens distortion. Zhang's method recovers them from a planar pattern at a few unknown orientations <Cite id="zhang-2000-calibration" />, and Kannala and Brandt's generic model covers wide-angle and fisheye lenses <Cite id="kannala-brandt-2006" />. Refit after any focus, resolution or crop change. AnyCalib estimates pixel rays from one image and fits several camera models to them, including pinhole and fisheye models; its formulation also handles cropped or stretched images <Cite id="anycalib-2025" />.

## Depth is a measurement model

Stereo depth error scales with the square of distance, and repetitive structures make matches ambiguous <Cite id="realsense-tuning-2026" />; the D400 datasheet adds saturation from specular reflections <Cite id="realsense-d400-datasheet-2026" />. Kinect random error grows from a few millimeters to about 4 cm at maximum range <Cite id="khoshelham-kinect-2012" />, and a joint depth-color calibration with a depth-distortion model beat the manufacturer's <Cite id="herrera-depth-color-2012" />.

Camera Depth Models instead learns a correction from RGB and raw sensor depth to metric depth, with synthetic sensor noise used during training <Cite id="camera-depth-models-2025" />.

## Hand-eye calibration

Hand-eye calibration finds the gripper-to-camera transform for a wrist camera, or base-to-camera for a fixed one. Shiu and Ahmad cast it as $AX = XB$ <Cite id="shiu-ahmad-1989" />, Tsai and Lenz solved it in about ${}100 + 64N$ arithmetic operations for $N$ robot stations <Cite id="tsai-lenz-1989" />, and Park and Martin derived closed-form exact and least-squares solutions <Cite id="park-martin-1994" />. Daniilidis represents the motions with dual quaternions and solves rotation and translation together using singular value decomposition <Cite id="daniilidis-1999" />.

<Image id="baxter-gripper-wrist-camera" />

OpenCV needs at least two motions with non-parallel rotation axes, so three poses, and strongly recommends many more <Cite id="opencv-hand-eye-docs-2026" />. MoveIt's tutorial reports accuracy plateaus after about 12 or 15 samples in most cases <Cite id="moveit-hand-eye-tutorial-2026" />.

<HandEyePoses className="my-6" />

Markerless methods now rival targets: DREAM's single-image accuracy is comparable to multi-frame offline calibration <Cite id="dream-2019" />, and Hydra reaches 5 mm task-space accuracy against 7 mm for classical methods <Cite id="hydra-hand-eye-2025" />. DRHeC's authors report 88.9% grasp success on a UR5e, 46.3 points above the differentiable-rendering method EasyHeC <Cite id="drhec-2026" /> <Cite id="easyhec-2023" />.

Kalib tracks a reference point on the robot, obtains its 3D positions from forward kinematics and solves a perspective-n-point problem for the camera transform <Cite id="kalib-2024" />.

## Kinematic and tool calibration

Manufacturing errors and joint compliance shift an assembled arm from its nominal [kinematics](/classical/kinematics) <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />. Nguyen and colleagues calibrated a humanoid from 31 chosen postures and cut RMS error 2.3-fold against the manufacturer's model <Cite id="humanoid-geometric-calibration-2025" />. OmniCalib found CAD wrist-camera extrinsics off by up to 10.56 mm and 1.74 degrees, and writes back only corrections its observability checks support <Cite id="omnicalib-2026" />.

## Time calibration

A late frame misplaces a moving arm. Kalibr estimates time offsets jointly with spatial transforms <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />, and IEEE 1588 synchronizes networked clocks to sub-microsecond accuracy <Cite id="ieee-1588-2019" />. On one RealSense D435 and Airbot Play rig, Realtime-VLA V2 measured camera, proprioception and motion delays of 55, 50 and 150 ms <Cite id="realtime-vla-v2-2026" />.

<TimeOffsetMiss className="my-6" />

## Dynamics and actuator calibration

Sim-to-real work calls this system identification. Atkeson, An and Hollerbach identified load and link inertial parameters by least squares and beat CAD-derived predictions <Cite id="atkeson-an-hollerbach-1986" />, and Gaz and colleagues first identified the Franka Panda's dynamics, joint friction and feasible parameters <Cite id="gaz-panda-dynamics-2019" />.

Swevers and colleagues design periodic excitation trajectories as finite Fourier series, enabling repeated-cycle averaging and analytic derivatives for parameter identification <Cite id="swevers-excitation-1997" />.

Hwangbo and colleagues found actuator dynamics central to ANYmal's transfer gap and learned an actuator network from real measurements <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />, and SPI-Active, which chooses identification data actively, beats baselines by 42 to 63% in locomotion transfer <Cite id="spi-active-2025" />. Without measured response, a dataset confuses policy and tracking error.

## Calibration versus visual servoing

Visual servoing puts the vision sensor inside the control loop and drives image features toward a target through a task function <Cite id="espiau-1992" />. Its interaction model, velocity commands and safety geometry still need consistent conventions.

## Drift and ownership

DROID's per-session checkerboard calibrations were not always accurate, and the dataset provides camera-to-base calibrations for about 36,000 scenes <Cite id="droid-2024" />. Most public datasets lack extrinsics; CalibAll recovered them for about 97,000 episodes across 16 datasets <Cite id="calib-all-2025" />. Store each calibration with hardware serials, camera settings, tool, software version, date, procedure and residuals, and redo it after a remount, collision, tool or firmware change.

## Configuration space Lozano-Pérez's 1983 reformulation moves planning from the workspace into configuration space. A configuration $q$ is one complete posture, the vector of joint values. The set $\mathcal{C}$ of all of them is 2D for a point robot in the plane and 7-dimensional for a 7-DoF arm . The configuration-space obstacle $\mathcal{C}_{obs}$ holds every configuration where the robot intersects an obstacle; the rest is free space : $$ \mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_{obs} \cup \mathcal{C}_{free}, \qquad \mathcal{C}_{free} = \mathcal{C} \setminus \mathcal{C}_{obs} $$ Shrinking the robot to a point and growing each obstacle by its shape reduces collision checking to point membership. Planning becomes the search for a continuous curve in $\mathcal{C}_{free}$ from $q_{start}$ to $q_{goal}$ . Explicit boundary or solid models of $\mathcal{C}_{obs}$ are difficult to build, though semi-algebraic models for chains and trees can be generated automatically. The basic semi-algebraic mover problem is PSPACE-hard when the number of degrees of freedom is unbounded . Hardness holds for a planar linkage with multiple links and for a multi-arm robot among 3D polyhedra; Canny's roadmap method is singly exponential . Sampling-based methods skip building $\mathcal{C}_{obs}$ by querying a collision checker and validating whole local paths, though closed-chain constraints make sampling difficult . MCVAMP addresses manifold constraints by projecting many samples in parallel with CPU vector instructions, including constraints for quasi-static humanoid motion . ## Sampling-based planning The probabilistic roadmap (PRM) of Kavraki, Svestka, Latombe, and Overmars samples configurations uniformly, keeps the collision-free ones as nodes and adds extra nodes where a heuristic marks the space as difficult. A local planner links nearby nodes, and queries become graph searches, so one roadmap serves many start-goal pairs . LaValle introduced the rapidly-exploring random tree in Iowa State Computer Science Technical Report 98-11, October 1998 . Each iteration samples a state, finds the nearest vertex under a chosen metric, picks a control input and integrates over a fixed time interval, keeping vertices and edge paths in free space. For dynamics $\dot{x}=f(x,u)$, the Euler step is $$ x_{new} \approx x + f(x,u)\Delta t $$ with starting state $x$ and input $u$; the report recommends a higher-order integrator such as Runge-Kutta . LaValle's 2006 book drops the step size: each sample connects to the nearest point on the tree's swath, the union of its edge paths, splitting an edge when needed . Nearest-neighbor selection gives RRT a Voronoi bias, because frontier vertices own larger Voronoi regions. The report leaves convergence rates open . LaValle and Kuffner's kinodynamic version steers with controls instead of straight lines . For differentially flat systems, FLASK plans in flat-output coordinates, where local boundary-value problems have closed-form solutions . Drag the shelf in the figure below and the tree of random safe steps regrows around it to the goal. Kuffner and LaValle's RRT-Connect grows two trees, rooted at the start and the goal . In the six manipulation problems of a 2023 comparison, it had the best overall success rate . pRRTC parallelizes RRT-Connect on the GPU, distributing both tree expansion and collision checking across threads . Probabilistic completeness means the chance of finding an existing solution approaches one as sampling continues, with no finite-budget guarantee . Karaman and Frazzoli prove it for simplified PRM (sPRM) and geometric RRT on $X=(0,1)^d$, $d\geq2$, assuming a solution with clearance $\delta>0$, uniform independent samples, a fixed sPRM radius, capped RRT steering and straight-line collision tests. A 1-nearest-neighbor sPRM is not probabilistically complete . OMPL 2.0.0, released April 6, 2026, added VAMP as a SIMD backend for planning speeds up to 25 kHz ; VAMP's authors report gains of more than 500x from fine-grained parallelism on 7 to 14 DoF robots . The library implements PRM and RRT, includes benchmarking tools and plugs into external collision checkers and visualizers . The OMPL 2.0 paper describes the broader update: hardware acceleration alongside planning with geometric constraints and temporal goals . ## Optimality: RRT\* Karaman and Frazzoli's 2011 analysis separates feasibility from cost. In an obstacle-free Euclidean example with steering distance at least the domain diameter, RRT's best cost converges almost surely to a suboptimal value. Their PRM result concerns a forest-building version that rejects connections inside a connected component. Fixed-radius sPRM, which allows them, is asymptotically optimal at greater computational cost . RRT\* adds least-cost parent selection and rewiring. A new vertex takes the cheapest collision-free parent among nearby vertices, and neighbors reattach to it only when that lowers their cost. With $n$ vertices, the connection radius is $$ r_n = \min\!\left\{\eta,\; \gamma\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{1/d}\right\}, $$ where $\eta>0$ caps the steering distance and $d\geq2$ is the dimension. Of the paper's two sufficient bounds on $\gamma$, the conservative one is $\gamma>4(\mu(X_{free})/\zeta_d)^{1/d}$, with free-space volume $\mu(X_{free})$ and unit-ball volume $\zeta_d$ . The result assumes a bounded Euclidean domain, uniform independent samples and straight-line connections, which excludes differential constraints. Cost must be positive, monotone under concatenation and at most a constant times path length. The optimum must have weak clearance, deforming continuously into paths with positive clearance, with cost continuous near it in a bounded-variation norm : $$ \mathbb{P}\!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}c_n=c^*\right)=1. $$ Here $c_n$ is the best cost after $n$ iterations, so a finite budget can return a suboptimal path. FMT* grows a tree over a fixed batch of samples with a lazy dynamic-programming recursion ordered by cost to arrive . AO-RRT-Connect puts RRT-Connect inside the AO-x framework to add asymptotic optimality while retaining its fast search for an initial feasible path . The non-optimality analysis assumes that optimal paths traverse a set of states of measure zero. Expected processing work is of order $n\log n$, within a constant factor of RRT, though RRT\* makes $O(\log n)$ collision checks per iteration to RRT's one . After a first solution, Informed RRT\* skips routes irrelevant to the query by sampling only the domain's intersection with $$ \hat{X}_f=\left\{x:\lVert x-x_{start}\rVert_2+\lVert x-x_{goal}\rVert_2\leq c_{best}\right\}. $$ This prolate hyperspheroid has the start and goal as foci and the best path length $c_{best}$ as transverse diameter. It contains every state on a strictly improving path, but its states need not be collision-free, so collision checks remain. Over 100 runs per variation with 60 seconds of refinement, it refined faster than RRT\*, and it gains nothing once the set covers the domain . BIT* combines batches of samples with heuristic search, ordering candidate connections by their potential solution cost and refining the approximation as more samples arrive . ## Trajectory optimization Trajectory optimization makes the trajectory the decision variable, with smoothness, clearance and task terms in the objective or constraints. Neither the objective nor an initial guess guarantees a collision-free result. CHOMP and TrajOpt both plan from infeasible guesses as well as refine existing trajectories . Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) poses planning as a mixed-integer program with a very tight convex relaxation, so in most cases a cheap rounding suffices for globally optimal trajectories . ### CHOMP: covariant gradient descent CHOMP combines an obstacle cost with an environment-independent prior on trajectory dynamics. In the discrete form, $\xi$ holds the interior waypoints, $K_d$ computes finite differences and $e_d$ accounts for the fixed endpoints : $$ \mathcal U(\xi)=f_{\mathrm{prior}}(\xi)+f_{\mathrm{obs}}(\xi), \qquad f_{\mathrm{prior}}(\xi)=\frac12\sum_{d=1}^{D} w_d\lVert K_d\xi+e_d\rVert^2. $$ The first-derivative term penalizes squared velocity; higher-order terms penalize other dynamics. The obstacle cost integrates a signed-distance penalty over the robot's body, weighted by arc length so that moving faster through a costly region cannot lower it. Covariant descent uses the inverse smoothness metric to spread each gradient step smoothly along the trajectory . On the first six joints of a seven-DoF Barrett WAM, CHOMP solved 99 of 105 problems from 15 endpoint configurations. On LittleDog it ran inside a footstep controller with a separate footstep planner and a ZMP preview controller seeding the trunk. Trajectories were computed before execution because worst-case optimization took about 1.5 times as long as execution . The paper also tests a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo variant and records finite-time local-minimum failures ; the 2013 journal CHOMP uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo against high-cost local minima and for probabilistic completeness, and respects hard trajectory constraints . STOMP improves a trajectory by sampling noisy alternatives and combining lower-cost samples; its obstacle and smoothness objective need not supply an analytic gradient . ### TrajOpt: penalties, trust regions, and collision limits TrajOpt solves a sequence of convex subproblems, with a kinematic objective summing squared displacements between successive waypoints. Nonlinear constraints enter an $\ell_1$ penalty whose coefficients grow in an outer loop as needed; linear constraints are imposed directly. With signed distance $\operatorname{sd}$ positive for separated objects, the collision penalty is $$ \max\!\left(d_{\mathrm{safe}}-\operatorname{sd},\,0\right). $$ It is nonzero inside the safety margin. Pairs out to $d_{\mathrm{check}}>d_{\mathrm{safe}}$ enter the linearized subproblem, including some with zero current penalty. A box trust region bounds each step, expanding when actual improvement matches the local model and shrinking otherwise . Waypoint checks can miss collisions between waypoints, so TrajOpt penalizes a swept volume: the convex hull of endpoint shapes, inflated for rotation. The rotation bound adds $d_{\mathrm{arc}}=r\phi^2/8$ to the safety margin, a correction omitted in experiments because it was well under 1 cm. The swept-volume gradient is not guaranteed accurate in 3D, and the implementation used Bullet with convex hulls of robot meshes and penalized self-collisions only at discrete times . ### What the TrajOpt benchmark measured The 2013 benchmark used four simulated MoveIt scenes with fixed endpoints: 198 seven-DoF PR2 arm problems with 11 timesteps and 96 eighteen-DoF full-body problems with 41. OMPL ran with default parameters and MoveIt's default smoother, and path length was normalized by the shortest path any planner found. Both tables give historical 2013 timings . On the arm, single-initialization TrajOpt solved fewer problems than either OMPL planner and multi-initialization TrajOpt the most. The tested CHOMP implementation came from its authors . The full-body comparison omits CHOMP, for which the authors lacked documentation or data. The 2014 journal extension also studies statically stable Atlas walking and curvature-constrained needle trajectories, which are separate experiments from the 2013 tables above . The introduction gives every planner ten seconds, while the experiments specify three seconds per CHOMP initialization and thirty seconds for full-body OMPL . cuRobo runs many parallel optimizer seeds on GPUs and solves difficult motion generation problems within 50 ms on average, 60x faster than state-of-the-art trajectory optimization . An industrial integration extends cuRobo to a robot on a gantry and builds collision environments from CAD digital twins, illustrating the extra modeling needed outside fixed-base benchmarks . ### Initial guesses and the two-stage pattern CHOMP and TrajOpt both need an initial trajectory and can stall in bad local minima. In CHOMP's tests, straight-line seeds often beat RRT seeds on the objective where collision removal succeeded; in TrajOpt's, multiple initializations changed success rates . Ratliff and colleagues describe PRM and RRT as commonly deployed in two phases: find a feasible path, then remove redundant or jerky motion . Shortcutting, a cheap second stage, repeatedly picks two trajectory points and tries to replace the segment between them with a shorter collision-free one . MR-POP uses a parallel GPU sampling planner to produce feasible multi-robot trajectories that can seed a trajectory optimizer . ## Where this meets the learned stack Motion Policy Networks trained on over 3 million motion planning problems in over 500,000 [environments](/world-models/generative-sim) . A 2026 survey finds that neural motion planners often struggle to generalize to unseen, out-of-distribution planning settings . Neural Motion Planning distills expert plans from simulated clutter into a reactive policy, then applies lightweight optimization when deploying the policy on a real arm . Deep Reactive Policy replaced AIT\* with cuRobo as its expert planner because GPU acceleration let it scale to 10 million expert trajectories. Its authors report that AIT\* achieved 0% success on all dynamic tasks, and cuRobo fell to 3.00% when the goal was temporarily obstructed . Ariadne, from Carnegie Mellon's Silong Yong, Guanya Shi and colleagues (October 2026, accepted at NeurIPS 2026), trains only on valid states, with no trajectories, and builds a path by following the geometry of the learned state manifold. On DualKUKA, where two 7-DoF arms must avoid obstacles and each other, it averaged 53.3% success across three environments, against 44.7% for RRT, 31.7% for a trajectory-trained Diffuser and 53.2% for PBDMP, which also receives the scene layout. Ariadne learns one planner per scene . Receding-horizon model-predictive control keeps optimization inside the feedback loop ; [reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc) weighs it against learned policies. Diffusion Policy represents a visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process run with receding-horizon control . [Control](/classical/control) and state estimation track the resulting trajectories and locate the robot. ## The runtime handoff contract A deployable planner needs the robot model, current state, collision geometry, allowed contacts, attached objects, joint and timing limits and a controller that can execute the result, and a path checked against a stale scene is unsafe. Time-Optimal Trajectory Generation (TOTG) computes the time-optimal trajectory that exactly follows a differentiable joint-space path within velocity and acceleration bounds , and MoveIt 2 has recommended it for time parameterization since January 2023 . Because TOTG sets no jerk limits, Ruckig, a real-time jerk-limited generator , can smooth its output . The cuRoboV2 authors note that fast planners output physically unexecutable trajectories, and report 99.7% success under a 3 kg payload against 72 to 77% for baselines . The [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) maps these artifacts onto the runtime graph. In hybrid systems a learned component proposes a goal, cost, waypoint or action chunk, and a planner or command gate checks what the model cannot certify. Validators fail too: MoveIt Pro 10.1.0 fixed a shortcut stage that let paths pass through obstacles between collision checks, and a ValidateTrajectory bug that checked the wrong robot configuration and risked passing a colliding trajectory as collision-free .

Validators fail too: MoveIt Pro 10.1.0 fixed a shortcut stage that let paths pass through obstacles between collision checks, and a ValidateTrajectory bug that checked the wrong robot configuration and risked passing a colliding trajectory as collision-free .

Perception for manipulation turns camera and depth data into object poses in the robot's own frame, through calibration, depth sensing, detection, segmentation and pose estimation, and [grasp planning](/classical/grasp-planning) computes grasps against those poses. DOPE's pose network was accurate enough for a real robot to grasp known household objects in clutter . ## An illustrative positioning budget Try the transparent bottle under "Adjust more": the depth term then dominates the budget. The instrument combines authored hand-eye, depth and pose magnitudes by root-sum-of-squares, with depth fixed at a 0.5 m standoff and the hand-eye term growing with working distance up to 1.5 m. Its 15 mm and 30 mm bands are teaching thresholds: a 90 mm opening around a 60 mm part leaves $(90-60)/2=15$ mm per side, and one reported assembly task had only 0.5 mm contact clearance .
## Calibration: what a pixel means A camera maps a 3D point onto a 2D sensor, and its intrinsics describe that mapping: focal length in pixels on each axis, the principal point and lens distortion. Zhang's 2000 method shows the camera a planar target at several unmeasured orientations. It models radial distortion and gives a closed-form solution followed by maximum-likelihood nonlinear refinement. Zhang contrasts it with classical techniques that need expensive equipment such as two or three orthogonal planes . ### Hand-eye calibration: what a pixel means to the robot Extrinsics place the camera relative to something else. Hand-eye calibration finds the flange-to-camera transform for a wrist camera, or base-to-camera for a fixed one. Shiu and Ahmad cast it as $AX = XB$, where $A$ is a robot motion, $B$ the camera's observed motion of a static target and $X$ the unknown transform . Tsai and Lenz gave an efficient closed-form technique that solves rotation first, then translation . Park and Martin derived closed-form exact and least-squares solutions with Lie theory . OpenCV's hand-eye calibration defaults to the Tsai and Lenz method, needs at least two motions with non-parallel rotation axes, so three poses, and strongly recommends many more . Tsai and Lenz's error analysis shows the lever arm: a 3 mrad rotation error at a 5 in camera-to-target distance gives a 15 mil translation error . The instrument's hand-eye term is a ray-to-plane offset at separation $d$ for a ray inclined by $\theta$ to the plane's normal, about 1.7 mm at 10 cm and 17 mm at 1 m for one degree: $$ e_\theta(d) = d \, \tan \theta $$ ## Depth sensing: what fails, and on what Stereo triangulates features matched between two images, so a featureless surface gives it nothing to match. Intel's RGBD depth cameras add an active texture projector to make matching unambiguous . The March 2026 RealSense D400 datasheet lists ±2% Z-accuracy up to 2 m for D410/D415 and D43x over an 80% region of interest at HD resolution. Accuracy compares valid pixels with ground truth over 80% of the depth field of view, and factory KPIs reflect typical conditions; these models are tested on a texture-less white target at the default 150 mW laser power and auto exposure . RealSense's D415/D435 tuning guide says D400 depth error scales with the square of distance. It advises moving closer while staying outside the minimum operating distance, MinZ. It describes resolution and range trade-offs when changing MinZ, and notes that focus and differing left and right views limit very-near matching . Learned models now estimate depth from images, alone or with a sparse sensor: Depth Pro predicts metric monocular depth without camera intrinsics, a 2.25-megapixel map in 0.3 seconds on a standard GPU . FoundationStereo combines diverse synthetic stereo pairs with a pretrained monocular depth prior and cost-volume filtering to improve transfer to unseen stereo scenes . Prompt Depth Anything instead supplies sparse depth from low-cost LiDAR as a metric prompt to a depth foundation model . For industrial 3D scanning, the PhoXi 3D Scanner L page lists 0.200 mm calibration accuracy and 0.190 mm temporal noise (both 1 σ), an 870 to 2150 mm scanning range and 250 to 2750 ms scanning time. These are separate specification fields for one model . Time of flight casts its own modulated near-infrared light and measures its round trip per pixel. Multi-path interference lets one pixel integrate light that arrived by several routes. The Azure Kinect DK documentation lists five causes of invalid depth: outside the IR illumination mask, saturated IR signal, low IR signal, filter outlier and multi-path interference. Invalid pixels carry depth zero. Ambiguous depth arises when light reflects from one wall onto another in a corner, and where foreground and background mix at object edges. Fast motion can increase edge invalidation . Microsoft announced the end of Azure Kinect DK production in August 2023, and support for its Sensor SDK ended in August 2024 . ### The failure taxonomy that decides how a cell is built - ClearGrasp starts from the observation that transparent objects "often appear as noisy or distorted approximations of the surfaces that lie behind them". It infers surface normals, transparent-surface masks and occlusion boundaries, then replaces the returned depth . - Specular reflections can saturate D400 images, and the D400f column says "Saturation mitigated" . Azure Kinect invalidates saturated IR pixels . - Dark surfaces and low light weaken the signal. Azure Kinect invalidates a pixel whose IR signal is too weak to generate depth . RealSense ties D4xx depth quality to the input images and warns of grainy low-light images, underexposure and overexposure. For its projected-pattern example, reducing background light with the projector on can raise the pattern's signal-to-noise ratio . - RealSense names fences and wire grids as scenes where left-right correspondence can become ambiguous. Its D4 processor compares the best and second-best match scores, and raising DSSecondPeakThreshold rejects more matches as zero depth . - Azure Kinect notes that a surface invalidated by multi-path from one camera view can reappear from another . The 2% figure is measured on a texture-less white target with the projector at default power , and the PhoXi page publishes no target condition for its 0.200 mm figure . Accuracy for transparent or specular surfaces is not disclosed in either datasheet. Depth yields a point cloud, an unordered set that a network must process without depending on input order. PointNet uses a shared per-point encoder and a symmetric pooling function . PointNet++ applies PointNet within radius neighbourhoods around sampled centroids, in coordinates relative to each centroid, building local features at growing scales. Density-adaptive variants combine scales where small neighbourhoods hold too few samples . ## Detection: from pixels to candidate objects Classical detectors return boxes over a class list fixed at training time. Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN with a branch that predicts an object mask in parallel with box recognition . OWLv2 scales open-vocabulary detection through self-training: an existing detector supplies pseudo-boxes for web image-text pairs, expanding training beyond human box annotations . Open-vocabulary detection removes the fixed list. Grounding DINO adds language-vision fusion to the DINO detector's feature enhancer, query selection and decoder and accepts category names or referring expressions. It performs weakly on referring expressions without REC training data. Its Swin-L model reports 52.5 AP on COCO 2017 validation after pretraining on O365, OpenImage and GoldG without COCO training images . Grounding DINO 1.5 separates a larger Pro model from an Edge variant designed for speed, reducing feature scales in the latter . DINOv2 learns image and patch features by self-supervised pretraining on the curated LVD-142M dataset. Its transfer evaluations freeze the encoder and train linear heads for classification and segmentation, and linear or DPT heads for depth . DINOv3 adds Gram anchoring to preserve the quality of dense features during long self-supervised training . ## Segmentation: the grounding layer A box around a mug also contains the table behind it, so a grasp planner needs the surface region that per-pixel labelling provides. Segment Anything (SAM, 2023) makes segmentation promptable; its default ViT-H model was trained on SA-1B, reported as 1.1 billion automatically generated masks on 11 million images. Point, box and mask prompts condition the decoder, and an ambiguous point can return several candidate masks for a part or a whole object. Fine structures and boundaries remain failure cases, and the heavy image encoder prevents overall real-time performance . SAM 2 extends prompting to video with a streaming memory of earlier predictions and prompted frames. Objects are inferred independently, and failures persist after shot changes or long occlusions, in crowded scenes and on thin, fast-moving details . SAM 3 accepts concept prompts such as a noun phrase or an example image and combines a detector with a memory-based tracker to segment matching instances . Grounded SAM feeds Grounding DINO's open-set boxes to SAM , and CNOS segments unseen objects by matching DINOv2 descriptors of SAM proposals against references built from CAD models . Promptable segmentation supplies object masks to MOKA and ReKep, two [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) with different perception stacks. MOKA proposes marked candidate points from GroundedSAM masks, then prompts a pretrained VLM to select grasp, function and target keypoints, waypoint regions and motion attributes. Calibrated depth lifts the points into the robot frame, and a separate grasp sampler and motion pipeline produce actions; the prompted method trains no robot policy . ReKep proposes semantic keypoints from DINOv2 features within SAM masks and calibrated RGB-D geometry. A large vision-language model writes Python sub-goal and path constraints from a marked image and an instruction, and a solver repeatedly plans end-effector motion from tracked keypoints. The solver penalizes constraint violations without guaranteeing physical feasibility, and rigidity assumptions and tracking failures remain limitations. Some evaluations use human annotations or disable tracking . RoboPoint instruction-tunes a VLM to predict image-space affordance points from synthetic object and free-space data mixed with real-image VQA and LVIS detection data. It needs no external detector at test time, though its robot pipeline adds depth, an end-effector offset and a motion planner . Dense Object Nets learns a descriptor for each RGB pixel, self-supervised by matches from static RGB-D reconstructions, and demonstrates correspondence across viewpoints and moderately deformable configurations. Class-consistent training generalizes across sufficiently similar hats, shoes and mugs, while instance-specific training distinguishes objects; for grasping, the gripper's 6-DoF orientation needs further information . ## 6-DoF pose estimation, and how to read a claim about it Pose estimation turns a mask into a rigid body with a position and orientation, and methods divide by what they assume about the object. Instance-level methods train on specific objects: PoseCNN localizes each object's centre, predicts its distance and regresses a rotation quaternion, with a loss that handles symmetric objects . DOPE, trained only on synthetic domain-randomized and photorealistic data, performs competitively with a network trained on real and synthetic data . Category-level methods such as NOCS estimate the pose and size of unseen instances in known categories with no exact CAD model at training or test time . Novel-object methods drop per-object training. SAM-6D first proposes instance masks with SAM, then estimates pose through partial-to-partial point matching against an object model . MegaPose uses render-and-compare against a CAD model supplied at test time , and FoundationPose works from a CAD model or a few reference images and reports results comparable to instance-level methods . Any6D uses one RGB-D anchor view to estimate an unfamiliar object's pose and size through render-and-compare refinement, without requiring its CAD model . SAM 3D goes further and infers object geometry, texture and layout from a single image; those generated surfaces include geometry that the camera did not observe . To read a pose result, check its evaluation protocol. The BOP Challenge 2020 evaluated 6D pose methods on RGB-D data and supplied physically based synthetic training images, making the training-data allowance part of the comparison . Hinterstoisser and colleagues evaluate a model $\mathcal M$ with ground-truth pose $(R,T)$ and estimate $(\tilde R,\tilde T)$ by averaging distances between corresponding transformed model points : $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx+T)-(\tilde R x+\tilde T) \rVert $$ An estimate is correct when $m \leq k_m d$, where $d$ is the model's diameter and $k_m$ a chosen coefficient; their LINEMOD evaluation uses $k_m=0.1$ . For the symmetry-aware pose error, each ground-truth-transformed point is matched to its nearest estimated-pose point before averaging : $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x_1 \in \mathcal M} \min_{x_2 \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx_1+T)-(\tilde R x_2+\tilde T) \rVert $$ They apply this rule to objects that are ambiguous, or look ambiguous from some views, naming "cup", "bowl", "box" and "glue" . CosyPose handles symmetries while matching object-pose hypotheses across images and jointly refining camera and object poses through object-level bundle adjustment . The BOP Challenge 2023 report scores 6-DoF localization differently: each dataset score averages the VSD, MSSD and MSPD recalls, each over several thresholds with a strict test $e < \theta_e$, and $AR_C$ averages seven core datasets (LM-O, T-LESS, ITODD, HB, YCB-V, TUD-L, IC-BIN) on a 0 to 100 scale. Seen and unseen tracks share the method, with object identities and instance counts supplied at test time, and the 2D-detection $AP_C$ averages over objects first . From 2017 to 2023, seen-object accuracy rose from 56.9 to 85.6 $AR_C$, a relative gain of over 50 percent. The endpoints are Vidal's point-pair-feature method with ICP and no training images, and GPose2023 with object-specific networks trained on PBR and real images . For unseen objects, GenFlow-MultiHypo16 led 2023's Task 4 with 67.4 $AR_C$, against 69.8 for the best 2020 seen-object entry, CosyPose, and the report calls these comparable across distinct tracks; average image times were 34.58 and 13.74 seconds on unmatched hardware. Task 4 still supplies mesh models for onboarding, capped at 5 minutes per object on one GPU with no real images of the objects, and GenFlow fails under heavy occlusion . In the BOP 2024 report, the best unseen-object method, FreeZeV2.1, is 22% more accurate on BOP-Classic-Core than GenFlow and 4% behind GPose2023, but takes 24.9 against 2.7 seconds per image, and the report names 2D detection as the main bottleneck for unseen objects . ## Visual servoing: image-based and position-based control Visual servoing uses vision inside the control loop, and Hutchinson, Hager and Corke's 1996 tutorial divides such systems into position-based and image-based classes . Espiau, Chaumette and Rives's 1992 paper applies a task-function framework to image-based control, with a task function designed for regulation that need not be the raw feature difference. Its interaction matrix relates feature rates to the camera's translational and rotational velocity in the camera frame. Convergence depends on task and model conditions, and neglecting target motion can leave a tracking error . For a fixed goal and motionless target, Chaumette and Hutchinson's Part I writes $\dot{s} = L_s v_c$, with $v_c$ the camera's six-component spatial velocity. Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) uses image features, and position-based visual servoing (PBVS) uses estimated pose. The IBVS point-feature interaction matrix still uses depth and camera intrinsics, estimated from current depths or depths at the desired pose . Redundant-feature IBVS is locally asymptotically stable when the interaction matrices have full rank and the estimated pseudoinverse times the true matrix meets a positivity condition; coarse estimates can change the camera path, while poor ones can make the system unstable. Large displacements can meet local minima or singularities, PBVS points can leave the field of view, and in PBVS pose-estimation errors affect final accuracy . Part II (2007) adds switching and planning methods that address visibility, occlusions and joint limits, for eye-in-hand and eye-to-hand systems . Bateux and colleagues fine-tuned a CNN to estimate the relative pose between current and desired images and kept a pose-based control law . Learned servoing can also aim the camera. EyeRobot 2.0, from Ken Goldberg (UC Berkeley) and colleagues (October 2026), swivels the two eye viewpoints of a single stereo camera to fixate a 3D point, with a gaze-servoing policy and a fixation selector both trained with RL on real data. It beat passive stereo by 40% in real trials and, when a grasped object hid the wrist views, more than doubled the success of policies that had them, 48% against 22% . ## Separate model error from geometric error Hand-eye accuracy depends on noise and motion range, so Enebuse and colleagues advise accounting for both when benchmarking or calibrating . A detector can keep stable image coordinates while the robot misses because the camera transform drifted, so each stage is checked in its own output first. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) defines the checks to rerun after a camera remount, and the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) shows where images, transforms and timestamps meet at runtime. ## What the end-to-end models replaced End-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) policies absorb the explicit pipeline into weights. Gemini Robotics is a VLA model that controls robots directly, built on an embodied-reasoning model that can detect objects, point, and predict trajectories, grasps and 3D bounding boxes . Such a policy needs no detector class or CAD model for a new object, and it has no hand-eye residual to re-solve when it misses a grasp by 8 mm. Some frontier systems keep geometric intermediates explicit, as the [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) did while a learned model produced the geometry: MolmoAct encodes observations into depth-aware perception tokens and generates editable trajectory traces before predicting low-level actions .

SAM 3 accepts concept prompts such as a noun phrase or an example image and combines a detector with a memory-based tracker to segment matching instances . Grounded SAM feeds Grounding DINO's open-set boxes to SAM , and CNOS segments unseen objects by matching DINOv2 descriptors of SAM proposals against references built from CAD models . ReKep proposes semantic keypoints from DINOv2 features within SAM masks and calibrated RGB-D geometry. A large vision-language model writes Python sub-goal and path constraints from a marked image and an instruction, and a solver repeatedly plans end-effector motion from tracked keypoints. The solver penalizes constraint violations without guaranteeing physical feasibility, and rigidity assumptions and tracking failures remain limitations. Some evaluations use human annotations or disable tracking . It needs no external detector at test time, though its robot pipeline adds depth, an end-effector offset and a motion planner . Class-consistent training generalizes across sufficiently similar hats, shoes and mugs, while instance-specific training distinguishes objects; for grasping, the gripper's 6-DoF orientation needs further information . ## 6-DoF pose estimation, and how to read a claim about it Pose estimation turns a mask into a rigid body with a position and orientation, and methods divide by what they assume about the object. Instance-level methods train on specific objects: PoseCNN localizes each object's centre, predicts its distance and regresses a rotation quaternion, with a loss that handles symmetric objects . DOPE, trained only on synthetic domain-randomized and photorealistic data, performs competitively with a network trained on real and synthetic data . Category-level methods such as NOCS estimate the pose and size of unseen instances in known categories with no exact CAD model at training or test time . Novel-object methods drop per-object training. SAM-6D first proposes instance masks with SAM, then estimates pose through partial-to-partial point matching against an object model . MegaPose uses render-and-compare against a CAD model supplied at test time , and FoundationPose works from a CAD model or a few reference images and reports results comparable to instance-level methods . Any6D uses one RGB-D anchor view to estimate an unfamiliar object's pose and size through render-and-compare refinement, without requiring its CAD model . SAM 3D goes further and infers object geometry, texture and layout from a single image; those generated surfaces include geometry that the camera did not observe . To read a pose result, check its evaluation protocol. Hinterstoisser and colleagues evaluate a model $\mathcal M$ with ground-truth pose $(R,T)$ and estimate $(\tilde R,\tilde T)$ by averaging distances between corresponding transformed model points : $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx+T)-(\tilde R x+\tilde T) \rVert $$ An estimate is correct when $m \leq k_m d$, where $d$ is the model's diameter and $k_m$ a chosen coefficient; their LINEMOD evaluation uses $k_m=0.1$ . For the symmetry-aware pose error, each ground-truth-transformed point is matched to its nearest estimated-pose point before averaging : $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x_1 \in \mathcal M} \min_{x_2 \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx_1+T)-(\tilde R x_2+\tilde T) \rVert $$ They apply this rule to objects that are ambiguous, or look ambiguous from some views, naming "cup", "bowl", "box" and "glue" . CosyPose handles symmetries while matching object-pose hypotheses across images and jointly refining camera and object poses through object-level bundle adjustment . The BOP Challenge 2020 evaluated 6D pose methods on RGB-D data and supplied physically based synthetic training images, making the training-data allowance part of the comparison . The BOP Challenge 2023 report scores 6-DoF localization differently: each dataset score averages the VSD, MSSD and MSPD recalls, each over several thresholds with a strict test $e < \theta_e$, and $AR_C$ averages seven core datasets (LM-O, T-LESS, ITODD, HB, YCB-V, TUD-L, IC-BIN) on a 0 to 100 scale. Seen and unseen tracks share the method, with object identities and instance counts supplied at test time, and the 2D-detection $AP_C$ averages over objects first . From 2017 to 2023, seen-object accuracy rose from 56.9 to 85.6 $AR_C$, a relative gain of over 50 percent. The endpoints are Vidal's point-pair-feature method with ICP and no training images, and GPose2023 with object-specific networks trained on PBR and real images . For unseen objects, GenFlow-MultiHypo16 led 2023's Task 4 with 67.4 $AR_C$, against 69.8 for the best 2020 seen-object entry, CosyPose, and the report calls these comparable across distinct tracks; average image times were 34.58 and 13.74 seconds on unmatched hardware. Task 4 still supplies mesh models for onboarding, capped at 5 minutes per object on one GPU with no real images of the objects, and GenFlow fails under heavy occlusion . Espiau, Chaumette and Rives's 1992 paper applies a task-function framework to image-based control, with a task function designed for regulation that need not be the raw feature difference. Its interaction matrix relates feature rates to the camera's translational and rotational velocity in the camera frame. Convergence depends on task and model conditions, and neglecting target motion can leave a tracking error . For a fixed goal and motionless target, Chaumette and Hutchinson's Part I writes $\dot{s} = L_s v_c$, with $v_c$ the camera's six-component spatial velocity. Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) uses image features, and position-based visual servoing (PBVS) uses estimated pose. The IBVS point-feature interaction matrix still uses depth and camera intrinsics, estimated from current depths or depths at the desired pose . Redundant-feature IBVS is locally asymptotically stable when the interaction matrices have full rank and the estimated pseudoinverse times the true matrix meets a positivity condition; coarse estimates can change the camera path, while poor ones can make the system unstable. Large displacements can meet local minima or singularities, PBVS points can leave the field of view, and in PBVS pose-estimation errors affect final accuracy . Part II (2007) adds switching and planning methods that address visibility, occlusions and joint limits, for eye-in-hand and eye-to-hand systems . Gemini Robotics is a VLA model that controls robots directly, built on an embodied-reasoning model that can detect objects, point, and predict trajectories, grasps and 3D bounding boxes . ROS 2 is the second generation of the Robot Operating System, a modular framework of freely available robot software, rebuilt because ROS 1 lacked production-grade features <Cite id="ros2-science-robotics-2022" />. Lyrical Luth, the current long-term-support release, shipped on 22 May 2026 and is supported until May 2031 <Cite id="ros2-lyrical-2026" /> <Cite id="ros2-distributions-2026" />.

<Image id="pr2-maker-faire-2011" />

<SelfCheck
  prompt="A fetch task takes 30 seconds, reports progress and may need cancelling. Which ROS 2 interface fits?"
  options={[
    {
      value: 'topic',
      label: 'Publish the request repeatedly on a topic',
      why: 'Topics fit continuous streams. This task needs acceptance, feedback, completion and cancellation semantics.'
    },
    {
      value: 'service',
      label: 'Block on a service call until it finishes',
      why: 'Services are intended for short request-response operations. A long task needs feedback and preemption without holding a synchronous request open.'
    },
    {
      value: 'action',
      label: 'Use a ROS action: goal, feedback, result and cancellation',
      why: 'Actions model long-running, preemptible work. The client can observe progress and cancel while the server owns execution.'
    }
  ]}
  answer="action"
  takeaway="Topics stream, services answer short requests, and actions manage long-running goals with feedback and cancellation."
/>

## The graph: nodes and typed interfaces

A node is one participant, such as a camera driver, policy server or controller bridge. Nodes talk through topics for continuous streams, services for short request-response calls, and actions for long-running goals with feedback, cancellation and a result <Cite id="ros2-interfaces-2026" />. A `geometry_msgs/PoseStamped` carries the timestamp and frame a bare array lacks, and REP 103 puts ROS on SI units <Cite id="rep-103-2010" />.

<Ros2Interfaces className="my-6" />

## QoS is part of the model input

ROS 2 inherits Quality of Service (QoS) from DDS <Cite id="ros2-dds-design-2014" />. The default profile keeps the last 10 messages and delivers reliably, while the sensor-data profile uses best effort and a smaller queue, because timely readings matter more than complete ones; lifespan silently drops messages older than its limit, and endpoints with incompatible policies never connect <Cite id="ros2-qos-2026" />.

End-to-end latency depends strongly on the DDS implementation, and ROS 2 can add 50% over raw DDS <Cite id="ros2-latency-2021" />. Since Kilted Kaiju (May 2025), Zenoh's `rmw_zenoh_cpp` is a Tier 1 middleware <Cite id="ros2-kilted-2025" />.

<QosQueueAge className="my-6" />

## Time and synchronization

Camera, depth, joint and force streams arrive at different rates, so inputs need acquisition and arrival timestamps. MCAP records a publish time and a log time for every message <Cite id="mcap-spec-2026" />.

Logging source, receipt and inference-completion times splits latency into sensing, transport, model execution and command delivery; ros2_tracing does it at an average overhead of 0.0033 ms per message <Cite id="ros2-tracing-2022" />. With `use_sim_time` set, ROS time follows the latest `/clock` message <Cite id="ros2-clock-design" />, so nodes that mix it with wall time see spurious timeouts. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers spatial and temporal alignment.

## tf2: the coordinate-frame graph

tf2 keeps a time-buffered tree of coordinate frames and transforms data between any two frames at any time <Cite id="tf2-docs-2026" />. A lookup at an image timestamp can wait for the transform; the tf2 tutorial raises an exception only if it is still missing after a 50 ms timeout <Cite id="tf2-time-tutorial-2026" />. Foote's original tf library makes this a distributed bookkeeping problem, tracking frame relationships through both space and time across a robot system <Cite id="tf-library-2013" />.

REP 105 defines `odom` as a drifting short-term reference and `map` as a frame whose poses can jump <Cite id="rep-105-2010" />, and camera optical frames take an `_optical` suffix and a different axis convention <Cite id="rep-103-2010" />. A policy trained on base-frame <Term id="end-effector">end-effector</Term> deltas cannot be sent tool-frame deltas in the same layout; *Modern Robotics* covers the geometry <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />.

## URDF, robot state and MoveIt

URDF, the most common robot-description format <Cite id="urdf-dataset-2023" />, lists links, joints, geometry and limits, and `robot_state_publisher` combines it with joint states to publish the frame tree. MoveIt 2's Planning Scene combines robot state, model and world geometry for kinematics, constraint and collision checks <Cite id="moveit-planning-scene-2026" />, so a learned policy can use it to plan or check collision-free motion.

## rosbag2 is the experiment record

rosbag2 records timestamped messages for replay, in MCAP by default since Iron Irwini <Cite id="ros2-iron-mcap-2023" />, and since Kilted it can replay in publication order instead of receipt order <Cite id="ros2-kilted-2025" />. Learning pipelines convert bags to episode formats such as RLDS <Cite id="rlds-2021" />.

## A production policy layout

A learned-policy graph can separate drivers, state assembly, a policy server, a command gate, a controller bridge and a supervisor. The supervisor can drive ROS 2 managed nodes, which leave a primary state only on an external request or an error <Cite id="ros2-lifecycle-design-2015" />. Inference stays outside the hard real-time loop unless its worst case fits, and ROS 2's real-time guidance keeps page faults, dynamic allocation and blocking synchronization out of that path <Cite id="ros2-realtime-docs-2026" />. Lyrical's EventsCBGExecutor cuts executor CPU overhead, but its event queue is unbounded <Cite id="ros2-executors-2026" />.

ROS-LLM connects language-model outputs to ROS actions and services, with feedback used to revise behavior sequences, trees or state machines <Cite id="ros-llm-2024" />.

<Ros2PolicyLayout className="my-6" />

Lyrical's `rosidl::Buffer` lets a `uint8[]` field live in GPU memory without changing the .msg file <Cite id="ros2-buffer-backends-2026" />. NVIDIA deprecated its NITROS transport on 21 September 2026 in its favor, with a CUDA backend <Cite id="isaac-ros-nitros-2026" />, because host round-trips add latency and use CPU and memory bandwidth <Cite id="isaac-ros-rosidl-buffer-2026" />.

## Navigation uses the same architecture

Nav2 uses a behavior tree to orchestrate planner, controller and recovery servers <Cite id="nav2-2020" />. Costmap 2D accepts sensor-processing plugins for AI outputs and semantic information <Cite id="nav2-costmap-2d-2026" />, so a learned local controller can reuse a classical one's costmap, goal interface, test harness and fallback. The [scene-representation module](/classical/scene-representation) explains the map choices. The Smac Planner implements cost-aware A*, Hybrid A* and state-lattice planning, allowing a navigation stack to select a search that respects the robot's motion constraints <Cite id="smac-planner-2024" />.

<Image id="clearpath-jackal-ugv-2020" />

## Common integration failures

Frequent failures include a policy deployed in a different frame from its training data, a queue that hides latency, two unarbitrated command publishers, bags without transforms, wall-time assumptions under `/clock`, and one node holding drivers, inference and hardware commands. DDS implementations interoperate only in limited circumstances, so a system should use one ROS version and one RMW implementation <Cite id="ros2-middleware-vendors-2026" />. Nodes are not guaranteed to communicate across distributions; Jazzy is supported until May 2029 and Humble until May 2027 <Cite id="ros2-distributions-2026" />. ROS 1 ended when Noetic reached end of life in May 2025 <Cite id="noetic-eol-2025" />.

Scene representation is how a robot stores what it knows about its surroundings so that planners, controllers and other consumers can query it <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Representations range from point clouds and occupancy grids to signed-distance fields, meshes and neural fields such as radiance fields and Gaussian splats <Cite id="cadena-2016" /><Cite id="neural-fields-survey-2024" />.

<Image id="ouster-lidar-point-cloud-sf" />

## The ladder, and what each rung can answer

Three queries separate the rungs: whether a cell is free for a planner, which way a surface faces for a contact solver, and what the scene looks like from a viewpoint the sensor never occupied. Cadena and colleagues judge representations by storage size, construction cost and usefulness for the task <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

<SceneRepresentationLadder className="my-6" />

### Point clouds and occupancy grids

A <Term id="point-cloud">point cloud</Term> is an unordered set of 3D points, and PointNet requires invariance to the order in which they arrive <Cite id="pointnet-2017" />. A region without points is either empty or unobserved, and the store cannot say which. CUT3R maintains a recurrent state while processing an image sequence and predicts metric pointmaps in a shared frame, including inferred views that were not directly observed <Cite id="cut3r-2025" />.

Moravec and Elfes projected wide-angle sonar readings from different sensors and robot positions onto a 2D <Term id="occupancy-grid">occupancy grid</Term>. Each reading marked a probably empty beam interior and an uncertain reflecting point near the measured range, and overlapping readings refined these constraints. Zero represented unknown occupancy, and negative and positive values probably empty and probably occupied cells <Cite id="moravec-elfes-1985" />. OctoMap carries the three states into 3D in a compressed octree <Cite id="octomap-2013" />. Step through the figure below to see one mug stored four ways.

<ExplainerFigure id="mug" />

### Signed-distance fields

Curless and Levoy fuse range images into a cumulative weighted <Term id="signed-distance-field">signed distance function</Term> and recover the surface at its zero crossing, truncating distance ramps and weights near observed points. Their hole-filling construction marks empty space with negative $D_{min}$ and unseen space with positive $D_{max}$, both at zero weight <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />. KinectFusion uses the opposite sign: positive toward visible free space and negative on the non-visible side <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />.

KinectFusion fused 11-bit, 640×480 Kinect depth frames at 30 Hz, tracking each frame against the global model by coarse-to-fine ICP and mapping at the sensor rate on a commodity GPU. A large plane filling most of the view can cause drift or tracking failure. Its projective TSDF caps visible-space values at the truncation distance $\mu$, leaves non-visible points beyond $\mu$ unmeasured and is exact at the surface, so fusion yields an approximate pseudo-Euclidean distance. Voxel hashing stores dense surface data only near observed regions and streams blocks through a spatial hash table, avoiding a fixed dense volume over the entire scene <Cite id="voxel-hashing-2013" />. Normals come from numerical derivatives near the zero level set, and ray marching finds surfaces by trilinear interpolation <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />.

<Image id="kinect-xbox-360-sensor" />

Trajectory optimizers need obstacle distances. Voxblox builds TSDFs faster than OctoMap builds its maps, then derives Euclidean signed distance fields (ESDFs) from them incrementally, more accurately than from occupancy <Cite id="voxblox-2016" />, and on GPUs nvblox reports up to 177x faster surface reconstruction and 31x faster distance-field computation <Cite id="nvblox-2023" />.

### Meshes, and then neural fields

A mesh adds connectivity, giving each face a normal and a renderable surface, but leaves holes where nothing was observed, and filling them invents geometry <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />.

NeRF fits a <Term id="neural-radiance-field">neural radiance field</Term> to a static scene from posed RGB photographs, intrinsics and scene bounds. Its MLP predicts density from position and colour from position and viewing direction, and differentiable volume rendering lets image error drive optimization <Cite id="nerf-2020" />. NeRF++ analyzes shape-radiance ambiguity and adapts the parameterization for 360-degree captures of unbounded scenes <Cite id="nerfpp-2020" />.

Instant NGP cut optimization cost with a multiresolution hash encoding, smaller networks and fully fused CUDA kernels, and rendered one scene at 1080p in 5 seconds over 128 samples and a large 360-degree scene at 10 frames per second on one RTX 3090 <Cite id="instant-ngp-2022" />. <Term id="gaussian-splatting">3D Gaussian splatting</Term> optimizes Gaussian positions, anisotropic covariances, opacities and spherical-harmonic appearance from calibrated photographs, then rasterizes by alpha-blending sorted splats. It reports real-time 1080p rendering, with results on an A6000 GPU <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />.

DUSt3R predicts dense pointmaps from a pair of RGB images without intrinsics or poses, in the first image's frame and at unknown scale, trained with geometric supervision from pretrained CroCo weights. For an image collection, it then optimizes the alignment of pairwise pointmaps in 3D <Cite id="dust3r-2024" />.

MASt3R adds matching descriptors to this 3D reconstruction approach and uses a fast reciprocal-matching procedure to obtain image correspondences <Cite id="mast3r-2024" />.

Feed-forward models now cover whole collections: VGGT infers cameras, point maps, depth maps and point tracks from one, a few or hundreds of views in under one second <Cite id="vggt-2025" />.

MapAnything accepts optional intrinsics, poses or depth alongside images and predicts metric geometry through separate depth, ray, camera and scale factors <Cite id="mapanything-2025" />. Pi3 avoids privileging one input view: its reconstruction is permutation-equivariant, with affine-invariant camera poses and scale-invariant local pointmaps <Cite id="pi3-2025" />.

Depth Anything 3 uses a depth-and-ray prediction target for arbitrary view collections, whether or not camera poses are supplied <Cite id="depth-anything-3-2025" />.

## A radiance field is geometry for rendering

The [world-models taxonomy](/world-models/taxonomy) treats a splat reconstruction as a learned renderer: appearance is learned and physics is not. In the original 3DGS, learned opacity is an image-space alpha-compositing weight with no free, occupied or unknown label, and the stored primitive is a volumetric Gaussian <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />. The paper names mesh reconstruction as an open direction <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />, and SuGaR then aligned Gaussians with surfaces and extracted meshes by Poisson reconstruction <Cite id="sugar-2023" />. 2D Gaussian Splatting instead uses oriented planar disks, ray-splat intersections and depth-distortion and normal regularizers to improve surface reconstruction <Cite id="2dgs-2024" />.

Simulators pair splats for appearance with separate physics: SplatSim renders with splats while PyBullet supplies physics <Cite id="splatsim-2024" />. Its authors report zero-shot real-world transfer of diffusion policies on four rigid-body tasks with a UR5 and Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, after manual robot segmentation and ICP alignment <Cite id="splatsim-2024" />. In RoboGSim's closed-loop evaluator, a policy acts on splat-rendered images while Isaac Sim handles inverse kinematics and physical interaction, from multi-view images, supplied MDH parameters and mesh assets <Cite id="robogsim-2024" />.

Other fields serve a planner directly. Dex-NeRF renders transparency-aware depth from learned density for a grasp planner, where a RealSense camera failed to compute depth for most transparent objects tested <Cite id="dex-nerf-2021" />. F3RM distills 2D foundation-model features into a 3D feature field so that language and a few demonstrations can guide grasping and placing <Cite id="f3rm-2023" />.

ParticleSplat, from Deepak Pathak (Carnegie Mellon) and colleagues (September 2026), encodes posed multi-view images into latent particles that decode to 3D Gaussians, trained with a novel-view synthesis objective. Object masks emerge without labels, moving a particle moves its object, and the representation improved downstream manipulation <Cite id="particlesplat-2026" />.

## SLAM: the system that builds the map

Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) builds such maps from sensor data while the robot moves without knowing its exact pose. Cadena and colleagues separate a sensor-dependent front end, which abstracts measurements and associates them with state variables, from a back end that performs inference and feeds information back for loop-closure detection and validation <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. [State estimation](/classical/state-estimation) covers the inference machinery.

<Image id="velodyne-hdl64-lidar-2009" />

Front ends are feature-based or direct. Monocular ORB-SLAM (2015) uses ORB features for tracking, local mapping, relocalization and loop closing, triangulating matched features and running local bundle adjustment. Its DBoW2 vocabulary proposes relocalization and loop candidates that need geometric validation <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />.

DBoW2 builds a vocabulary tree from binary features, combining image retrieval with geometric checks to reject visually similar but inconsistent places <Cite id="dbow2-2012" />.

ORB-SLAM3 supports stereo, RGB-D and visual-inertial modes with pinhole or fisheye cameras and MAP-based IMU initialization. It starts a new map after persistent tracking loss and merges maps only after geometric and covisibility checks, plus gravity-direction checks for mature visual-inertial maps. Low texture remains the main failure case, and slow motion can delay inertial initialization <Cite id="orb-slam3-2021" />.

Direct Sparse Odometry skips the detector and optimizes photometric error over sampled pixels jointly with geometry <Cite id="dso-2018" />. It can sample any region with intensity gradient, including near-featureless walls, and gains from calibrating exposure, vignetting and camera response <Cite id="dso-2018" />.

Learned systems keep classical machinery: DROID-SLAM iterates camera pose and per-pixel depth through a dense bundle-adjustment layer <Cite id="droid-slam-2021" />.

MASt3R-SLAM builds tracking, local fusion, loop closure and global optimization around a learned two-view reconstruction prior <Cite id="mast3r-slam-2024" />. SLAM3R predicts pointmaps for overlapping video windows and aligns them into a global reconstruction without explicitly solving camera parameters <Cite id="slam3r-2024" />.

VGGT-SLAM instead aligns submaps with projective transforms, accounting for the reconstruction ambiguity that remains when monocular cameras are uncalibrated <Cite id="vggt-slam-2025" />.

Revisiting mapped landmarks can reduce odometric drift and in some cases correct it, and visual-inertial methods drift less than wheel odometry <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Monocular ORB-SLAM validates a <Term id="loop-closure">loop closure</Term> geometrically, then spreads its error with similarity alignment and Essential Graph optimization <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />.

<LoopClosure className="my-6" />

<Term id="place-recognition">Place recognition</Term> asks whether the current image matches a stored place, and motion information can also inform that belief. Viewpoint, illumination and seasonal changes alter one place's appearance, and different places can look alike, which is perceptual aliasing <Cite id="lowry-2016-place-recognition" />. AnyLoc builds place descriptors by aggregating frozen self-supervised features, without training a network specifically for visual place recognition <Cite id="anyloc-2023" />.

Perceptual aliasing can create false-positive associations that corrupt back-end estimates, while false negatives discard useful measurements. Robust losses and loop-closure validation mitigate outliers, though failures remain that depend on initialization <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Graduated non-convexity offers another route: it gradually sharpens a robust objective while using non-minimal solvers, avoiding a required initial guess in the tested estimation problems <Cite id="gnc-2019" />.

In the back end, Square Root SAM estimates the trajectory and landmark map jointly by MAP inference, which under Gaussian models with known data associations is sparse nonlinear least squares. It solves successive linearized systems by QR or Cholesky, and variable ordering controls fill-in <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. iSAM2 adds incremental reordering and relinearization on a Bayes tree. Thresholded updates trade some accuracy for speed, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve <Cite id="kaess-2012" />.

Smoothing suits loop closure because relinearizing the past requires the past to stay in the graph. Cadena and colleagues contrast sparse landmark maps with dense models suited to obstacle avoidance, and cite octrees and voxel hashing as efficient volumetric storage. Two rooms can look identical to a 2D laser yet differ to a camera. Severe illumination changes defeat bag-of-words methods, and active range cameras work in dark, untextured scenes but face range and external-light limits <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

The iMAP system learns a scene-specific MLP from scratch at room scale from a handheld RGB-D stream. It tracks at 10 Hz and maps at 2 Hz on a desktop CPU and GPU, retaining keyframes for replay <Cite id="imap-2021" />. NICE-SLAM uses hierarchical feature grids with pretrained geometry decoders, reconstructs a multi-room apartment and performs no loop closure <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />. Its 47 ms tracking and 130 ms mapping times use small pixel samples on an RTX 3090 <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />.

SplaTAM maps with 3D Gaussians from an RGB-D camera and uses a silhouette mask to determine whether areas were previously mapped <Cite id="splatam-2023" />.

Gaussian Splatting SLAM uses Gaussians for tracking as well as mapping, optimizing the camera directly against them and adding geometric checks for incremental monocular reconstruction <Cite id="monogs-2023" />.

AMB3R-SLAM separates a lightweight tracking front end from a hierarchical back end that enforces local, intermediate and global consistency over long trajectories <Cite id="amb3r-slam-2026" />.

## The deployed answer: costmaps and two planners

A navigation stack plans over a <Term id="costmap">costmap</Term>: occupancy from the map and live sensors, inflated by the robot's footprint. Lu, Hershberger and Smart's layered costmaps keep an ordered list of semantically separate layers and accumulate them into a master 2D costmap. Each update gathers the layers' bounds, then lets each layer write the master grid within them, and a configuration setting decides whether sensed obstacles overwrite static-map costs <Cite id="layered-costmaps-2014" />.

Navigation2, built on ROS 2, uses a layered costmap. Cartographer supplies a 2D LiDAR mapping example: branch-and-bound scan-to-submap matching produces loop-closure constraints during mapping <Cite id="cartographer-2016" />. Its global planner computes a shortest route to the goal, and a separate controller computes a local path and control signals, each a plugin in an asynchronous server <Cite id="nav2-2020" />.

The layered costmap's `track_unknown_space` option defaults to false, which treats unknown space as free; keeping the unknown state requires enabling it <Cite id="nav2-costmap-2d-2026" />. The planning algorithms are those of [motion planning](/classical/motion-planning) on a 2D grid.

## A representation is a service contract

[Perception](/classical/perception) locates objects in the current frame <Cite id="conceptgraphs-2023" />. Consumers issue different queries: localization needs stable landmarks <Cite id="cadena-2016" />, collision checking needs occupied volume and a conservative update rule <Cite id="octomap-2013" />, grasping needs surface pose and identity, and rendering needs appearance <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

Hydra stacks rungs in one real-time system, building a local ESDF, extracting a topological map of places from it and segmenting places into rooms <Cite id="hydra-2022" />.

ConceptFusion fuses pixel-aligned foundation-model features into a 3D map that can be queried through text, images, audio or geometry, without additional training <Cite id="conceptfusion-2023" />.

SceneLM, from Jitendra Malik (UC Berkeley), Marco Pavone and colleagues (September 2026), keeps the whole map as a structured text list of objects that one vision-language model edits after each image. On language-grounded retrieval and localization benchmarks it performed competitively with complete mapping pipelines, with a map 6 to 12 times more compact, and it ran online on an edge device aboard a quadruped <Cite id="scenelm-2026" />.

Ledger, from Shravan Chaudhari, Homanga Bharadhwaj and colleagues at Johns Hopkins (October 2026), keeps a persistent 3D object memory from a person's egocentric video: each object's resting locations, its moves and a short description, retained after it leaves view. A language model answering from these records as text, without the images, raised GPT-5.4's HD-EPIC accuracy from 29.7% to 42.6%, and on Ego4D the memory located objects with a median error of 0.99 m where it returned a prediction <Cite id="ledger-2026" />.

A deployed map publishes its frame, timestamp, resolution, unknown-state convention, update rate and invalidation rule. In MoveIt 2, the planning scene holds the robot's current state, its model and the world representation for collision checking <Cite id="moveit-planning-scene-2026" />, and attached or removed objects must reach it before motion; the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers transforms and the planning scene. A scene representation answers what is present now, while a world model must answer how state changes under an action, as the [simulator comparison](/world-models/world-models-vs-simulators) sets out.
