Dex-NeRF renders transparency-aware depth from learned density for a grasp planner, where a RealSense camera failed to compute depth for most transparent objects tested <Cite id="dex-nerf-2021" />. F3RM distills 2D foundation-model features into a 3D feature field so that language and a few demonstrations can guide grasping and placing <Cite id="f3rm-2023" />.

ParticleSplat, from Deepak Pathak (Carnegie Mellon) and colleagues (September 2026), encodes posed multi-view images into latent particles that decode to 3D Gaussians, trained with a novel-view synthesis objective. Object masks emerge without labels, moving a particle moves its object, and the representation improved downstream manipulation <Cite id="particlesplat-2026" />.

## SLAM: the system that builds the map

Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) builds such maps from sensor data while the robot moves without knowing its exact pose. Cadena and colleagues separate a sensor-dependent front end, which abstracts measurements and associates them with state variables, from a back end that performs inference and feeds information back for loop-closure detection and validation <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. [State estimation](/classical/state-estimation) covers the inference machinery.

<Image id="velodyne-hdl64-lidar-2009" />

Front ends are feature-based or direct. Monocular ORB-SLAM (2015) uses ORB features for tracking, local mapping, relocalization and loop closing, triangulating matched features and running local bundle adjustment. Its DBoW2 vocabulary proposes relocalization and loop candidates that need geometric validation <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />.

DBoW2 builds a vocabulary tree from binary features, combining image retrieval with geometric checks to reject visually similar but inconsistent places <Cite id="dbow2-2012" />.

ORB-SLAM3 supports stereo, RGB-D and visual-inertial modes with pinhole or fisheye cameras and MAP-based IMU initialization. It starts a new map after persistent tracking loss and merges maps only after geometric and covisibility checks, plus gravity-direction checks for mature visual-inertial maps. Low texture remains the main failure case, and slow motion can delay inertial initialization <Cite id="orb-slam3-2021" />.

Direct Sparse Odometry skips the detector and optimizes photometric error over sampled pixels jointly with geometry <Cite id="dso-2018" />. It can sample any region with intensity gradient, including near-featureless walls, and gains from calibrating exposure, vignetting and camera response <Cite id="dso-2018" />.

Learned systems keep classical machinery: DROID-SLAM iterates camera pose and per-pixel depth through a dense bundle-adjustment layer <Cite id="droid-slam-2021" />.

MASt3R-SLAM builds tracking, local fusion, loop closure and global optimization around a learned two-view reconstruction prior <Cite id="mast3r-slam-2024" />. SLAM3R predicts pointmaps for overlapping video windows and aligns them into a global reconstruction without explicitly solving camera parameters <Cite id="slam3r-2024" />.

VGGT-SLAM instead aligns submaps with projective transforms, accounting for the reconstruction ambiguity that remains when monocular cameras are uncalibrated <Cite id="vggt-slam-2025" />.

Revisiting mapped landmarks can reduce odometric drift and in some cases correct it, and visual-inertial methods drift less than wheel odometry <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Monocular ORB-SLAM validates a <Term id="loop-closure">loop closure</Term> geometrically, then spreads its error with similarity alignment and Essential Graph optimization <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />.

<LoopClosure className="my-6" />

<Term id="place-recognition">Place recognition</Term> asks whether the current image matches a stored place, and motion information can also inform that belief. Viewpoint, illumination and seasonal changes alter one place's appearance, and different places can look alike, which is perceptual aliasing <Cite id="lowry-2016-place-recognition" />. AnyLoc builds place descriptors by aggregating frozen self-supervised features, without training a network specifically for visual place recognition <Cite id="anyloc-2023" />.

Perceptual aliasing can create false-positive associations that corrupt back-end estimates, while false negatives discard useful measurements. Robust losses and loop-closure validation mitigate outliers, though failures remain that depend on initialization <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Graduated non-convexity offers another route: it gradually sharpens a robust objective while using non-minimal solvers, avoiding a required initial guess in the tested estimation problems <Cite id="gnc-2019" />.

In the back end, Square Root SAM estimates the trajectory and landmark map jointly by MAP inference, which under Gaussian models with known data associations is sparse nonlinear least squares. It solves successive linearized systems by QR or Cholesky, and variable ordering controls fill-in <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. iSAM2 adds incremental reordering and relinearization on a Bayes tree. Thresholded updates trade some accuracy for speed, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve <Cite id="kaess-2012" />.

Smoothing suits loop closure because relinearizing the past requires the past to stay in the graph. Cadena and colleagues contrast sparse landmark maps with dense models suited to obstacle avoidance, and cite octrees and voxel hashing as efficient volumetric storage. Two rooms can look identical to a 2D laser yet differ to a camera. Severe illumination changes defeat bag-of-words methods, and active range cameras work in dark, untextured scenes but face range and external-light limits <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

The iMAP system learns a scene-specific MLP from scratch at room scale from a handheld RGB-D stream. It tracks at 10 Hz and maps at 2 Hz on a desktop CPU and GPU, retaining keyframes for replay <Cite id="imap-2021" />. NICE-SLAM uses hierarchical feature grids with pretrained geometry decoders, reconstructs a multi-room apartment and performs no loop closure <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />. Its 47 ms tracking and 130 ms mapping times use small pixel samples on an RTX 3090 <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />.

SplaTAM maps with 3D Gaussians from an RGB-D camera and uses a silhouette mask to determine whether areas were previously mapped <Cite id="splatam-2023" />.

Gaussian Splatting SLAM uses Gaussians for tracking as well as mapping, optimizing the camera directly against them and adding geometric checks for incremental monocular reconstruction <Cite id="monogs-2023" />.

AMB3R-SLAM separates a lightweight tracking front end from a hierarchical back end that enforces local, intermediate and global consistency over long trajectories <Cite id="amb3r-slam-2026" />.

Cartographer supplies a 2D LiDAR mapping example: branch-and-bound scan-to-submap matching produces loop-closure constraints during mapping <Cite id="cartographer-2016" />.

## The deployed answer: costmaps and two planners

A navigation stack plans over a <Term id="costmap">costmap</Term>: occupancy from the map and live sensors, inflated by the robot's footprint. Lu, Hershberger and Smart's layered costmaps keep an ordered list of semantically separate layers and accumulate them into a master 2D costmap. Each update gathers the layers' bounds, then lets each layer write the master grid within them, and a configuration setting decides whether sensed obstacles overwrite static-map costs <Cite id="layered-costmaps-2014" />.

Navigation2, built on ROS 2, uses a layered costmap. Its global planner computes a shortest route to the goal, and a separate controller computes a local path and control signals, each a plugin in an asynchronous server <Cite id="nav2-2020" />.

The layered costmap's `track_unknown_space` option defaults to false, which treats unknown space as free; keeping the unknown state requires enabling it <Cite id="nav2-costmap-2d-2026" />. The planning algorithms are those of [motion planning](/classical/motion-planning) on a 2D grid.

## A representation is a service contract

[Perception](/classical/perception) locates objects in the current frame <Cite id="conceptgraphs-2023" />. Consumers issue different queries: localization needs stable landmarks <Cite id="cadena-2016" />, collision checking needs occupied volume and a conservative update rule <Cite id="octomap-2013" />, grasping needs surface pose and identity, and rendering needs appearance <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

Hydra stacks rungs in one real-time system, building a local ESDF, extracting a topological map of places from it and segmenting places into rooms <Cite id="hydra-2022" />.

ConceptFusion fuses pixel-aligned foundation-model features into a 3D map that can be queried through text, images, audio or geometry, without additional training <Cite id="conceptfusion-2023" />.

SceneLM, from Jitendra Malik (UC Berkeley), Marco Pavone and colleagues (September 2026), keeps the whole map as a structured text list of objects that one vision-language model edits after each image. On language-grounded retrieval and localization benchmarks it performed competitively with complete mapping pipelines, with a map 6 to 12 times more compact, and it ran online on an edge device aboard a quadruped <Cite id="scenelm-2026" />.

Ledger, from Shravan Chaudhari, Homanga Bharadhwaj and colleagues at Johns Hopkins (October 2026), keeps a persistent 3D object memory from a person's egocentric video: each object's resting locations, its moves and a short description, retained after it leaves view. A language model answering from these records as text, without the images, raised GPT-5.4's HD-EPIC accuracy from 29.7% to 42.6%, and on Ego4D the memory located objects with a median error of 0.99 m where it returned a prediction <Cite id="ledger-2026" />.

A deployed map publishes its frame, timestamp, resolution, unknown-state convention, update rate and invalidation rule. In MoveIt 2, the planning scene holds the robot's current state, its model and the world representation for collision checking <Cite id="moveit-planning-scene-2026" />, and attached or removed objects must reach it before motion; the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers transforms and the planning scene. A scene representation answers what is present now, while a world model must answer how state changes under an action, as the [simulator comparison](/world-models/world-models-vs-simulators) sets out.

Includes a step-through motion scene of one predict-and-update cycle." domain: classical slug: state-estimation order: 4 status: published lastReviewed: "2026-08-17" citations: - kalman-1960-filter - mcgee-schmidt-1985 - thrun-2005 - smith-1990 - julier-uhlmann-1997 - kschischang-2001 - dellaert-kaess-2006 - kaess-2008 - kaess-2012 - cadena-2016 - forster-2017 - gtsam-2026 - mesh-mcl-construction-2026 - gordon-salmond-smith-1993 - dellaert-mcl-1999 - kalman-bucy-1961 - julier-uhlmann-2004 - li-mourikis-2013 - hartley-inekf-2019 - eqvio-2022 - gtsam-4-3-2026 - rauch-tung-striebel-1965 - grisetti-gmapping-2007 - msckf-2007 - okvis-2014 - backprop-kf-2016 - tlio-2020 - airio-2025 - mac-vo-2024 - tartan-imu-2025 - gait-2026 - mast3r-slam-2024 - planet-2018 - dreamerv3-nature-2025 - li-mourikis-temporal-2014 - li-rolling-shutter-2013 - openvins-2020 - kalibr-2013 - grandtour-2026 - ssio-2026 - humanoidpose-2026 seeAlso: - "rl-sim2real/legged-locomotion" - "adjacent/autonomous-vehicles" --- import { KalmanPredictUpdate } from '@/components/motion/scenes/kalman-predict-update'; import { Clip } from '@/components/motion/clip'; import { LinearizationGap } from '@/components/interactive/linearization-gap'; import { ExplainerFigure } from '@/components/explainers/explainer-figure'; State estimation computes a robot's state, such as its [configuration](/classical/kinematics) or velocity over ground, from noisy, biased and intermittent sensor readings, and [planning](/classical/motion-planning) and [control](/classical/control) assume that state is known. Probabilistic estimators report a belief, so each estimate carries its uncertainty .
## The Bayes filter A belief $bel(x_t)$ is a probability distribution over the state, kept current by two alternating steps. The predict step pushes the belief through the process model, given the control $u_t$ : $$ \overline{bel}(x_t) = \int p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}) \, bel(x_{t-1}) \, dx_{t-1} $$ The update step folds in the measurement $z_t$ through the sensor model $p(z_t \mid x_t)$ and sharpens the belief where the measurement points : $$ bel(x_t) = \eta \, p(z_t \mid x_t) \, \overline{bel}(x_t) $$ with normalizer $\eta$. This recursion is the Bayes filter, which Thrun, Burgard and Fox call the basis of virtually every technique in their book, and each tractable filter adds assumptions or approximations that make the integral computable . The bootstrap filter of Gordon, Salmond and Smith drops the linearity and Gaussian-noise assumptions and applies to any state transition or measurement model . Drive the robot in the figure below: its cloud of doubt grows as it moves and shrinks when it spots a landmark. ## The Kalman filter The 1960 Kalman filter reduces the recursion to matrix algebra by assuming linear process and measurement models and Gaussian noise : $$ x_t = A_t x_{t-1} + B_t u_t + w_t, \qquad z_t = C_t x_t + v_t $$ with $w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q_t)$ and $v_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R_t)$; Probabilistic Robotics swaps the two symbols. A Gaussian belief then stays Gaussian, so the recursion tracks only a mean and covariance. Predict : $$ \bar{\mu}_t = A_t \mu_{t-1} + B_t u_t, \qquad \bar{\Sigma}_t = A_t \Sigma_{t-1} A_t^{\top} + Q_t $$ Update, through the Kalman gain $K_t$ : $$ K_t = \bar{\Sigma}_t C_t^{\top} \left( C_t \bar{\Sigma}_t C_t^{\top} + R_t \right)^{-1} $$ $$ \mu_t = \bar{\mu}_t + K_t \left( z_t - C_t \bar{\mu}_t \right), \qquad \Sigma_t = \left( I - K_t C_t \right) \bar{\Sigma}_t $$ The gain is prior uncertainty over prior-plus-sensor uncertainty: a filter that trusts its model gets a small gain and mostly ignores the sensor, and one that trusts its sensor gets a gain near one. Under linear-Gaussian assumptions the recursion is the minimum-variance estimator, and Kalman's projection-based derivation makes it the best linear estimator with white noise even without Gaussian noise . Kalman and Bucy's continuous-time formulation evolves the error covariance through a Riccati differential equation, whose solution determines the optimal filter . McGee and Schmidt's 1985 NASA history credits Schmidt's Ames group with adapting the filter to nonlinear circumlunar navigation in the early 1960s. By early 1961 simulations supported the approach, though operation on available flight computers was unverified. The report separates this work from Battin's Apollo studies at MIT and Potter's square-root implementation used in Apollo. Primary Apollo navigation used ground radar, with an onboard backup . ## The extended Kalman filter Real robots are nonlinear: joint angles enter through sines and cosines, so the models become $x_t = g(x_{t-1}, u_t) + w_t$ and $z_t = h(x_t) + v_t$. The extended Kalman filter keeps the Gaussian belief, linearizes both models about the current estimate with their Jacobians $G_t = \partial g / \partial x$ and $H_t = \partial h / \partial x$, and propagates the covariance through the tangent system : $$ \bar{\Sigma}_t = G_t \Sigma_{t-1} G_t^{\top} + Q_t, \qquad K_t = \bar{\Sigma}_t H_t^{\top} \left( H_t \bar{\Sigma}_t H_t^{\top} + R_t \right)^{-1} $$ The mean moves through the true maps $g$ and $h$; only the covariance takes the linearized route . The Ames group moved from linearizing about a nominal reference trajectory to relinearizing about the *current estimated state*, which they hoped would bring "substantial advantages". An accidentally off-nominal simulation converged after initial overshoots, and the report names this modification the extended Kalman filter. It also discusses instability from round-off, inadequate statistical models and nonlinearities . Linearization holds near the estimate, which is itself uncertain, so where the nonlinearity is strong over the region the covariance covers, $\Sigma$ stops describing the true error, and the filter grows overconfident and can diverge . Julier and Uhlmann summarize 35 years of experience: the EKF is difficult to implement and tune, and reliable only for systems almost linear on the time scale of the updates . Li and Mourikis proved that standard EKF visual-inertial odometry is inconsistent because of how its Jacobians are computed, so it underestimates its uncertainty . The unscented Kalman filter of Julier and Uhlmann keeps the Gaussian and pushes deterministically chosen sample points through the true nonlinearity . Particle filters drop the Gaussian assumption and carry the belief as a set of particles . Invariant filters on Lie groups remove the dependence on the estimate: in the contact-aided invariant EKF, neither the linearized error dynamics nor the linearized observation model depends on the current state estimate . EqVIO applies an equivariant filter to visual-inertial odometry, using the system's symmetries to reduce linearization error and improve consistency . ## Factor graphs: keep the whole trajectory Rauch, Tung and Striebel related filtered and smoothed estimates in 1965 and showed numerically that smoothing reduces errors . In EKF-based SLAM, marginalizing old poses commits their linearized information to a Gaussian approximation that cannot be relinearized later. Full smoothing keeps the trajectory and can relinearize, though nonlinear optimization is not guaranteed to reach the global minimum . The posterior over the trajectory $X = \{x_0, \dots, x_T\}$ is a product of factors, one per measurement or motion constraint : $$ p(X \mid Z) \propto \prod_i \phi_i(X_i) $$ Drawn as a bipartite graph of variable and factor nodes, this is a factor graph. Kschischang, Frey, and Loeliger's 2001 paper unified inference on such graphs under the sum-product algorithm . With Gaussian factors, the most probable trajectory solves one sparse nonlinear least-squares problem : $$ X^{\star} = \arg\min_X \sum_i \left\lVert h_i(X_i) - z_i \right\rVert_{\Sigma_i}^2 $$ Dellaert and Kaess's 2006 Square Root SAM jointly estimates the SLAM trajectory and landmark map, assuming known data associations, Gaussian models, a uniform landmark prior and a fixed initial frame. It solves successive linearized systems, by QR on the measurement Jacobian or Cholesky on the information matrix, and variable ordering sets fill-in and cost . The iSAM method updates only the part of the factorization a new measurement touches . iSAM2 adds a Bayes tree with incremental reordering and relinearization: an update re-eliminates the affected cliques and their ancestors, then reattaches unaffected subtrees. Thresholds trade accuracy for computation, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve . GTSAM is a BSD-licensed C++ library that implements sensor fusion for robotics and computer vision using factor graphs . Version 4.3 moved to C++17 and added experimental CUDA nonlinear optimization and several legged-state-estimation implementations . Building on Lupton and Sukkarieh's preintegration, Forster and colleagues' on-manifold version collapses anywhere from a few to hundreds of IMU readings between two keyframes into one factor . Cadena and colleagues describe a classical SLAM period from 1986 to 2004, with EKF, Rao-Blackwellised particle-filter and maximum-likelihood approaches, and an algorithmic-analysis period from 2004 to 2015 . In Rao-Blackwellized grid mapping, each particle carries its own map . Smith, Self and Cheeseman's stochastic map stores estimated spatial relationships together with their uncertainties and updates them incrementally as measurements arrive . The survey treats MAP estimation, often over factor graphs, as the de facto standard but notes EKF systems with state-of-the-art performance. The gap shrinks when EKF linearization is accurate, sliding windows are used and inconsistency is addressed, and graphs still face unbounded growth and information loss under sparsification . The MSCKF sliding-window filter keeps 3D feature positions out of the state and is optimal up to linearization errors , while OKVIS argues that nonlinear optimization offers superior accuracy and stays tractable through sparsity . [Scene representation and mapping](/classical/scene-representation) covers what a robot keeps from the estimate. ## Where this meets the learned stack Learned components mostly enter classical estimators as measurements with uncertainty. Backprop KF makes the filter itself differentiable, representing its belief-parameter updates as a computation graph that can be trained from raw observations . TLIO regresses 3D displacement and its uncertainty from IMU data and fuses both into a stochastic cloning EKF , and MAC-VO learns a metrics-aware keypoint covariance and uses it to weight pose graph optimization . AirIO preserves body-frame IMU measurements and encodes attitude, combining learned IMU correction with an uncertainty-aware EKF for aerial robots . A September 2026 paper from Linus Kramer, William Talbot, Olga Vysotska and Marco Hutter is an example. For robots on construction sites, they replace the observation model of a Monte Carlo localization particle filter with a network that matches LiDAR scans against the building mesh, trained only on scans simulated inside that mesh. On real-world datasets it outperformed diffusion-based and ScanContext++ baselines at 18 ms per call . GAIT estimates legged-robot state without an explicit contact estimator and outperforms contact-aided model-based methods on a Unitree Go1 . Yuheng Qiu, Pieter Abbeel, Guanya Shi and colleagues at Amazon FAR, Carnegie Mellon and three other universities (October 2026) train inertial odometry from scratch without velocity or position labels: a teacher integrates the IMU over each short window, and a pose graph over many windows refines the targets . On six datasets from pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds and a humanoid, average velocity error came within 0.07 m/s of a supervised network of the same architecture, though its trajectory error on the EuRoC drone flights was 10.23 m against the supervised network's 3.72 m . The teacher used a reference attitude to remove gravity, and the IMU bias must be calibrated . Jiaxi Jiang, Marco Hutter, Christian Holz and colleagues at ETH Zurich (October 2026) estimate a humanoid's joint angles and world-space motion from ordinary video, training the pose decoder only on 128,000 synthetic images of sixteen humanoids . With no real pose labels, joint-angle error on three real humanoids was 18 to 32% below the best baseline on each . [Latent-dynamics world models](/world-models/latent-dynamics) act as learned belief states. PlaNet's latent dynamics model has deterministic and stochastic transition components trained with variational inference . DreamerV3 learns a model of the environment and improves its behaviour by imagining future scenarios . ## Timing is part of the state Fusing visual and inertial measurements requires each measurement's precise sampling time , and most consumer cameras use rolling shutters that capture each pixel row at a slightly different time . The camera-IMU offset can be a state variable, locally identifiable except in a few degenerate motions ; OpenVINS calibrates it in its sliding-window filter , and Kalibr estimates time offsets to a fraction of the smallest measurement period . Persistent directional residuals in per-sensor innovations point to calibration or timing bias instead of random noise. GrandTour, which its authors call the largest open-access legged-robotics dataset, supplies RTK-GNSS and total-station ground truth . The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers temporal residuals, and the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers timestamped interfaces.

In EKF-based SLAM, marginalizing old poses commits their linearized information to a Gaussian approximation that cannot be relinearized later. Full smoothing keeps the trajectory and can relinearize, though nonlinear optimization is not guaranteed to reach the global minimum . The posterior over the trajectory $X = \{x_0, \dots, x_T\}$ is a product of factors, one per measurement or motion constraint : $$ p(X \mid Z) \propto \prod_i \phi_i(X_i) $$ Drawn as a bipartite graph of variable and factor nodes, this is a factor graph. Kschischang, Frey, and Loeliger's 2001 paper unified inference on such graphs under the sum-product algorithm . With Gaussian factors, the most probable trajectory solves one sparse nonlinear least-squares problem : $$ X^{\star} = \arg\min_X \sum_i \left\lVert h_i(X_i) - z_i \right\rVert_{\Sigma_i}^2 $$ Dellaert and Kaess's 2006 Square Root SAM jointly estimates the SLAM trajectory and landmark map, assuming known data associations, Gaussian models, a uniform landmark prior and a fixed initial frame. It solves successive linearized systems, by QR on the measurement Jacobian or Cholesky on the information matrix, and variable ordering sets fill-in and cost . The iSAM method updates only the part of the factorization a new measurement touches . iSAM2 adds a Bayes tree with incremental reordering and relinearization: an update re-eliminates the affected cliques and their ancestors, then reattaches unaffected subtrees. Thresholds trade accuracy for computation, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve . GTSAM is a BSD-licensed C++ library that implements sensor fusion for robotics and computer vision using factor graphs . Version 4.3 moved to C++17 and added experimental CUDA nonlinear optimization and several legged-state-estimation implementations . Building on Lupton and Sukkarieh's preintegration, Forster and colleagues' on-manifold version collapses anywhere from a few to hundreds of IMU readings between two keyframes into one factor . Cadena and colleagues describe a classical SLAM period from 1986 to 2004, with EKF, Rao-Blackwellised particle-filter and maximum-likelihood approaches, and an algorithmic-analysis period from 2004 to 2015 . In Rao-Blackwellized grid mapping, each particle carries its own map . Smith, Self and Cheeseman's stochastic map stores estimated spatial relationships together with their uncertainties and updates them incrementally as measurements arrive . The survey treats MAP estimation, often over factor graphs, as the de facto standard but notes EKF systems with state-of-the-art performance. The gap shrinks when EKF linearization is accurate, sliding windows are used and inconsistency is addressed, and graphs still face unbounded growth and information loss under sparsification . Its central test, force closure, asks whether the origin lies inside the convex hull of the contact wrenches ; the distance to that hull's boundary is the standard quality metric . ## The wrench space, live ## Contact models
A contact model says which forces a fingertip can transmit; Salisbury and Roth modeled several finger-contact types for three-fingered hands . A frictionless point contact pushes only along the surface normal. A point contact with friction obeys Coulomb's law: the tangential force can reach $\mu$ times the normal force before the contact slides . $$ \lVert f^t \rVert \le \mu \, f^n $$ The admissible forces form the friction cone around the inward normal, with half-angle $\alpha = \arctan \mu$. In the plane the cone is a wedge; in space it is a quadratic cone, and approximating it by a polyhedral one keeps the analysis linear . A soft-finger contact adds a torsional moment about the normal, bounded by a torsional coefficient times the normal load . Kao, Lynch and Burdick extend contact analysis to pressure distributions and friction limit surfaces, which also describe soft contacts and nonprehensile manipulation such as pushing . Tilt the grip in the figure below and pick a surface to find where the pinch lets go. Cutkosky's taxonomy separates power grasps, which wrap the object for stability, from precision grasps, which hold it in the fingertips for dexterity . GraspQP reports that simplified force-closure analysis favors power grasps . ## The grasp wrench space [Perception](/classical/perception) supplies the object pose. A contact force both pushes and twists the object, so its wrench stacks the force over its moment about the object's reference frame : $$ w_i = \begin{bmatrix} f_i \\ r_i \times f_i \end{bmatrix} $$ In the plane this is $(f_x, f_y, \tau)$ with $\tau = r_x f_y - r_y f_x$ . The primitive wrenches lie along the cone edges at unit normal force. If each contact's force is limited separately, the grasp wrench space is the convex hull of the Minkowski sum of the contacts' primitive wrenches . If the total force is limited, it is the convex hull of their union : $$ \mathcal{W} = \operatorname{conv}\left\{ w_{ij} \right\}, \qquad w_{ij} = \begin{bmatrix} n_i \pm \mu \, t_i \\ r_i \times (n_i \pm \mu \, t_i) \end{bmatrix} $$ Testing whether the origin lies inside this polytope is a ray-shooting problem dual to a linear program . Han, Trinkle and Li formulate friction-cone constraints as linear matrix inequalities, giving convex optimization problems for closure, wrench feasibility under joint-effort limits and contact-force optimization . ## Force closure A grasp has force closure when the contacts can resist any external wrench, so the object's motion is fully constrained . That holds exactly when the hull contains a neighborhood of the origin : $$ \exists \, \varepsilon > 0 : \quad B_\varepsilon(0) \subset \mathcal{W} $$ An origin on the boundary leaves a disturbance the grasp cannot resist. Bicchi separates form closure, a geometric property, from force closure involving the grasping device, and connects the latter to equilibrium and stability . Uncertainty in friction and contact position can be disastrous for closure . Without friction the cone collapses to the normal ray, and form closure, closure by geometry alone, needs at least four wrenches in the plane and seven in space, as Reuleaux noted in 1875 and Somoff in 1897 . Markenscoff, Ni and Papadimitriou showed that four fingers suffice for any planar object with a piecewise smooth boundary except a circle, twelve for any spatial object without rotational symmetry, and seven under very general conditions . Mishra, Schwartz and Sharir analyze frictionless positive grips under equilibrium, constant external wrenches and varying external wrenches, and give synthesis algorithms for polyhedral and polygonal objects . With Coulomb friction, three fingers are necessary and sufficient to grasp any planar object, and four in space, under the most relaxed assumptions; a particular object can need fewer . Nguyen's antipodal grasp theorem settles the two-finger planar case: such a grasp with friction is force closure if and only if the line between the contacts lies inside both friction cones . A differentiable estimator later made force closure an optimization objective that tests closure within milliseconds for arbitrary hands . ## Grasp quality: the epsilon metric Ferrari and Canny turned the binary test into a number: the quality $\varepsilon$ is the radius of the largest origin-centered ball inside the grasp wrench space . $$ \varepsilon = \min_{F_k \in \partial \mathcal{W}} \; \operatorname{dist}\!\left( 0, F_k \right) $$ Because the hull is a polytope, $\varepsilon$ is the distance from the origin to its nearest facet , and with an $l$-edge polyhedral cone it is an approximation . Kirkpatrick, Mishra and Yap connect grasp efficiency to a quantitative Steinitz theorem: selecting a limited subset of wrenches shrinks the origin-centered ball that their hull can contain . With unit normal forces, $\varepsilon$ is the worst-case disturbance the grasp absorbs per unit of contact force, at the nominal friction. In FIRMGrasp's tests, 53% of nominally force-closed grasps lost closure in the adverse friction tail , and in a shake test the nominal margin ranked a successful grasp above a failed one with probability only 0.53 . In most cases the grasp most robust to pose error is not the one with the highest $\varepsilon$ . Predicting grasp stability well required a combination of metrics . Roa and Suárez review measures based on contact locations and hand configuration and show that the largest-minimum resisted wrench depends on the torque origin and on the force-torque metric. A grasp optimal under a shared total-force limit need not be optimal under per-finger limits, and most of their analysis is quasi-static . FRoGGeR's min-weight metric approximates $\varepsilon$ differentiably and synthesizes grasps in a median 0.834 s . Li and Sastry's task-oriented metric instead represents the required task as an ellipsoid in wrench space, so the grasp is judged against expected loading directions . ## Reading the hull The lab draws the object and each contact's friction cone beside the grasp wrench space projected from $(f_x, f_y, \tau)$, turns the origin ring green under force closure and reports $\varepsilon$. The default tripod of top, right and bottom contacts is force closure at $\mu = 0.7$. Without the bottom contact, the top-right pair's connecting line sits 45 degrees from each normal, outside cones of half-angle $\arctan 0.7 \approx 35$ degrees, so it fails Nguyen's test . Sliding contact 2 onto the bottom edge makes the pair antipodal and restores closure for any positive friction, and lowering $\mu$ lowers $\varepsilon$. ## Where this meets the learned stack Dex-Net 2.0 labels synthetic data with analytic metrics: 6.7 million datapoints from 1,500 object models, positive when expected $\varepsilon$ under object-pose, gripper-pose and friction uncertainty exceeds 0.002 and no collision is modeled. Its GQ-CNN takes a grasp-aligned depth crop and the gripper depth, and predicts robustness without regressing $\varepsilon$ . The planner samples antipodal parallel-jaw candidates from depth gradients and executes the most robust [reachable](/classical/kinematics), [collision-free](/classical/motion-planning) one. It assumes isolated rigid objects on a planar worksurface and one depth camera with known intrinsics. On an ABB YuMi with silicone fingertips and a Primesense Carmine 1.08, a success meant the object stayed held through lifting, transport and shaking . On eight 3D-printed adversarial objects, GQ-L-Adv, fine-tuned on synthetic examples of them, succeeded in 93% of 80 trials. A separate CEM-augmented run of 100 trials on 40 novel household objects, including articulated and deformable ones, reported 94% success and 99% precision: 68 of 69 grasps rated above 50% robustness succeeded. The two evaluations cannot be pooled, and missing depth on thin parts and object collisions remained failure modes . Dex-Net 4.0 cleared bins of up to 25 novel objects with over 95% reliability at more than 300 mean picks per hour . DexGraspNet 2.0 holds 427 million grasps , and GraspGen-X, a diffusion grasp generator trained on procedural grippers and 2 billion grasps, generalized zero-shot to novel real grippers . Learned [diffusion policies](/manipulation/diffusion-policy) take contacts from data, but dexterous data pipelines still solve contact mechanics: BODex synthesizes over 49 grasps per second on one RTX 3090 GPU , and DexEvolve's authors note that analytic synthesis rests on simplifying assumptions that yield infeasible grasps, which high-fidelity simulation must filter out . A 2026 [controller](/classical/control) enforces the quality margin during execution, keeping a median 94% of it at 0.09 ms per solve . [Sim-to-real transfer](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion) remained hard for dexterous grasping: Get a Grip found most multi-finger methods degrading on hardware . DexGraspNet 2.0 transferred zero-shot to real clutter at 90.7% success , and RobustDexGrasp, trained in simulation, reached 94.6% on 512 real objects . DexGraspVLA reports over 90% success in thousands of unseen cluttered scenes . Adding wrench and tactile feedback to vision raised one policy from 14 to 24 successes in 25 real trials . GENESIS-Handover, from Marco Hutter (ETH Zurich) and colleagues (October 2026), chooses how a robot presents an object by matching generated task-specific grips to the person's live hand . On a legged manipulator, handovers needing no adjustment rose from 6 to 16 of 60 against AFT-Handover .

Robot calibration estimates the parameters that make a robot's measurements and commands agree on the physical world. Classical kinematic calibration has four steps: modeling, measurement, identification and correction <Cite id="roth-mooring-ravani-1987" />.

## The calibration chain

A manipulation system chains <Term id="camera-intrinsics">camera intrinsics</Term>, depth alignment, extrinsics, joint zeroes, link and tool parameters, payload, timing and actuator response. FoundationPose tracks novel-object poses with or without a model <Cite id="foundationpose-2024" />, but a wrong hand-eye transform still misplaces the grasp.

<CalibrationChain className="my-6" />

## Camera intrinsics

Intrinsics map pixels to rays through focal lengths, principal point and lens distortion. Zhang's method recovers them from a planar pattern at a few unknown orientations <Cite id="zhang-2000-calibration" />, and Kannala and Brandt's generic model covers wide-angle and fisheye lenses <Cite id="kannala-brandt-2006" />. Refit after any focus, resolution or crop change.

## Depth is a measurement model

Stereo depth error scales with the square of distance, and repetitive structures make matches ambiguous <Cite id="realsense-tuning-2026" />; the D400 datasheet adds saturation from specular reflections <Cite id="realsense-d400-datasheet-2026" />. Kinect random error grows from a few millimeters to about 4 cm at maximum range <Cite id="khoshelham-kinect-2012" />, and a joint depth-color calibration with a depth-distortion model beat the manufacturer's <Cite id="herrera-depth-color-2012" />.

## Hand-eye calibration

Hand-eye calibration finds the gripper-to-camera transform for a wrist camera, or base-to-camera for a fixed one. Shiu and Ahmad cast it as $AX = XB$ <Cite id="shiu-ahmad-1989" />, Tsai and Lenz solved it in about ${}100 + 64N$ arithmetic operations for $N$ robot stations <Cite id="tsai-lenz-1989" />, and Park and Martin derived closed-form exact and least-squares solutions <Cite id="park-martin-1994" />.

<Image id="baxter-gripper-wrist-camera" />

OpenCV needs at least two motions with non-parallel rotation axes, so three poses, and strongly recommends many more <Cite id="opencv-hand-eye-docs-2026" />. MoveIt's tutorial reports accuracy plateaus after about 12 or 15 samples in most cases <Cite id="moveit-hand-eye-tutorial-2026" />.

<HandEyePoses className="my-6" />

Markerless methods now rival targets: DREAM's single-image accuracy is comparable to multi-frame offline calibration <Cite id="dream-2019" />, and Hydra reaches 5 mm task-space accuracy against 7 mm for classical methods <Cite id="hydra-hand-eye-2025" />. ## Kinematic and tool calibration

Manufacturing errors and joint compliance shift an assembled arm from its nominal [kinematics](/classical/kinematics) <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />. Nguyen and colleagues calibrated a humanoid from 31 chosen postures and cut RMS error 2.3-fold against the manufacturer's model <Cite id="humanoid-geometric-calibration-2025" />. OmniCalib found CAD wrist-camera extrinsics off by up to 10.56 mm and 1.74 degrees, and writes back only corrections its observability checks support <Cite id="omnicalib-2026" />.

## Time calibration

A late frame misplaces a moving arm. Kalibr estimates time offsets jointly with spatial transforms <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />, and IEEE 1588 synchronizes networked clocks to sub-microsecond accuracy <Cite id="ieee-1588-2019" />. On one RealSense D435 and Airbot Play rig, Realtime-VLA V2 measured camera, proprioception and motion delays of 55, 50 and 150 ms <Cite id="realtime-vla-v2-2026" />.

<TimeOffsetMiss className="my-6" />

## Dynamics and actuator calibration

Sim-to-real work calls this system identification. Atkeson, An and Hollerbach identified load and link inertial parameters by least squares and beat CAD-derived predictions <Cite id="atkeson-an-hollerbach-1986" />, and Gaz and colleagues first identified the Franka Panda's dynamics, joint friction and feasible parameters <Cite id="gaz-panda-dynamics-2019" />.

Hwangbo and colleagues found actuator dynamics central to ANYmal's transfer gap and learned an actuator network from real measurements <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />, and SPI-Active, which chooses identification data actively, beats baselines by 42 to 63% in locomotion transfer <Cite id="spi-active-2025" />. Without measured response, a dataset confuses policy and tracking error.

## Calibration versus visual servoing

Visual servoing puts the vision sensor inside the control loop and drives image features toward a target through a task function <Cite id="espiau-1992" />. Its interaction model, velocity commands and safety geometry still need consistent conventions.

## Drift and ownership

DROID's per-session checkerboard calibrations were not always accurate, and the dataset provides camera-to-base calibrations for about 36,000 scenes <Cite id="droid-2024" />. Most public datasets lack extrinsics; CalibAll recovered them for about 97,000 episodes across 16 datasets <Cite id="calib-all-2025" />. Store each calibration with hardware serials, camera settings, tool, software version, date, procedure and residuals, and redo it after a remount, collision, tool or firmware change.

Forward kinematics maps joint angles to the end-effector pose through a unique composition of transforms, and inverse kinematics maps a pose back to joint angles, with no solution, one, or many .
## Forward kinematics [A serial arm is a chain](/how-robots-work/#arm) of rigid links and joints, with a coordinate frame on each link. A rigid transform packs a rotation $R$ and a translation $p$ into one matrix : $$ T = \begin{bmatrix} R & p \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ The ordered product of one transform per joint carries the base frame to the tool frame : $$ T_0^{n}(q) = T_0^1(q_1)\,T_1^2(q_2)\,\cdots\,T_{n-1}^{n}(q_n) $$ The map is smooth in the joint angles and cheap to evaluate . In the plane, each link is a vector of length $l_i$ along the cumulative angle, and the end effector sits at their sum : $$ x = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l_i \cos\left(q_1 + \cdots + q_i\right) \qquad y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l_i \sin\left(q_1 + \cdots + q_i\right) $$ Moving one joint moves every later link, the dependence the Jacobian captures . ## Denavit-Hartenberg parameters Denavit and Hartenberg's 1955 matrix notation describes the kinematics of all lower-pair mechanisms . LaValle gives the Denavit-Hartenberg convention four parameters per revolute joint: an offset along a rotation axis, an angle about it, the distance between successive axes, and the angle between them . The example here writes the last two $a_i$ and $\alpha_i$. Standard and modified variants coexist . The standard form is : $$ A_i = \mathrm{Rot}_z(\theta_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_z(d_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_x(a_i)\,\mathrm{Rot}_x(\alpha_i) $$ $$ \def\arraystretch{0.9} A_i = \begin{bmatrix} R_i & t_i \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad t_i = \begin{bmatrix} a_i\cos\theta_i \\ a_i\sin\theta_i \\ d_i \end{bmatrix} $$ $$ \def\arraystretch{0.9} R_i = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_i & -\sin\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & \sin\theta_i\sin\alpha_i \\ \sin\theta_i & \cos\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & -\cos\theta_i\sin\alpha_i \\ 0 & \sin\alpha_i & \cos\alpha_i \end{bmatrix} $$ A planar arm has zero twists and offsets, leaving link lengths and angles . DH parameters are ill-conditioned when consecutive axes are nearly parallel . Product-of-exponentials (POE) parameters vary smoothly as the axes change : POE, which Brockett applied to manipulators in 1984, treats each joint as a screw about a fixed axis, the form Modern Robotics uses . The 3D playground reads the SO-101 chain from its URDF, the most common description format, where each joint carries an origin transform and a rotation axis . ## The Jacobian The Jacobian relates joint velocities to end-effector velocity, one column per joint : $$ \dot{x} = J(q)\,\dot{q} $$ In Modern Robotics' space Jacobian, column $i$ is joint $i$'s screw axis at the current pose, in base-frame coordinates . A revolute joint with unit axis $\omega_i$ through point $p_i$ gives the first form, and a prismatic joint sliding along unit direction $v_i$ the second : $$ J_i = \begin{bmatrix} \omega_i \\ -\omega_i \times p_i \end{bmatrix} \qquad J_i = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ v_i \end{bmatrix} $$ The transpose maps an end-effector wrench to balancing joint torques, $\tau = J^{T}(q)\,F$ . At singularities, such as a fully extended arm, the Jacobian loses rank, and nearby a modest end-effector speed demands unbounded joint speeds ; Yoshikawa's 1985 manipulability measure scores how well an arm can position and orient its end effector . Whitney's resolved motion rate control (1969) let an operator command hand motion along task axes , with the inverse Jacobian giving joint rates: $$ \dot{q} = J^{-1}(q)\,\dot{x} $$ A redundant arm uses the pseudoinverse $J^{+} = J^{T}(JJ^{T})^{-1}$, whose spare freedom can serve goals such as avoiding joint limits , ranked against the end-effector task in Siciliano and Slotine's task-priority framework . Near singular points, Nakamura and Hanafusa's singularity-robust inverse returns a motion close to the desired path . ## Inverse kinematics Inverse kinematics seeks $q$ with $k(q) = x_d$ for a target $x_d$. The map is nonlinear: a reachable target can have several configurations, such as elbow left or right, a redundant arm has a continuum, and an unreachable target has none . Move the shoulder slider in the figure below to trace the hand's path, then drag the cup and watch the arm work out an angle for every joint. Closed forms exist for special geometries, such as six-revolute arms with intersecting wrist axes . A general 6R arm reduces to one minimum-degree polynomial in a single joint variable , which Manocha and Canny's 1994 algorithm solved in 11 ms on average on an IBM RS/6000 workstation , and Diankov's IKFast generates closed-form solvers that answer in about 6 microseconds, against about 10 milliseconds for most numerical solvers . The general tool is iterative: linearize, step, repeat : $$ \Delta x = J(q)\,\Delta q \qquad \Delta q = J^{+}(q)\,\Delta x $$ KDL's pseudoinverse solver repeatedly reports false failures on humanoids, and TRAC-IK finds solutions much more often . cuRobo solves over 7,000 collision-free IK queries per second , and for redundant arms IKFlow samples 2,000 solutions in under 10 ms, within 10 mm and 2 degrees of exact . The [3D kinematics playground](/playground) solves IK on TheRobotStudio's SO-101 arm with a live residual and iteration count . ## The same geometry, inside learned policies [Action chunking](/manipulation/action-chunking) with ACT predicts 14 joint-space targets for two 6-DoF arms and their grippers , while OpenVLA predicts 7-dimensional single-arm end-effector actions , and Diffusion Policy did consistently better with position than velocity actions . Across 13,000+ real rollouts and 500+ models, delta actions consistently helped, joint space favored stability, and task space favored generalization . GR00T N1 uses embodiment-specific action decoders: in its simulation benchmarks a Panda arm acts in relative end-effector position and rotation, and the GR-1 humanoid in joint positions . NVIDIA says N1.7 shares one relative end-effector action space across robot and human data . Quaternions and Euler angles are discontinuous and hard for networks to learn, while 5D and 6D rotation representations are continuous . Teleoperation runs through the same chain: a GELLO leader copies its target arm's kinematic structure , and retargeting artifacts such as foot sliding reduce the robustness of humanoid tracking policies . ## Treat coordinate frames as an API A Cartesian action must name its frame, units, rotation representation, composition order, and whether it is absolute or relative; a joint action needs joint order, signs, limits and controller semantics. ROS REP 103 makes frames right-handed, with x forward, y left and z up , and REP 105 separates the drifting `odom` frame from the `map` frame, which can jump . Round-trip kinematics tests and versioned URDF and calibration files keep the contract testable. LeRobot calibrates SO-101 leader and follower arms to read the same values in the same pose, so a network trained on one robot works on another . See the [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) and the [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces).

A revolute joint with unit axis $\omega_i$ through point $p_i$ gives the first form, and a prismatic joint sliding along unit direction $v_i$ the second : $$ J_i = \begin{bmatrix} \omega_i \\ -\omega_i \times p_i \end{bmatrix} \qquad J_i = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ v_i \end{bmatrix} $$ The transpose maps an end-effector wrench to balancing joint torques, $\tau = J^{T}(q)\,F$ . At singularities, such as a fully extended arm, the Jacobian loses rank, and nearby a modest end-effector speed demands unbounded joint speeds ; Yoshikawa's 1985 manipulability measure scores how well an arm can position and orient its end effector . Whitney's resolved motion rate control (1969) let an operator command hand motion along task axes , with the inverse Jacobian giving joint rates: $$ \dot{q} = J^{-1}(q)\,\dot{x} $$ A redundant arm uses the pseudoinverse $J^{+} = J^{T}(JJ^{T})^{-1}$, whose spare freedom can serve goals such as avoiding joint limits , ranked against the end-effector task in Siciliano and Slotine's task-priority framework . Near singular points, Nakamura and Hanafusa's singularity-robust inverse returns a motion close to the desired path . Wampler's damped least-squares formulation makes the tradeoff explicit: reduce pose error while penalizing the size of the corrective joint motion . ## Inverse kinematics Inverse kinematics seeks $q$ with $k(q) = x_d$ for a target $x_d$. The map is nonlinear: a reachable target can have several configurations, such as elbow left or right, a redundant arm has a continuum, and an unreachable target has none . Move the shoulder slider in the figure below to trace the hand's path, then drag the cup and watch the arm work out an angle for every joint. Closed forms exist for special geometries, such as six-revolute arms with intersecting wrist axes . A general 6R arm reduces to one minimum-degree polynomial in a single joint variable , which Manocha and Canny's 1994 algorithm solved in 11 ms on average on an IBM RS/6000 workstation , and Diankov's IKFast generates closed-form solvers that answer in about 6 microseconds, against about 10 milliseconds for most numerical solvers . The general tool is iterative: linearize, step, repeat : $$ \Delta x = J(q)\,\Delta q \qquad \Delta q = J^{+}(q)\,\Delta x $$ KDL's pseudoinverse solver repeatedly reports false failures on humanoids, and TRAC-IK finds solutions much more often . cuRobo solves over 7,000 collision-free IK queries per second , and for redundant arms IKFlow samples 2,000 solutions in under 10 ms, within 10 mm and 2 degrees of exact . The [3D kinematics playground](/playground) solves IK on TheRobotStudio's SO-101 arm with a live residual and iteration count . PyRoki expresses inverse kinematics, retargeting and planning as modular variables and costs in a nonlinear least-squares solver, with CPU, GPU and TPU execution . ## The same geometry, inside learned policies [Action chunking](/manipulation/action-chunking) with ACT predicts 14 joint-space targets for two 6-DoF arms and their grippers , while OpenVLA predicts 7-dimensional single-arm end-effector actions , and Diffusion Policy did consistently better with position than velocity actions . Across 13,000+ real rollouts and 500+ models, delta actions consistently helped, joint space favored stability, and task space favored generalization . GR00T N1 uses embodiment-specific action decoders: in its simulation benchmarks a Panda arm acts in relative end-effector position and rotation, and the GR-1 humanoid in joint positions . NVIDIA says N1.7 shares one relative end-effector action space across robot and human data . Quaternions and Euler angles are discontinuous and hard for networks to learn, while 5D and 6D rotation representations are continuous . Teleoperation runs through the same chain: a GELLO leader copies its target arm's kinematic structure , and retargeting artifacts such as foot sliding reduce the robustness of humanoid tracking policies . ## Treat coordinate frames as an API A Cartesian action must name its frame, units, rotation representation, composition order, and whether it is absolute or relative; a joint action needs joint order, signs, limits and controller semantics. ROS REP 103 makes frames right-handed, with x forward, y left and z up , and REP 105 separates the drifting `odom` frame from the `map` frame, which can jump . Round-trip kinematics tests and versioned URDF and calibration files keep the contract testable. LeRobot calibrates SO-101 leader and follower arms to read the same values in the same pose, so a network trained on one robot works on another . See the [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) and the [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces).

## Configuration space Lozano-Pérez's 1983 reformulation moves planning from the workspace into configuration space. A configuration $q$ is one complete posture, the vector of joint values. The set $\mathcal{C}$ of all of them is 2D for a point robot in the plane and 7-dimensional for a 7-DoF arm . The configuration-space obstacle $\mathcal{C}_{obs}$ holds every configuration where the robot intersects an obstacle; the rest is free space : $$ \mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_{obs} \cup \mathcal{C}_{free}, \qquad \mathcal{C}_{free} = \mathcal{C} \setminus \mathcal{C}_{obs} $$ Shrinking the robot to a point and growing each obstacle by its shape reduces collision checking to point membership. Planning becomes the search for a continuous curve in $\mathcal{C}_{free}$ from $q_{start}$ to $q_{goal}$ . Explicit boundary or solid models of $\mathcal{C}_{obs}$ are difficult to build, though semi-algebraic models for chains and trees can be generated automatically. The basic semi-algebraic mover problem is PSPACE-hard when the number of degrees of freedom is unbounded . Hardness holds for a planar linkage with multiple links and for a multi-arm robot among 3D polyhedra; Canny's roadmap method is singly exponential . Sampling-based methods skip building $\mathcal{C}_{obs}$ by querying a collision checker and validating whole local paths, though closed-chain constraints make sampling difficult . ## Sampling-based planning The probabilistic roadmap (PRM) of Kavraki, Svestka, Latombe, and Overmars samples configurations uniformly, keeps the collision-free ones as nodes and adds extra nodes where a heuristic marks the space as difficult. A local planner links nearby nodes, and queries become graph searches, so one roadmap serves many start-goal pairs . LaValle introduced the rapidly-exploring random tree in Iowa State Computer Science Technical Report 98-11, October 1998 . Each iteration samples a state, finds the nearest vertex under a chosen metric, picks a control input and integrates over a fixed time interval, keeping vertices and edge paths in free space. For dynamics $\dot{x}=f(x,u)$, the Euler step is $$ x_{new} \approx x + f(x,u)\Delta t $$ with starting state $x$ and input $u$; the report recommends a higher-order integrator such as Runge-Kutta . LaValle's 2006 book drops the step size: each sample connects to the nearest point on the tree's swath, the union of its edge paths, splitting an edge when needed . Nearest-neighbor selection gives RRT a Voronoi bias, because frontier vertices own larger Voronoi regions. The report leaves convergence rates open . LaValle and Kuffner's kinodynamic version steers with controls instead of straight lines . Drag the shelf in the figure below and the tree of random safe steps regrows around it to the goal. Kuffner and LaValle's RRT-Connect grows two trees, rooted at the start and the goal . In the six manipulation problems of a 2023 comparison, it had the best overall success rate . Probabilistic completeness means the chance of finding an existing solution approaches one as sampling continues, with no finite-budget guarantee . Karaman and Frazzoli prove it for simplified PRM (sPRM) and geometric RRT on $X=(0,1)^d$, $d\geq2$, assuming a solution with clearance $\delta>0$, uniform independent samples, a fixed sPRM radius, capped RRT steering and straight-line collision tests. A 1-nearest-neighbor sPRM is not probabilistically complete . OMPL 2.0.0, released April 6, 2026, added VAMP as a SIMD backend for planning speeds up to 25 kHz ; VAMP's authors report gains of more than 500x from fine-grained parallelism on 7 to 14 DoF robots . The library implements PRM and RRT, includes benchmarking tools and plugs into external collision checkers and visualizers . ## Optimality: RRT\* Karaman and Frazzoli's 2011 analysis separates feasibility from cost. In an obstacle-free Euclidean example with steering distance at least the domain diameter, RRT's best cost converges almost surely to a suboptimal value. Their PRM result concerns a forest-building version that rejects connections inside a connected component. Fixed-radius sPRM, which allows them, is asymptotically optimal at greater computational cost . RRT\* adds least-cost parent selection and rewiring. A new vertex takes the cheapest collision-free parent among nearby vertices, and neighbors reattach to it only when that lowers their cost. With $n$ vertices, the connection radius is $$ r_n = \min\!\left\{\eta,\; \gamma\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{1/d}\right\}, $$ where $\eta>0$ caps the steering distance and $d\geq2$ is the dimension. Of the paper's two sufficient bounds on $\gamma$, the conservative one is $\gamma>4(\mu(X_{free})/\zeta_d)^{1/d}$, with free-space volume $\mu(X_{free})$ and unit-ball volume $\zeta_d$ . The result assumes a bounded Euclidean domain, uniform independent samples and straight-line connections, which excludes differential constraints. Cost must be positive, monotone under concatenation and at most a constant times path length. The optimum must have weak clearance, deforming continuously into paths with positive clearance, with cost continuous near it in a bounded-variation norm : $$ \mathbb{P}\!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}c_n=c^*\right)=1. $$ Here $c_n$ is the best cost after $n$ iterations, so a finite budget can return a suboptimal path. The non-optimality analysis assumes that optimal paths traverse a set of states of measure zero. Expected processing work is of order $n\log n$, within a constant factor of RRT, though RRT\* makes $O(\log n)$ collision checks per iteration to RRT's one . After a first solution, Informed RRT\* skips routes irrelevant to the query by sampling only the domain's intersection with $$ \hat{X}_f=\left\{x:\lVert x-x_{start}\rVert_2+\lVert x-x_{goal}\rVert_2\leq c_{best}\right\}. $$ This prolate hyperspheroid has the start and goal as foci and the best path length $c_{best}$ as transverse diameter. It contains every state on a strictly improving path, but its states need not be collision-free, so collision checks remain. Over 100 runs per variation with 60 seconds of refinement, it refined faster than RRT\*, and it gains nothing once the set covers the domain . ## Trajectory optimization Trajectory optimization makes the trajectory the decision variable, with smoothness, clearance and task terms in the objective or constraints. Neither the objective nor an initial guess guarantees a collision-free result. CHOMP and TrajOpt both plan from infeasible guesses as well as refine existing trajectories . Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) poses planning as a mixed-integer program with a very tight convex relaxation, so in most cases a cheap rounding suffices for globally optimal trajectories . ### CHOMP: covariant gradient descent CHOMP combines an obstacle cost with an environment-independent prior on trajectory dynamics. In the discrete form, $\xi$ holds the interior waypoints, $K_d$ computes finite differences and $e_d$ accounts for the fixed endpoints : $$ \mathcal U(\xi)=f_{\mathrm{prior}}(\xi)+f_{\mathrm{obs}}(\xi), \qquad f_{\mathrm{prior}}(\xi)=\frac12\sum_{d=1}^{D} w_d\lVert K_d\xi+e_d\rVert^2. $$ The first-derivative term penalizes squared velocity; higher-order terms penalize other dynamics. The obstacle cost integrates a signed-distance penalty over the robot's body, weighted by arc length so that moving faster through a costly region cannot lower it. Covariant descent uses the inverse smoothness metric to spread each gradient step smoothly along the trajectory . On the first six joints of a seven-DoF Barrett WAM, CHOMP solved 99 of 105 problems from 15 endpoint configurations. On LittleDog it ran inside a footstep controller with a separate footstep planner and a ZMP preview controller seeding the trunk. Trajectories were computed before execution because worst-case optimization took about 1.5 times as long as execution . The paper also tests a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo variant and records finite-time local-minimum failures ; the 2013 journal CHOMP uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo against high-cost local minima and for probabilistic completeness, and respects hard trajectory constraints . ### TrajOpt: penalties, trust regions, and collision limits TrajOpt solves a sequence of convex subproblems, with a kinematic objective summing squared displacements between successive waypoints. Nonlinear constraints enter an $\ell_1$ penalty whose coefficients grow in an outer loop as needed; linear constraints are imposed directly. With signed distance $\operatorname{sd}$ positive for separated objects, the collision penalty is $$ \max\!\left(d_{\mathrm{safe}}-\operatorname{sd},\,0\right). $$ It is nonzero inside the safety margin. Pairs out to $d_{\mathrm{check}}>d_{\mathrm{safe}}$ enter the linearized subproblem, including some with zero current penalty. A box trust region bounds each step, expanding when actual improvement matches the local model and shrinking otherwise . Waypoint checks can miss collisions between waypoints, so TrajOpt penalizes a swept volume: the convex hull of endpoint shapes, inflated for rotation. The rotation bound adds $d_{\mathrm{arc}}=r\phi^2/8$ to the safety margin, a correction omitted in experiments because it was well under 1 cm. The swept-volume gradient is not guaranteed accurate in 3D, and the implementation used Bullet with convex hulls of robot meshes and penalized self-collisions only at discrete times . ### What the TrajOpt benchmark measured The 2013 benchmark used four simulated MoveIt scenes with fixed endpoints: 198 seven-DoF PR2 arm problems with 11 timesteps and 96 eighteen-DoF full-body problems with 41. OMPL ran with default parameters and MoveIt's default smoother, and path length was normalized by the shortest path any planner found. Both tables give historical 2013 timings . On the arm, single-initialization TrajOpt solved fewer problems than either OMPL planner and multi-initialization TrajOpt the most. The tested CHOMP implementation came from its authors . The full-body comparison omits CHOMP, for which the authors lacked documentation or data. The introduction gives every planner ten seconds, while the experiments specify three seconds per CHOMP initialization and thirty seconds for full-body OMPL . cuRobo runs many parallel optimizer seeds on GPUs and solves difficult motion generation problems within 50 ms on average, 60x faster than state-of-the-art trajectory optimization . ### Initial guesses and the two-stage pattern CHOMP and TrajOpt both need an initial trajectory and can stall in bad local minima. In CHOMP's tests, straight-line seeds often beat RRT seeds on the objective where collision removal succeeded; in TrajOpt's, multiple initializations changed success rates . Ratliff and colleagues describe PRM and RRT as commonly deployed in two phases: find a feasible path, then remove redundant or jerky motion . Shortcutting, a cheap second stage, repeatedly picks two trajectory points and tries to replace the segment between them with a shorter collision-free one . ## Where this meets the learned stack Motion Policy Networks trained on over 3 million motion planning problems in over 500,000 [environments](/world-models/generative-sim) . A 2026 survey finds that neural motion planners often struggle to generalize to unseen, out-of-distribution planning settings . Deep Reactive Policy replaced AIT\* with cuRobo as its expert planner because GPU acceleration let it scale to 10 million expert trajectories. Its authors report that AIT\* achieved 0% success on all dynamic tasks, and cuRobo fell to 3.00% when the goal was temporarily obstructed . Ariadne, from Carnegie Mellon's Silong Yong, Guanya Shi and colleagues (October 2026, accepted at NeurIPS 2026), trains only on valid states, with no trajectories, and builds a path by following the geometry of the learned state manifold. On DualKUKA, where two 7-DoF arms must avoid obstacles and each other, it averaged 53.3% success across three environments, against 44.7% for RRT, 31.7% for a trajectory-trained Diffuser and 53.2% for PBDMP, which also receives the scene layout. Ariadne learns one planner per scene . Receding-horizon model-predictive control keeps optimization inside the feedback loop ; [reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc) weighs it against learned policies. Diffusion Policy represents a visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process run with receding-horizon control . [Control](/classical/control) and state estimation track the resulting trajectories and locate the robot. ## The runtime handoff contract A deployable planner needs the robot model, current state, collision geometry, allowed contacts, attached objects, joint and timing limits and a controller that can execute the result, and a path checked against a stale scene is unsafe. Time-Optimal Trajectory Generation (TOTG) computes the time-optimal trajectory that exactly follows a differentiable joint-space path within velocity and acceleration bounds , and MoveIt 2 has recommended it for time parameterization since January 2023 . Because TOTG sets no jerk limits, Ruckig, a real-time jerk-limited generator , can smooth its output . The cuRoboV2 authors note that fast planners output physically unexecutable trajectories, and report 99.7% success under a 3 kg payload against 72 to 77% for baselines . The [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) maps these artifacts onto the runtime graph. In hybrid systems a learned component proposes a goal, cost, waypoint or action chunk, and a planner or command gate checks what the model cannot certify. Validators fail too: MoveIt Pro 10.1.0 fixed a shortcut stage that let paths pass through obstacles between collision checks, and a ValidateTrajectory bug that checked the wrong robot configuration and risked passing a colliding trajectory as collision-free .

Pairs out to $d_{\mathrm{check}}>d_{\mathrm{safe}}$ enter the linearized subproblem, including some with zero current penalty. A box trust region bounds each step, expanding when actual improvement matches the local model and shrinking otherwise . Waypoint checks can miss collisions between waypoints, so TrajOpt penalizes a swept volume: the convex hull of endpoint shapes, inflated for rotation. The rotation bound adds $d_{\mathrm{arc}}=r\phi^2/8$ to the safety margin, a correction omitted in experiments because it was well under 1 cm. The swept-volume gradient is not guaranteed accurate in 3D, and the implementation used Bullet with convex hulls of robot meshes and penalized self-collisions only at discrete times . ### What the TrajOpt benchmark measured The 2013 benchmark used four simulated MoveIt scenes with fixed endpoints: 198 seven-DoF PR2 arm problems with 11 timesteps and 96 eighteen-DoF full-body problems with 41. OMPL ran with default parameters and MoveIt's default smoother, and path length was normalized by the shortest path any planner found. Both tables give historical 2013 timings . On the arm, single-initialization TrajOpt solved fewer problems than either OMPL planner and multi-initialization TrajOpt the most. The tested CHOMP implementation came from its authors . The full-body comparison omits CHOMP, for which the authors lacked documentation or data. The introduction gives every planner ten seconds, while the experiments specify three seconds per CHOMP initialization and thirty seconds for full-body OMPL . The 2014 journal extension also studies statically stable Atlas walking and curvature-constrained needle trajectories, which are separate experiments from the 2013 tables above . cuRobo runs many parallel optimizer seeds on GPUs and solves difficult motion generation problems within 50 ms on average, 60x faster than state-of-the-art trajectory optimization . An industrial integration extends cuRobo to a robot on a gantry and builds collision environments from CAD digital twins, illustrating the extra modeling needed outside fixed-base benchmarks . ### Initial guesses and the two-stage pattern CHOMP and TrajOpt both need an initial trajectory and can stall in bad local minima. In CHOMP's tests, straight-line seeds often beat RRT seeds on the objective where collision removal succeeded; in TrajOpt's, multiple initializations changed success rates . Ratliff and colleagues describe PRM and RRT as commonly deployed in two phases: find a feasible path, then remove redundant or jerky motion . Shortcutting, a cheap second stage, repeatedly picks two trajectory points and tries to replace the segment between them with a shorter collision-free one . MR-POP uses a parallel GPU sampling planner to produce feasible multi-robot trajectories that can seed a trajectory optimizer . ## Where this meets the learned stack Motion Policy Networks trained on over 3 million motion planning problems in over 500,000 [environments](/world-models/generative-sim) . A 2026 survey finds that neural motion planners often struggle to generalize to unseen, out-of-distribution planning settings . Neural Motion Planning distills expert plans from simulated clutter into a reactive policy, then applies lightweight optimization when deploying the policy on a real arm . Deep Reactive Policy replaced AIT\* with cuRobo as its expert planner because GPU acceleration let it scale to 10 million expert trajectories. Its authors report that AIT\* achieved 0% success on all dynamic tasks, and cuRobo fell to 3.00% when the goal was temporarily obstructed . Ariadne, from Carnegie Mellon's Silong Yong, Guanya Shi and colleagues (October 2026, accepted at NeurIPS 2026), trains only on valid states, with no trajectories, and builds a path by following the geometry of the learned state manifold. On DualKUKA, where two 7-DoF arms must avoid obstacles and each other, it averaged 53.3% success across three environments, against 44.7% for RRT, 31.7% for a trajectory-trained Diffuser and 53.2% for PBDMP, which also receives the scene layout. Ariadne learns one planner per scene . Receding-horizon model-predictive control keeps optimization inside the feedback loop ; [reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc) weighs it against learned policies. Diffusion Policy represents a visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process run with receding-horizon control . [Control](/classical/control) and state estimation track the resulting trajectories and locate the robot. ## The runtime handoff contract A deployable planner needs the robot model, current state, collision geometry, allowed contacts, attached objects, joint and timing limits and a controller that can execute the result, and a path checked against a stale scene is unsafe. Time-Optimal Trajectory Generation (TOTG) computes the time-optimal trajectory that exactly follows a differentiable joint-space path within velocity and acceleration bounds , and MoveIt 2 has recommended it for time parameterization since January 2023 . Because TOTG sets no jerk limits, Ruckig, a real-time jerk-limited generator , can smooth its output . The cuRoboV2 authors note that fast planners output physically unexecutable trajectories, and report 99.7% success under a 3 kg payload against 72 to 77% for baselines . The [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) maps these artifacts onto the runtime graph. In hybrid systems a learned component proposes a goal, cost, waypoint or action chunk, and a planner or command gate checks what the model cannot certify. Validators fail too: MoveIt Pro 10.1.0 fixed a shortcut stage that let paths pass through obstacles between collision checks, and a ValidateTrajectory bug that checked the wrong robot configuration and risked passing a colliding trajectory as collision-free .
