Perception for manipulation turns camera and depth data into object poses in the robot's own frame, through calibration, depth sensing, detection, segmentation and pose estimation, and [grasp planning](/classical/grasp-planning) computes grasps against those poses. DOPE's pose network was accurate enough for a real robot to grasp known household objects in clutter . ## An illustrative positioning budget Try the transparent bottle under "Adjust more": the depth term then dominates the budget. The instrument combines authored hand-eye, depth and pose magnitudes by root-sum-of-squares, with depth fixed at a 0.5 m standoff and the hand-eye term growing with working distance up to 1.5 m. Its 15 mm and 30 mm bands are teaching thresholds: a 90 mm opening around a 60 mm part leaves $(90-60)/2=15$ mm per side, and one reported assembly task had only 0.5 mm contact clearance .
## Calibration: what a pixel means A camera maps a 3D point onto a 2D sensor, and its intrinsics describe that mapping: focal length in pixels on each axis, the principal point and lens distortion. Zhang's 2000 method shows the camera a planar target at several unmeasured orientations. It models radial distortion and gives a closed-form solution followed by maximum-likelihood nonlinear refinement. Zhang contrasts it with classical techniques that need expensive equipment such as two or three orthogonal planes . ### Hand-eye calibration: what a pixel means to the robot Extrinsics place the camera relative to something else. Hand-eye calibration finds the flange-to-camera transform for a wrist camera, or base-to-camera for a fixed one. Shiu and Ahmad cast it as $AX = XB$, where $A$ is a robot motion, $B$ the camera's observed motion of a static target and $X$ the unknown transform . Tsai and Lenz gave an efficient closed-form technique that solves rotation first, then translation . Park and Martin derived closed-form exact and least-squares solutions with Lie theory . OpenCV's hand-eye calibration defaults to the Tsai and Lenz method, needs at least two motions with non-parallel rotation axes, so three poses, and strongly recommends many more . Tsai and Lenz's error analysis shows the lever arm: a 3 mrad rotation error at a 5 in camera-to-target distance gives a 15 mil translation error . The instrument's hand-eye term is a ray-to-plane offset at separation $d$ for a ray inclined by $\theta$ to the plane's normal, about 1.7 mm at 10 cm and 17 mm at 1 m for one degree: $$ e_\theta(d) = d \, \tan \theta $$ ## Depth sensing: what fails, and on what Stereo triangulates features matched between two images, so a featureless surface gives it nothing to match. Intel's RGBD depth cameras add an active texture projector to make matching unambiguous . The March 2026 RealSense D400 datasheet lists ±2% Z-accuracy up to 2 m for D410/D415 and D43x over an 80% region of interest at HD resolution. Accuracy compares valid pixels with ground truth over 80% of the depth field of view, and factory KPIs reflect typical conditions; these models are tested on a texture-less white target at the default 150 mW laser power and auto exposure . RealSense's D415/D435 tuning guide says D400 depth error scales with the square of distance. It advises moving closer while staying outside the minimum operating distance, MinZ. It describes resolution and range trade-offs when changing MinZ, and notes that focus and differing left and right views limit very-near matching . Learned models now estimate depth from images, alone or with a sparse sensor: Depth Pro predicts metric monocular depth without camera intrinsics, a 2.25-megapixel map in 0.3 seconds on a standard GPU . For industrial 3D scanning, the PhoXi 3D Scanner L page lists 0.200 mm calibration accuracy and 0.190 mm temporal noise (both 1 σ), an 870 to 2150 mm scanning range and 250 to 2750 ms scanning time. These are separate specification fields for one model . Time of flight casts its own modulated near-infrared light and measures its round trip per pixel. Multi-path interference lets one pixel integrate light that arrived by several routes. The Azure Kinect DK documentation lists five causes of invalid depth: outside the IR illumination mask, saturated IR signal, low IR signal, filter outlier and multi-path interference. Invalid pixels carry depth zero. Ambiguous depth arises when light reflects from one wall onto another in a corner, and where foreground and background mix at object edges. Fast motion can increase edge invalidation . Microsoft announced the end of Azure Kinect DK production in August 2023, and support for its Sensor SDK ended in August 2024 . ### The failure taxonomy that decides how a cell is built - ClearGrasp starts from the observation that transparent objects "often appear as noisy or distorted approximations of the surfaces that lie behind them". It infers surface normals, transparent-surface masks and occlusion boundaries, then replaces the returned depth . - Specular reflections can saturate D400 images, and the D400f column says "Saturation mitigated" . Azure Kinect invalidates saturated IR pixels . - Dark surfaces and low light weaken the signal. Azure Kinect invalidates a pixel whose IR signal is too weak to generate depth . RealSense ties D4xx depth quality to the input images and warns of grainy low-light images, underexposure and overexposure. For its projected-pattern example, reducing background light with the projector on can raise the pattern's signal-to-noise ratio . - RealSense names fences and wire grids as scenes where left-right correspondence can become ambiguous. Its D4 processor compares the best and second-best match scores, and raising DSSecondPeakThreshold rejects more matches as zero depth . - Azure Kinect notes that a surface invalidated by multi-path from one camera view can reappear from another . The 2% figure is measured on a texture-less white target with the projector at default power , and the PhoXi page publishes no target condition for its 0.200 mm figure . Accuracy for transparent or specular surfaces is not disclosed in either datasheet. Depth yields a point cloud, an unordered set that a network must process without depending on input order. PointNet uses a shared per-point encoder and a symmetric pooling function . PointNet++ applies PointNet within radius neighbourhoods around sampled centroids, in coordinates relative to each centroid, building local features at growing scales. Density-adaptive variants combine scales where small neighbourhoods hold too few samples . ## Detection: from pixels to candidate objects Classical detectors return boxes over a class list fixed at training time. Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN with a branch that predicts an object mask in parallel with box recognition . Open-vocabulary detection removes the fixed list. Grounding DINO adds language-vision fusion to the DINO detector's feature enhancer, query selection and decoder and accepts category names or referring expressions. It performs weakly on referring expressions without REC training data. Its Swin-L model reports 52.5 AP on COCO 2017 validation after pretraining on O365, OpenImage and GoldG without COCO training images . DINOv2 learns image and patch features by self-supervised pretraining on the curated LVD-142M dataset. Its transfer evaluations freeze the encoder and train linear heads for classification and segmentation, and linear or DPT heads for depth . ## Segmentation: the grounding layer A box around a mug also contains the table behind it, so a grasp planner needs the surface region that per-pixel labelling provides. Segment Anything (SAM, 2023) makes segmentation promptable; its default ViT-H model was trained on SA-1B, reported as 1.1 billion automatically generated masks on 11 million images. Point, box and mask prompts condition the decoder, and an ambiguous point can return several candidate masks for a part or a whole object. Fine structures and boundaries remain failure cases, and the heavy image encoder prevents overall real-time performance . SAM 2 extends prompting to video with a streaming memory of earlier predictions and prompted frames. Objects are inferred independently, and failures persist after shot changes or long occlusions, in crowded scenes and on thin, fast-moving details . Grounded SAM feeds Grounding DINO's open-set boxes to SAM , and CNOS segments unseen objects by matching DINOv2 descriptors of SAM proposals against references built from CAD models . Promptable segmentation supplies object masks to MOKA and ReKep, two [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) with different perception stacks. MOKA proposes marked candidate points from GroundedSAM masks, then prompts a pretrained VLM to select grasp, function and target keypoints, waypoint regions and motion attributes. Calibrated depth lifts the points into the robot frame, and a separate grasp sampler and motion pipeline produce actions; the prompted method trains no robot policy . ReKep proposes semantic keypoints from DINOv2 features within SAM masks and calibrated RGB-D geometry. A large vision-language model writes Python sub-goal and path constraints from a marked image and an instruction, and a solver repeatedly plans end-effector motion from tracked keypoints. The solver penalizes constraint violations without guaranteeing physical feasibility, and rigidity assumptions and tracking failures remain limitations. Some evaluations use human annotations or disable tracking . RoboPoint instruction-tunes a VLM to predict image-space affordance points from synthetic object and free-space data mixed with real-image VQA and LVIS detection data. It needs no external detector at test time, though its robot pipeline adds depth, an end-effector offset and a motion planner . Dense Object Nets learns a descriptor for each RGB pixel, self-supervised by matches from static RGB-D reconstructions, and demonstrates correspondence across viewpoints and moderately deformable configurations. Class-consistent training generalizes across sufficiently similar hats, shoes and mugs, while instance-specific training distinguishes objects; for grasping, the gripper's 6-DoF orientation needs further information . ## 6-DoF pose estimation, and how to read a claim about it Pose estimation turns a mask into a rigid body with a position and orientation, and methods divide by what they assume about the object. Instance-level methods train on specific objects: PoseCNN localizes each object's centre, predicts its distance and regresses a rotation quaternion, with a loss that handles symmetric objects . DOPE, trained only on synthetic domain-randomized and photorealistic data, performs competitively with a network trained on real and synthetic data . Category-level methods such as NOCS estimate the pose and size of unseen instances in known categories with no exact CAD model at training or test time . Novel-object methods drop per-object training. MegaPose uses render-and-compare against a CAD model supplied at test time , and FoundationPose works from a CAD model or a few reference images and reports results comparable to instance-level methods . To read a pose result, check its evaluation protocol. Hinterstoisser and colleagues evaluate a model $\mathcal M$ with ground-truth pose $(R,T)$ and estimate $(\tilde R,\tilde T)$ by averaging distances between corresponding transformed model points : $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx+T)-(\tilde R x+\tilde T) \rVert $$ An estimate is correct when $m \leq k_m d$, where $d$ is the model's diameter and $k_m$ a chosen coefficient; their LINEMOD evaluation uses $k_m=0.1$ . For the symmetry-aware pose error, each ground-truth-transformed point is matched to its nearest estimated-pose point before averaging : $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x_1 \in \mathcal M} \min_{x_2 \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx_1+T)-(\tilde R x_2+\tilde T) \rVert $$ They apply this rule to objects that are ambiguous, or look ambiguous from some views, naming "cup", "bowl", "box" and "glue" . The BOP Challenge 2023 report scores 6-DoF localization differently: each dataset score averages the VSD, MSSD and MSPD recalls, each over several thresholds with a strict test $e < \theta_e$, and $AR_C$ averages seven core datasets (LM-O, T-LESS, ITODD, HB, YCB-V, TUD-L, IC-BIN) on a 0 to 100 scale. Seen and unseen tracks share the method, with object identities and instance counts supplied at test time, and the 2D-detection $AP_C$ averages over objects first . From 2017 to 2023, seen-object accuracy rose from 56.9 to 85.6 $AR_C$, a relative gain of over 50 percent. The endpoints are Vidal's point-pair-feature method with ICP and no training images, and GPose2023 with object-specific networks trained on PBR and real images . For unseen objects, GenFlow-MultiHypo16 led 2023's Task 4 with 67.4 $AR_C$, against 69.8 for the best 2020 seen-object entry, CosyPose, and the report calls these comparable across distinct tracks; average image times were 34.58 and 13.74 seconds on unmatched hardware. Task 4 still supplies mesh models for onboarding, capped at 5 minutes per object on one GPU with no real images of the objects, and GenFlow fails under heavy occlusion . In the BOP 2024 report, the best unseen-object method, FreeZeV2.1, is 22% more accurate on BOP-Classic-Core than GenFlow and 4% behind GPose2023, but takes 24.9 against 2.7 seconds per image, and the report names 2D detection as the main bottleneck for unseen objects . ## Visual servoing: image-based and position-based control Visual servoing uses vision inside the control loop, and Hutchinson, Hager and Corke's 1996 tutorial divides such systems into position-based and image-based classes . Espiau, Chaumette and Rives's 1992 paper applies a task-function framework to image-based control, with a task function designed for regulation that need not be the raw feature difference. Its interaction matrix relates feature rates to the camera's translational and rotational velocity in the camera frame. Convergence depends on task and model conditions, and neglecting target motion can leave a tracking error . For a fixed goal and motionless target, Chaumette and Hutchinson's Part I writes $\dot{s} = L_s v_c$, with $v_c$ the camera's six-component spatial velocity. Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) uses image features, and position-based visual servoing (PBVS) uses estimated pose. The IBVS point-feature interaction matrix still uses depth and camera intrinsics, estimated from current depths or depths at the desired pose . Redundant-feature IBVS is locally asymptotically stable when the interaction matrices have full rank and the estimated pseudoinverse times the true matrix meets a positivity condition; coarse estimates can change the camera path, while poor ones can make the system unstable. Large displacements can meet local minima or singularities, PBVS points can leave the field of view, and in PBVS pose-estimation errors affect final accuracy . Part II (2007) adds switching and planning methods that address visibility, occlusions and joint limits, for eye-in-hand and eye-to-hand systems . Bateux and colleagues fine-tuned a CNN to estimate the relative pose between current and desired images and kept a pose-based control law . Learned servoing can also aim the camera. EyeRobot 2.0, from Ken Goldberg (UC Berkeley) and colleagues (October 2026), swivels the two eye viewpoints of a single stereo camera to fixate a 3D point, with a gaze-servoing policy and a fixation selector both trained with RL on real data. It beat passive stereo by 40% in real trials and, when a grasped object hid the wrist views, more than doubled the success of policies that had them, 48% against 22% . ## Separate model error from geometric error Hand-eye accuracy depends on noise and motion range, so Enebuse and colleagues advise accounting for both when benchmarking or calibrating . A detector can keep stable image coordinates while the robot misses because the camera transform drifted, so each stage is checked in its own output first. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) defines the checks to rerun after a camera remount, and the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) shows where images, transforms and timestamps meet at runtime. ## What the end-to-end models replaced End-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) policies absorb the explicit pipeline into weights. Gemini Robotics is a VLA model that controls robots directly, built on an embodied-reasoning model that can detect objects, point, and predict trajectories, grasps and 3D bounding boxes . Such a policy needs no detector class or CAD model for a new object, and it has no hand-eye residual to re-solve when it misses a grasp by 8 mm. Some frontier systems keep geometric intermediates explicit, as the [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) did while a learned model produced the geometry: MolmoAct encodes observations into depth-aware perception tokens and generates editable trajectory traces before predicting low-level actions .

PointNet++ applies PointNet within radius neighbourhoods around sampled centroids, in coordinates relative to each centroid, building local features at growing scales. Density-adaptive variants combine scales where small neighbourhoods hold too few samples . ## Detection: from pixels to candidate objects Classical detectors return boxes over a class list fixed at training time. Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN with a branch that predicts an object mask in parallel with box recognition . Open-vocabulary detection removes the fixed list. OWLv2 scales open-vocabulary detection through self-training: an existing detector supplies pseudo-boxes for web image-text pairs, expanding training beyond human box annotations . Grounding DINO adds language-vision fusion to the DINO detector's feature enhancer, query selection and decoder and accepts category names or referring expressions. It performs weakly on referring expressions without REC training data. Its Swin-L model reports 52.5 AP on COCO 2017 validation after pretraining on O365, OpenImage and GoldG without COCO training images . Grounding DINO 1.5 separates a larger Pro model from an Edge variant designed for speed, reducing feature scales in the latter . DINOv2 learns image and patch features by self-supervised pretraining on the curated LVD-142M dataset. Its transfer evaluations freeze the encoder and train linear heads for classification and segmentation, and linear or DPT heads for depth . DINOv3 adds Gram anchoring to preserve the quality of dense features during long self-supervised training . ## Segmentation: the grounding layer A box around a mug also contains the table behind it, so a grasp planner needs the surface region that per-pixel labelling provides. Segment Anything (SAM, 2023) makes segmentation promptable; its default ViT-H model was trained on SA-1B, reported as 1.1 billion automatically generated masks on 11 million images. Point, box and mask prompts condition the decoder, and an ambiguous point can return several candidate masks for a part or a whole object. Fine structures and boundaries remain failure cases, and the heavy image encoder prevents overall real-time performance . SAM 2 extends prompting to video with a streaming memory of earlier predictions and prompted frames. Objects are inferred independently, and failures persist after shot changes or long occlusions, in crowded scenes and on thin, fast-moving details . SAM 3 accepts concept prompts such as a noun phrase or an example image and combines a detector with a memory-based tracker to segment matching instances . Grounded SAM feeds Grounding DINO's open-set boxes to SAM , and CNOS segments unseen objects by matching DINOv2 descriptors of SAM proposals against references built from CAD models . Promptable segmentation supplies object masks to MOKA and ReKep, two [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) with different perception stacks. MOKA proposes marked candidate points from GroundedSAM masks, then prompts a pretrained VLM to select grasp, function and target keypoints, waypoint regions and motion attributes. Calibrated depth lifts the points into the robot frame, and a separate grasp sampler and motion pipeline produce actions; the prompted method trains no robot policy . ReKep proposes semantic keypoints from DINOv2 features within SAM masks and calibrated RGB-D geometry. A large vision-language model writes Python sub-goal and path constraints from a marked image and an instruction, and a solver repeatedly plans end-effector motion from tracked keypoints. The solver penalizes constraint violations without guaranteeing physical feasibility, and rigidity assumptions and tracking failures remain limitations. Some evaluations use human annotations or disable tracking . RoboPoint instruction-tunes a VLM to predict image-space affordance points from synthetic object and free-space data mixed with real-image VQA and LVIS detection data. It needs no external detector at test time, though its robot pipeline adds depth, an end-effector offset and a motion planner . Dense Object Nets learns a descriptor for each RGB pixel, self-supervised by matches from static RGB-D reconstructions, and demonstrates correspondence across viewpoints and moderately deformable configurations. Class-consistent training generalizes across sufficiently similar hats, shoes and mugs, while instance-specific training distinguishes objects; for grasping, the gripper's 6-DoF orientation needs further information . ## 6-DoF pose estimation, and how to read a claim about it Pose estimation turns a mask into a rigid body with a position and orientation, and methods divide by what they assume about the object. Instance-level methods train on specific objects: PoseCNN localizes each object's centre, predicts its distance and regresses a rotation quaternion, with a loss that handles symmetric objects . DOPE, trained only on synthetic domain-randomized and photorealistic data, performs competitively with a network trained on real and synthetic data . Category-level methods such as NOCS estimate the pose and size of unseen instances in known categories with no exact CAD model at training or test time . Novel-object methods drop per-object training. SAM-6D first proposes instance masks with SAM, then estimates pose through partial-to-partial point matching against an object model . MegaPose uses render-and-compare against a CAD model supplied at test time , and FoundationPose works from a CAD model or a few reference images and reports results comparable to instance-level methods . Any6D uses one RGB-D anchor view to estimate an unfamiliar object's pose and size through render-and-compare refinement, without requiring its CAD model . SAM 3D goes further and infers object geometry, texture and layout from a single image; those generated surfaces include geometry that the camera did not observe . To read a pose result, check its evaluation protocol. Hinterstoisser and colleagues evaluate a model $\mathcal M$ with ground-truth pose $(R,T)$ and estimate $(\tilde R,\tilde T)$ by averaging distances between corresponding transformed model points : $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx+T)-(\tilde R x+\tilde T) \rVert $$ An estimate is correct when $m \leq k_m d$, where $d$ is the model's diameter and $k_m$ a chosen coefficient; their LINEMOD evaluation uses $k_m=0.1$ . For the symmetry-aware pose error, each ground-truth-transformed point is matched to its nearest estimated-pose point before averaging : $$ m = \operatorname{avg}_{x_1 \in \mathcal M} \min_{x_2 \in \mathcal M} \lVert (Rx_1+T)-(\tilde R x_2+\tilde T) \rVert $$ They apply this rule to objects that are ambiguous, or look ambiguous from some views, naming "cup", "bowl", "box" and "glue" . CosyPose handles symmetries while matching object-pose hypotheses across images and jointly refining camera and object poses through object-level bundle adjustment . The BOP Challenge 2020 evaluated 6D pose methods on RGB-D data and supplied physically based synthetic training images, making the training-data allowance part of the comparison . The BOP Challenge 2023 report scores 6-DoF localization differently: each dataset score averages the VSD, MSSD and MSPD recalls, each over several thresholds with a strict test $e < \theta_e$, and $AR_C$ averages seven core datasets (LM-O, T-LESS, ITODD, HB, YCB-V, TUD-L, IC-BIN) on a 0 to 100 scale. Seen and unseen tracks share the method, with object identities and instance counts supplied at test time, and the 2D-detection $AP_C$ averages over objects first . From 2017 to 2023, seen-object accuracy rose from 56.9 to 85.6 $AR_C$, a relative gain of over 50 percent. The endpoints are Vidal's point-pair-feature method with ICP and no training images, and GPose2023 with object-specific networks trained on PBR and real images . For unseen objects, GenFlow-MultiHypo16 led 2023's Task 4 with 67.4 $AR_C$, against 69.8 for the best 2020 seen-object entry, CosyPose, and the report calls these comparable across distinct tracks; average image times were 34.58 and 13.74 seconds on unmatched hardware. Task 4 still supplies mesh models for onboarding, capped at 5 minutes per object on one GPU with no real images of the objects, and GenFlow fails under heavy occlusion . In the BOP 2024 report, the best unseen-object method, FreeZeV2.1, is 22% more accurate on BOP-Classic-Core than GenFlow and 4% behind GPose2023, but takes 24.9 against 2.7 seconds per image, and the report names 2D detection as the main bottleneck for unseen objects . ## Visual servoing: image-based and position-based control Visual servoing uses vision inside the control loop, and Hutchinson, Hager and Corke's 1996 tutorial divides such systems into position-based and image-based classes . Espiau, Chaumette and Rives's 1992 paper applies a task-function framework to image-based control, with a task function designed for regulation that need not be the raw feature difference. Its interaction matrix relates feature rates to the camera's translational and rotational velocity in the camera frame. Convergence depends on task and model conditions, and neglecting target motion can leave a tracking error . For a fixed goal and motionless target, Chaumette and Hutchinson's Part I writes $\dot{s} = L_s v_c$, with $v_c$ the camera's six-component spatial velocity. Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) uses image features, and position-based visual servoing (PBVS) uses estimated pose. The IBVS point-feature interaction matrix still uses depth and camera intrinsics, estimated from current depths or depths at the desired pose . Redundant-feature IBVS is locally asymptotically stable when the interaction matrices have full rank and the estimated pseudoinverse times the true matrix meets a positivity condition; coarse estimates can change the camera path, while poor ones can make the system unstable. Large displacements can meet local minima or singularities, PBVS points can leave the field of view, and in PBVS pose-estimation errors affect final accuracy . Part II (2007) adds switching and planning methods that address visibility, occlusions and joint limits, for eye-in-hand and eye-to-hand systems . Bateux and colleagues fine-tuned a CNN to estimate the relative pose between current and desired images and kept a pose-based control law . Learned servoing can also aim the camera. EyeRobot 2.0, from Ken Goldberg (UC Berkeley) and colleagues (October 2026), swivels the two eye viewpoints of a single stereo camera to fixate a 3D point, with a gaze-servoing policy and a fixation selector both trained with RL on real data. It beat passive stereo by 40% in real trials and, when a grasped object hid the wrist views, more than doubled the success of policies that had them, 48% against 22% . ## Separate model error from geometric error Hand-eye accuracy depends on noise and motion range, so Enebuse and colleagues advise accounting for both when benchmarking or calibrating . A detector can keep stable image coordinates while the robot misses because the camera transform drifted, so each stage is checked in its own output first. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) defines the checks to rerun after a camera remount, and the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) shows where images, transforms and timestamps meet at runtime. ## What the end-to-end models replaced End-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) policies absorb the explicit pipeline into weights. Gemini Robotics is a VLA model that controls robots directly, built on an embodied-reasoning model that can detect objects, point, and predict trajectories, grasps and 3D bounding boxes . Such a policy needs no detector class or CAD model for a new object, and it has no hand-eye residual to re-solve when it misses a grasp by 8 mm. Some frontier systems keep geometric intermediates explicit, as the [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) did while a learned model produced the geometry: MolmoAct encodes observations into depth-aware perception tokens and generates editable trajectory traces before predicting low-level actions .

ROS 2 is the second generation of the Robot Operating System, a modular framework of freely available robot software, rebuilt because ROS 1 lacked production-grade features <Cite id="ros2-science-robotics-2022" />. Lyrical Luth, the current long-term-support release, shipped on 22 May 2026 and is supported until May 2031 <Cite id="ros2-lyrical-2026" /> <Cite id="ros2-distributions-2026" />.

<Image id="pr2-maker-faire-2011" />

<SelfCheck
  prompt="A fetch task takes 30 seconds, reports progress and may need cancelling. Which ROS 2 interface fits?"
  options={[
    {
      value: 'topic',
      label: 'Publish the request repeatedly on a topic',
      why: 'Topics fit continuous streams. This task needs acceptance, feedback, completion and cancellation semantics.'
    },
    {
      value: 'service',
      label: 'Block on a service call until it finishes',
      why: 'Services are intended for short request-response operations. A long task needs feedback and preemption without holding a synchronous request open.'
    },
    {
      value: 'action',
      label: 'Use a ROS action: goal, feedback, result and cancellation',
      why: 'Actions model long-running, preemptible work. The client can observe progress and cancel while the server owns execution.'
    }
  ]}
  answer="action"
  takeaway="Topics stream, services answer short requests, and actions manage long-running goals with feedback and cancellation."
/>

## The graph: nodes and typed interfaces

A node is one participant, such as a camera driver, policy server or controller bridge. Nodes talk through topics for continuous streams, services for short request-response calls, and actions for long-running goals with feedback, cancellation and a result <Cite id="ros2-interfaces-2026" />. A `geometry_msgs/PoseStamped` carries the timestamp and frame a bare array lacks, and REP 103 puts ROS on SI units <Cite id="rep-103-2010" />.

<Ros2Interfaces className="my-6" />

## QoS is part of the model input

ROS 2 inherits Quality of Service (QoS) from DDS <Cite id="ros2-dds-design-2014" />. The default profile keeps the last 10 messages and delivers reliably, while the sensor-data profile uses best effort and a smaller queue, because timely readings matter more than complete ones; lifespan silently drops messages older than its limit, and endpoints with incompatible policies never connect <Cite id="ros2-qos-2026" />.

End-to-end latency depends strongly on the DDS implementation, and ROS 2 can add 50% over raw DDS <Cite id="ros2-latency-2021" />. Since Kilted Kaiju (May 2025), Zenoh's `rmw_zenoh_cpp` is a Tier 1 middleware <Cite id="ros2-kilted-2025" />.

<QosQueueAge className="my-6" />

## Time and synchronization

Camera, depth, joint and force streams arrive at different rates, so inputs need acquisition and arrival timestamps. MCAP records a publish time and a log time for every message <Cite id="mcap-spec-2026" />.

Logging source, receipt and inference-completion times splits latency into sensing, transport, model execution and command delivery; ros2_tracing does it at an average overhead of 0.0033 ms per message <Cite id="ros2-tracing-2022" />. With `use_sim_time` set, ROS time follows the latest `/clock` message <Cite id="ros2-clock-design" />, so nodes that mix it with wall time see spurious timeouts. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers spatial and temporal alignment.

## tf2: the coordinate-frame graph

tf2 keeps a time-buffered tree of coordinate frames and transforms data between any two frames at any time <Cite id="tf2-docs-2026" />. A lookup at an image timestamp can wait for the transform; the tf2 tutorial raises an exception only if it is still missing after a 50 ms timeout <Cite id="tf2-time-tutorial-2026" />.

REP 105 defines `odom` as a drifting short-term reference and `map` as a frame whose poses can jump <Cite id="rep-105-2010" />, and camera optical frames take an `_optical` suffix and a different axis convention <Cite id="rep-103-2010" />. A policy trained on base-frame <Term id="end-effector">end-effector</Term> deltas cannot be sent tool-frame deltas in the same layout; *Modern Robotics* covers the geometry <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />.

## URDF, robot state and MoveIt

URDF, the most common robot-description format <Cite id="urdf-dataset-2023" />, lists links, joints, geometry and limits, and `robot_state_publisher` combines it with joint states to publish the frame tree. MoveIt 2's Planning Scene combines robot state, model and world geometry for kinematics, constraint and collision checks <Cite id="moveit-planning-scene-2026" />, so a learned policy can use it to plan or check collision-free motion.

## rosbag2 is the experiment record

rosbag2 records timestamped messages for replay, in MCAP by default since Iron Irwini <Cite id="ros2-iron-mcap-2023" />, and since Kilted it can replay in publication order instead of receipt order <Cite id="ros2-kilted-2025" />. Learning pipelines convert bags to episode formats such as RLDS <Cite id="rlds-2021" />.

## A production policy layout

A learned-policy graph can separate drivers, state assembly, a policy server, a command gate, a controller bridge and a supervisor. The supervisor can drive ROS 2 managed nodes, which leave a primary state only on an external request or an error <Cite id="ros2-lifecycle-design-2015" />. Inference stays outside the hard real-time loop unless its worst case fits, and ROS 2's real-time guidance keeps page faults, dynamic allocation and blocking synchronization out of that path <Cite id="ros2-realtime-docs-2026" />. Lyrical's EventsCBGExecutor cuts executor CPU overhead, but its event queue is unbounded <Cite id="ros2-executors-2026" />.

<Ros2PolicyLayout className="my-6" />

Lyrical's `rosidl::Buffer` lets a `uint8[]` field live in GPU memory without changing the .msg file <Cite id="ros2-buffer-backends-2026" />. NVIDIA deprecated its NITROS transport on 21 September 2026 in its favor, with a CUDA backend <Cite id="isaac-ros-nitros-2026" />, because host round-trips add latency and use CPU and memory bandwidth <Cite id="isaac-ros-rosidl-buffer-2026" />.

## Navigation uses the same architecture

Nav2 uses a behavior tree to orchestrate planner, controller and recovery servers <Cite id="nav2-2020" />. Costmap 2D accepts sensor-processing plugins for AI outputs and semantic information <Cite id="nav2-costmap-2d-2026" />, so a learned local controller can reuse a classical one's costmap, goal interface, test harness and fallback. The [scene-representation module](/classical/scene-representation) explains the map choices.

<Image id="clearpath-jackal-ugv-2020" />

## Common integration failures

Frequent failures include a policy deployed in a different frame from its training data, a queue that hides latency, two unarbitrated command publishers, bags without transforms, wall-time assumptions under `/clock`, and one node holding drivers, inference and hardware commands. DDS implementations interoperate only in limited circumstances, so a system should use one ROS version and one RMW implementation <Cite id="ros2-middleware-vendors-2026" />. Nodes are not guaranteed to communicate across distributions; Jazzy is supported until May 2029 and Humble until May 2027 <Cite id="ros2-distributions-2026" />. ROS 1 ended when Noetic reached end of life in May 2025 <Cite id="noetic-eol-2025" />.

## Common integration failures

Frequent failures include a policy deployed in a different frame from its training data, a queue that hides latency, two unarbitrated command publishers, bags without transforms, wall-time assumptions under `/clock`, and one node holding drivers, inference and hardware commands. DDS implementations interoperate only in limited circumstances, so a system should use one ROS version and one RMW implementation <Cite id="ros2-middleware-vendors-2026" />. Nodes are not guaranteed to communicate across distributions; Jazzy is supported until May 2029 and Humble until May 2027 <Cite id="ros2-distributions-2026" />. Scene representation is how a robot stores what it knows about its surroundings so that planners, controllers and other consumers can query it <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Representations range from point clouds and occupancy grids to signed-distance fields, meshes and neural fields such as radiance fields and Gaussian splats <Cite id="cadena-2016" /><Cite id="neural-fields-survey-2024" />.

<Image id="ouster-lidar-point-cloud-sf" />

## The ladder, and what each rung can answer

Three queries separate the rungs: whether a cell is free for a planner, which way a surface faces for a contact solver, and what the scene looks like from a viewpoint the sensor never occupied. Cadena and colleagues judge representations by storage size, construction cost and usefulness for the task <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

<SceneRepresentationLadder className="my-6" />

### Point clouds and occupancy grids

A <Term id="point-cloud">point cloud</Term> is an unordered set of 3D points, and PointNet requires invariance to the order in which they arrive <Cite id="pointnet-2017" />. A region without points is either empty or unobserved, and the store cannot say which.

Moravec and Elfes projected wide-angle sonar readings from different sensors and robot positions onto a 2D <Term id="occupancy-grid">occupancy grid</Term>. Each reading marked a probably empty beam interior and an uncertain reflecting point near the measured range, and overlapping readings refined these constraints. Zero represented unknown occupancy, and negative and positive values probably empty and probably occupied cells <Cite id="moravec-elfes-1985" />. OctoMap carries the three states into 3D in a compressed octree <Cite id="octomap-2013" />. Step through the figure below to see one mug stored four ways.

<ExplainerFigure id="mug" />

### Signed-distance fields

Curless and Levoy fuse range images into a cumulative weighted <Term id="signed-distance-field">signed distance function</Term> and recover the surface at its zero crossing, truncating distance ramps and weights near observed points. Their hole-filling construction marks empty space with negative $D_{min}$ and unseen space with positive $D_{max}$, both at zero weight <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />. KinectFusion uses the opposite sign: positive toward visible free space and negative on the non-visible side <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />.

KinectFusion fused 11-bit, 640×480 Kinect depth frames at 30 Hz, tracking each frame against the global model by coarse-to-fine ICP and mapping at the sensor rate on a commodity GPU. A large plane filling most of the view can cause drift or tracking failure. Its projective TSDF caps visible-space values at the truncation distance $\mu$, leaves non-visible points beyond $\mu$ unmeasured and is exact at the surface, so fusion yields an approximate pseudo-Euclidean distance. Normals come from numerical derivatives near the zero level set, and ray marching finds surfaces by trilinear interpolation <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />.

<Image id="kinect-xbox-360-sensor" />

Trajectory optimizers need obstacle distances. Voxblox builds TSDFs faster than OctoMap builds its maps, then derives Euclidean signed distance fields (ESDFs) from them incrementally, more accurately than from occupancy <Cite id="voxblox-2016" />, and on GPUs nvblox reports up to 177x faster surface reconstruction and 31x faster distance-field computation <Cite id="nvblox-2023" />.

### Meshes, and then neural fields

A mesh adds connectivity, giving each face a normal and a renderable surface, but leaves holes where nothing was observed, and filling them invents geometry <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />.

NeRF fits a <Term id="neural-radiance-field">neural radiance field</Term> to a static scene from posed RGB photographs, intrinsics and scene bounds. Its MLP predicts density from position and colour from position and viewing direction, and differentiable volume rendering lets image error drive optimization <Cite id="nerf-2020" />.

Instant NGP cut optimization cost with a multiresolution hash encoding, smaller networks and fully fused CUDA kernels, and rendered one scene at 1080p in 5 seconds over 128 samples and a large 360-degree scene at 10 frames per second on one RTX 3090 <Cite id="instant-ngp-2022" />. <Term id="gaussian-splatting">3D Gaussian splatting</Term> optimizes Gaussian positions, anisotropic covariances, opacities and spherical-harmonic appearance from calibrated photographs, then rasterizes by alpha-blending sorted splats. It reports real-time 1080p rendering, with results on an A6000 GPU <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />.

DUSt3R predicts dense pointmaps from a pair of RGB images without intrinsics or poses, in the first image's frame and at unknown scale, trained with geometric supervision from pretrained CroCo weights. For an image collection, it then optimizes the alignment of pairwise pointmaps in 3D <Cite id="dust3r-2024" />.

Feed-forward models now cover whole collections: VGGT infers cameras, point maps, depth maps and point tracks from one, a few or hundreds of views in under one second <Cite id="vggt-2025" />.

## A radiance field is geometry for rendering

The [world-models taxonomy](/world-models/taxonomy) treats a splat reconstruction as a learned renderer: appearance is learned and physics is not. In the original 3DGS, learned opacity is an image-space alpha-compositing weight with no free, occupied or unknown label, and the stored primitive is a volumetric Gaussian <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />. The paper names mesh reconstruction as an open direction <Cite id="3dgs-2023" />, and SuGaR then aligned Gaussians with surfaces and extracted meshes by Poisson reconstruction <Cite id="sugar-2023" />.

Simulators pair splats for appearance with separate physics: SplatSim renders with splats while PyBullet supplies physics <Cite id="splatsim-2024" />. Its authors report zero-shot real-world transfer of diffusion policies on four rigid-body tasks with a UR5 and Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, after manual robot segmentation and ICP alignment <Cite id="splatsim-2024" />. In RoboGSim's closed-loop evaluator, a policy acts on splat-rendered images while Isaac Sim handles inverse kinematics and physical interaction, from multi-view images, supplied MDH parameters and mesh assets <Cite id="robogsim-2024" />.

Other fields serve a planner directly. Dex-NeRF renders transparency-aware depth from learned density for a grasp planner, where a RealSense camera failed to compute depth for most transparent objects tested <Cite id="dex-nerf-2021" />.

ParticleSplat, from Deepak Pathak (Carnegie Mellon) and colleagues (September 2026), encodes posed multi-view images into latent particles that decode to 3D Gaussians, trained with a novel-view synthesis objective. Object masks emerge without labels, moving a particle moves its object, and the representation improved downstream manipulation <Cite id="particlesplat-2026" />.

## SLAM: the system that builds the map

Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) builds such maps from sensor data while the robot moves without knowing its exact pose. Cadena and colleagues separate a sensor-dependent front end, which abstracts measurements and associates them with state variables, from a back end that performs inference and feeds information back for loop-closure detection and validation <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. [State estimation](/classical/state-estimation) covers the inference machinery.

<Image id="velodyne-hdl64-lidar-2009" />

Front ends are feature-based or direct. Monocular ORB-SLAM (2015) uses ORB features for tracking, local mapping, relocalization and loop closing, triangulating matched features and running local bundle adjustment. Its DBoW2 vocabulary proposes relocalization and loop candidates that need geometric validation <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />.

ORB-SLAM3 supports stereo, RGB-D and visual-inertial modes with pinhole or fisheye cameras and MAP-based IMU initialization. It starts a new map after persistent tracking loss and merges maps only after geometric and covisibility checks, plus gravity-direction checks for mature visual-inertial maps. Low texture remains the main failure case, and slow motion can delay inertial initialization <Cite id="orb-slam3-2021" />.

Direct Sparse Odometry skips the detector and optimizes photometric error over sampled pixels jointly with geometry <Cite id="dso-2018" />. It can sample any region with intensity gradient, including near-featureless walls, and gains from calibrating exposure, vignetting and camera response <Cite id="dso-2018" />.

Learned systems keep classical machinery: DROID-SLAM iterates camera pose and per-pixel depth through a dense bundle-adjustment layer <Cite id="droid-slam-2021" />.

Revisiting mapped landmarks can reduce odometric drift and in some cases correct it, and visual-inertial methods drift less than wheel odometry <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Monocular ORB-SLAM validates a <Term id="loop-closure">loop closure</Term> geometrically, then spreads its error with similarity alignment and Essential Graph optimization <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />.

<LoopClosure className="my-6" />

<Term id="place-recognition">Place recognition</Term> asks whether the current image matches a stored place, and motion information can also inform that belief. Viewpoint, illumination and seasonal changes alter one place's appearance, and different places can look alike, which is perceptual aliasing <Cite id="lowry-2016-place-recognition" />.

Perceptual aliasing can create false-positive associations that corrupt back-end estimates, while false negatives discard useful measurements. Robust losses and loop-closure validation mitigate outliers, though failures remain that depend on initialization <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

In the back end, Square Root SAM estimates the trajectory and landmark map jointly by MAP inference, which under Gaussian models with known data associations is sparse nonlinear least squares. It solves successive linearized systems by QR or Cholesky, and variable ordering controls fill-in <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. iSAM2 adds incremental reordering and relinearization on a Bayes tree. Thresholded updates trade some accuracy for speed, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve <Cite id="kaess-2012" />.

Smoothing suits loop closure because relinearizing the past requires the past to stay in the graph. Cadena and colleagues contrast sparse landmark maps with dense models suited to obstacle avoidance, and cite octrees and voxel hashing as efficient volumetric storage. Two rooms can look identical to a 2D laser yet differ to a camera. Severe illumination changes defeat bag-of-words methods, and active range cameras work in dark, untextured scenes but face range and external-light limits <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

The iMAP system learns a scene-specific MLP from scratch at room scale from a handheld RGB-D stream. It tracks at 10 Hz and maps at 2 Hz on a desktop CPU and GPU, retaining keyframes for replay <Cite id="imap-2021" />. NICE-SLAM uses hierarchical feature grids with pretrained geometry decoders, reconstructs a multi-room apartment and performs no loop closure <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />. Its 47 ms tracking and 130 ms mapping times use small pixel samples on an RTX 3090 <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />.

SplaTAM maps with 3D Gaussians from an RGB-D camera and uses a silhouette mask to determine whether areas were previously mapped <Cite id="splatam-2023" />.

## The deployed answer: costmaps and two planners

A navigation stack plans over a <Term id="costmap">costmap</Term>: occupancy from the map and live sensors, inflated by the robot's footprint. Lu, Hershberger and Smart's layered costmaps keep an ordered list of semantically separate layers and accumulate them into a master 2D costmap. Each update gathers the layers' bounds, then lets each layer write the master grid within them, and a configuration setting decides whether sensed obstacles overwrite static-map costs <Cite id="layered-costmaps-2014" />.

Navigation2, built on ROS 2, uses a layered costmap. Its global planner computes a shortest route to the goal, and a separate controller computes a local path and control signals, each a plugin in an asynchronous server <Cite id="nav2-2020" />.

The layered costmap's `track_unknown_space` option defaults to false, which treats unknown space as free; keeping the unknown state requires enabling it <Cite id="nav2-costmap-2d-2026" />. The planning algorithms are those of [motion planning](/classical/motion-planning) on a 2D grid.

## A representation is a service contract

[Perception](/classical/perception) locates objects in the current frame <Cite id="conceptgraphs-2023" />. Consumers issue different queries: localization needs stable landmarks <Cite id="cadena-2016" />, collision checking needs occupied volume and a conservative update rule <Cite id="octomap-2013" />, grasping needs surface pose and identity, and rendering needs appearance <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

Hydra stacks rungs in one real-time system, building a local ESDF, extracting a topological map of places from it and segmenting places into rooms <Cite id="hydra-2022" />.

SceneLM, from Jitendra Malik (UC Berkeley), Marco Pavone and colleagues (September 2026), keeps the whole map as a structured text list of objects that one vision-language model edits after each image. On language-grounded retrieval and localization benchmarks it performed competitively with complete mapping pipelines, with a map 6 to 12 times more compact, and it ran online on an edge device aboard a quadruped <Cite id="scenelm-2026" />.

Ledger, from Shravan Chaudhari, Homanga Bharadhwaj and colleagues at Johns Hopkins (October 2026), keeps a persistent 3D object memory from a person's egocentric video: each object's resting locations, its moves and a short description, retained after it leaves view. A language model answering from these records as text, without the images, raised GPT-5.4's HD-EPIC accuracy from 29.7% to 42.6%, and on Ego4D the memory located objects with a median error of 0.99 m where it returned a prediction <Cite id="ledger-2026" />.

A deployed map publishes its frame, timestamp, resolution, unknown-state convention, update rate and invalidation rule. In MoveIt 2, the planning scene holds the robot's current state, its model and the world representation for collision checking <Cite id="moveit-planning-scene-2026" />, and attached or removed objects must reach it before motion; the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers transforms and the planning scene. A scene representation answers what is present now, while a world model must answer how state changes under an action, as the [simulator comparison](/world-models/world-models-vs-simulators) sets out.

ORB-SLAM3 supports stereo, RGB-D and visual-inertial modes with pinhole or fisheye cameras and MAP-based IMU initialization. It starts a new map after persistent tracking loss and merges maps only after geometric and covisibility checks, plus gravity-direction checks for mature visual-inertial maps. Low texture remains the main failure case, and slow motion can delay inertial initialization <Cite id="orb-slam3-2021" />.

Direct Sparse Odometry skips the detector and optimizes photometric error over sampled pixels jointly with geometry <Cite id="dso-2018" />. It can sample any region with intensity gradient, including near-featureless walls, and gains from calibrating exposure, vignetting and camera response <Cite id="dso-2018" />.

Learned systems keep classical machinery: DROID-SLAM iterates camera pose and per-pixel depth through a dense bundle-adjustment layer <Cite id="droid-slam-2021" />.

MASt3R-SLAM builds tracking, local fusion, loop closure and global optimization around a learned two-view reconstruction prior <Cite id="mast3r-slam-2024" />. SLAM3R predicts pointmaps for overlapping video windows and aligns them into a global reconstruction without explicitly solving camera parameters <Cite id="slam3r-2024" />.

VGGT-SLAM instead aligns submaps with projective transforms, accounting for the reconstruction ambiguity that remains when monocular cameras are uncalibrated <Cite id="vggt-slam-2025" />.

Revisiting mapped landmarks can reduce odometric drift and in some cases correct it, and visual-inertial methods drift less than wheel odometry <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Monocular ORB-SLAM validates a <Term id="loop-closure">loop closure</Term> geometrically, then spreads its error with similarity alignment and Essential Graph optimization <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />.

<LoopClosure className="my-6" />

<Term id="place-recognition">Place recognition</Term> asks whether the current image matches a stored place, and motion information can also inform that belief. Viewpoint, illumination and seasonal changes alter one place's appearance, and different places can look alike, which is perceptual aliasing <Cite id="lowry-2016-place-recognition" />. AnyLoc builds place descriptors by aggregating frozen self-supervised features, without training a network specifically for visual place recognition <Cite id="anyloc-2023" />.

Perceptual aliasing can create false-positive associations that corrupt back-end estimates, while false negatives discard useful measurements. Robust losses and loop-closure validation mitigate outliers, though failures remain that depend on initialization <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Graduated non-convexity offers another route: it gradually sharpens a robust objective while using non-minimal solvers, avoiding a required initial guess in the tested estimation problems <Cite id="gnc-2019" />.

In the back end, Square Root SAM estimates the trajectory and landmark map jointly by MAP inference, which under Gaussian models with known data associations is sparse nonlinear least squares. It solves successive linearized systems by QR or Cholesky, and variable ordering controls fill-in <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. iSAM2 adds incremental reordering and relinearization on a Bayes tree. Thresholded updates trade some accuracy for speed, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve <Cite id="kaess-2012" />.

Smoothing suits loop closure because relinearizing the past requires the past to stay in the graph. Cadena and colleagues contrast sparse landmark maps with dense models suited to obstacle avoidance, and cite octrees and voxel hashing as efficient volumetric storage. Two rooms can look identical to a 2D laser yet differ to a camera. Severe illumination changes defeat bag-of-words methods, and active range cameras work in dark, untextured scenes but face range and external-light limits <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

The iMAP system learns a scene-specific MLP from scratch at room scale from a handheld RGB-D stream. It tracks at 10 Hz and maps at 2 Hz on a desktop CPU and GPU, retaining keyframes for replay <Cite id="imap-2021" />. NICE-SLAM uses hierarchical feature grids with pretrained geometry decoders, reconstructs a multi-room apartment and performs no loop closure <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />. Its 47 ms tracking and 130 ms mapping times use small pixel samples on an RTX 3090 <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />.

SplaTAM maps with 3D Gaussians from an RGB-D camera and uses a silhouette mask to determine whether areas were previously mapped <Cite id="splatam-2023" />.

Gaussian Splatting SLAM uses Gaussians for tracking as well as mapping, optimizing the camera directly against them and adding geometric checks for incremental monocular reconstruction <Cite id="monogs-2023" />.

AMB3R-SLAM separates a lightweight tracking front end from a hierarchical back end that enforces local, intermediate and global consistency over long trajectories <Cite id="amb3r-slam-2026" />.

Cartographer supplies a 2D LiDAR mapping example: branch-and-bound scan-to-submap matching produces loop-closure constraints during mapping <Cite id="cartographer-2016" />.

## The deployed answer: costmaps and two planners

A navigation stack plans over a <Term id="costmap">costmap</Term>: occupancy from the map and live sensors, inflated by the robot's footprint. Lu, Hershberger and Smart's layered costmaps keep an ordered list of semantically separate layers and accumulate them into a master 2D costmap. Each update gathers the layers' bounds, then lets each layer write the master grid within them, and a configuration setting decides whether sensed obstacles overwrite static-map costs <Cite id="layered-costmaps-2014" />.

Navigation2, built on ROS 2, uses a layered costmap. Its global planner computes a shortest route to the goal, and a separate controller computes a local path and control signals, each a plugin in an asynchronous server <Cite id="nav2-2020" />.

The layered costmap's `track_unknown_space` option defaults to false, which treats unknown space as free; keeping the unknown state requires enabling it <Cite id="nav2-costmap-2d-2026" />. The planning algorithms are those of [motion planning](/classical/motion-planning) on a 2D grid.

## A representation is a service contract

[Perception](/classical/perception) locates objects in the current frame <Cite id="conceptgraphs-2023" />. Consumers issue different queries: localization needs stable landmarks <Cite id="cadena-2016" />, collision checking needs occupied volume and a conservative update rule <Cite id="octomap-2013" />, grasping needs surface pose and identity, and rendering needs appearance <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

Hydra stacks rungs in one real-time system, building a local ESDF, extracting a topological map of places from it and segmenting places into rooms <Cite id="hydra-2022" />.

ConceptFusion fuses pixel-aligned foundation-model features into a 3D map that can be queried through text, images, audio or geometry, without additional training <Cite id="conceptfusion-2023" />.

SceneLM, from Jitendra Malik (UC Berkeley), Marco Pavone and colleagues (September 2026), keeps the whole map as a structured text list of objects that one vision-language model edits after each image. On language-grounded retrieval and localization benchmarks it performed competitively with complete mapping pipelines, with a map 6 to 12 times more compact, and it ran online on an edge device aboard a quadruped <Cite id="scenelm-2026" />.

Ledger, from Shravan Chaudhari, Homanga Bharadhwaj and colleagues at Johns Hopkins (October 2026), keeps a persistent 3D object memory from a person's egocentric video: each object's resting locations, its moves and a short description, retained after it leaves view. A language model answering from these records as text, without the images, raised GPT-5.4's HD-EPIC accuracy from 29.7% to 42.6%, and on Ego4D the memory located objects with a median error of 0.99 m where it returned a prediction <Cite id="ledger-2026" />.

A deployed map publishes its frame, timestamp, resolution, unknown-state convention, update rate and invalidation rule. In MoveIt 2, the planning scene holds the robot's current state, its model and the world representation for collision checking <Cite id="moveit-planning-scene-2026" />, and attached or removed objects must reach it before motion; the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers transforms and the planning scene. A scene representation answers what is present now, while a world model must answer how state changes under an action, as the [simulator comparison](/world-models/world-models-vs-simulators) sets out.

Includes a step-through motion scene of one predict-and-update cycle." domain: classical slug: state-estimation order: 4 status: published lastReviewed: "2026-08-17" citations: - kalman-1960-filter - mcgee-schmidt-1985 - thrun-2005 - smith-1990 - julier-uhlmann-1997 - kschischang-2001 - dellaert-kaess-2006 - kaess-2008 - kaess-2012 - cadena-2016 - forster-2017 - gtsam-2026 - mesh-mcl-construction-2026 - gordon-salmond-smith-1993 - dellaert-mcl-1999 - kalman-bucy-1961 - julier-uhlmann-2004 - li-mourikis-2013 - hartley-inekf-2019 - eqvio-2022 - gtsam-4-3-2026 - rauch-tung-striebel-1965 - grisetti-gmapping-2007 - msckf-2007 - okvis-2014 - backprop-kf-2016 - tlio-2020 - airio-2025 - mac-vo-2024 - tartan-imu-2025 - gait-2026 - mast3r-slam-2024 - planet-2018 - dreamerv3-nature-2025 - li-mourikis-temporal-2014 - li-rolling-shutter-2013 - openvins-2020 - kalibr-2013 - grandtour-2026 - ssio-2026 - humanoidpose-2026 seeAlso: - "rl-sim2real/legged-locomotion" - "adjacent/autonomous-vehicles" --- import { KalmanPredictUpdate } from '@/components/motion/scenes/kalman-predict-update'; import { Clip } from '@/components/motion/clip'; import { LinearizationGap } from '@/components/interactive/linearization-gap'; import { ExplainerFigure } from '@/components/explainers/explainer-figure'; State estimation computes a robot's state, such as its [configuration](/classical/kinematics) or velocity over ground, from noisy, biased and intermittent sensor readings, and [planning](/classical/motion-planning) and [control](/classical/control) assume that state is known. Probabilistic estimators report a belief, so each estimate carries its uncertainty .
## The Bayes filter A belief $bel(x_t)$ is a probability distribution over the state, kept current by two alternating steps. The predict step pushes the belief through the process model, given the control $u_t$ : $$ \overline{bel}(x_t) = \int p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}) \, bel(x_{t-1}) \, dx_{t-1} $$ The update step folds in the measurement $z_t$ through the sensor model $p(z_t \mid x_t)$ and sharpens the belief where the measurement points : $$ bel(x_t) = \eta \, p(z_t \mid x_t) \, \overline{bel}(x_t) $$ with normalizer $\eta$. This recursion is the Bayes filter, which Thrun, Burgard and Fox call the basis of virtually every technique in their book, and each tractable filter adds assumptions or approximations that make the integral computable . The bootstrap filter of Gordon, Salmond and Smith drops the linearity and Gaussian-noise assumptions and applies to any state transition or measurement model . Drive the robot in the figure below: its cloud of doubt grows as it moves and shrinks when it spots a landmark. ## The Kalman filter The 1960 Kalman filter reduces the recursion to matrix algebra by assuming linear process and measurement models and Gaussian noise : $$ x_t = A_t x_{t-1} + B_t u_t + w_t, \qquad z_t = C_t x_t + v_t $$ with $w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q_t)$ and $v_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R_t)$; Probabilistic Robotics swaps the two symbols. A Gaussian belief then stays Gaussian, so the recursion tracks only a mean and covariance. Predict : $$ \bar{\mu}_t = A_t \mu_{t-1} + B_t u_t, \qquad \bar{\Sigma}_t = A_t \Sigma_{t-1} A_t^{\top} + Q_t $$ Update, through the Kalman gain $K_t$ : $$ K_t = \bar{\Sigma}_t C_t^{\top} \left( C_t \bar{\Sigma}_t C_t^{\top} + R_t \right)^{-1} $$ $$ \mu_t = \bar{\mu}_t + K_t \left( z_t - C_t \bar{\mu}_t \right), \qquad \Sigma_t = \left( I - K_t C_t \right) \bar{\Sigma}_t $$ The gain is prior uncertainty over prior-plus-sensor uncertainty: a filter that trusts its model gets a small gain and mostly ignores the sensor, and one that trusts its sensor gets a gain near one. Under linear-Gaussian assumptions the recursion is the minimum-variance estimator, and Kalman's projection-based derivation makes it the best linear estimator with white noise even without Gaussian noise . McGee and Schmidt's 1985 NASA history credits Schmidt's Ames group with adapting the filter to nonlinear circumlunar navigation in the early 1960s. By early 1961 simulations supported the approach, though operation on available flight computers was unverified. The report separates this work from Battin's Apollo studies at MIT and Potter's square-root implementation used in Apollo. Primary Apollo navigation used ground radar, with an onboard backup . ## The extended Kalman filter Real robots are nonlinear: joint angles enter through sines and cosines, so the models become $x_t = g(x_{t-1}, u_t) + w_t$ and $z_t = h(x_t) + v_t$. The extended Kalman filter keeps the Gaussian belief, linearizes both models about the current estimate with their Jacobians $G_t = \partial g / \partial x$ and $H_t = \partial h / \partial x$, and propagates the covariance through the tangent system : $$ \bar{\Sigma}_t = G_t \Sigma_{t-1} G_t^{\top} + Q_t, \qquad K_t = \bar{\Sigma}_t H_t^{\top} \left( H_t \bar{\Sigma}_t H_t^{\top} + R_t \right)^{-1} $$ The mean moves through the true maps $g$ and $h$; only the covariance takes the linearized route . The Ames group moved from linearizing about a nominal reference trajectory to relinearizing about the *current estimated state*, which they hoped would bring "substantial advantages". An accidentally off-nominal simulation converged after initial overshoots, and the report names this modification the extended Kalman filter. It also discusses instability from round-off, inadequate statistical models and nonlinearities . Linearization holds near the estimate, which is itself uncertain, so where the nonlinearity is strong over the region the covariance covers, $\Sigma$ stops describing the true error, and the filter grows overconfident and can diverge . Julier and Uhlmann summarize 35 years of experience: the EKF is difficult to implement and tune, and reliable only for systems almost linear on the time scale of the updates . Li and Mourikis proved that standard EKF visual-inertial odometry is inconsistent because of how its Jacobians are computed, so it underestimates its uncertainty . The unscented Kalman filter of Julier and Uhlmann keeps the Gaussian and pushes deterministically chosen sample points through the true nonlinearity . Particle filters drop the Gaussian assumption and carry the belief as a set of particles . Invariant filters on Lie groups remove the dependence on the estimate: in the contact-aided invariant EKF, neither the linearized error dynamics nor the linearized observation model depends on the current state estimate . ## Factor graphs: keep the whole trajectory Rauch, Tung and Striebel related filtered and smoothed estimates in 1965 and showed numerically that smoothing reduces errors . In EKF-based SLAM, marginalizing old poses commits their linearized information to a Gaussian approximation that cannot be relinearized later. Full smoothing keeps the trajectory and can relinearize, though nonlinear optimization is not guaranteed to reach the global minimum . The posterior over the trajectory $X = \{x_0, \dots, x_T\}$ is a product of factors, one per measurement or motion constraint : $$ p(X \mid Z) \propto \prod_i \phi_i(X_i) $$ Drawn as a bipartite graph of variable and factor nodes, this is a factor graph. Kschischang, Frey, and Loeliger's 2001 paper unified inference on such graphs under the sum-product algorithm . With Gaussian factors, the most probable trajectory solves one sparse nonlinear least-squares problem : $$ X^{\star} = \arg\min_X \sum_i \left\lVert h_i(X_i) - z_i \right\rVert_{\Sigma_i}^2 $$ Dellaert and Kaess's 2006 Square Root SAM jointly estimates the SLAM trajectory and landmark map, assuming known data associations, Gaussian models, a uniform landmark prior and a fixed initial frame. It solves successive linearized systems, by QR on the measurement Jacobian or Cholesky on the information matrix, and variable ordering sets fill-in and cost . The iSAM method updates only the part of the factorization a new measurement touches . iSAM2 adds a Bayes tree with incremental reordering and relinearization: an update re-eliminates the affected cliques and their ancestors, then reattaches unaffected subtrees. Thresholds trade accuracy for computation, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve . GTSAM is a BSD-licensed C++ library that implements sensor fusion for robotics and computer vision using factor graphs . Version 4.3 moved to C++17 and added experimental CUDA nonlinear optimization and several legged-state-estimation implementations . Building on Lupton and Sukkarieh's preintegration, Forster and colleagues' on-manifold version collapses anywhere from a few to hundreds of IMU readings between two keyframes into one factor . Cadena and colleagues describe a classical SLAM period from 1986 to 2004, with EKF, Rao-Blackwellised particle-filter and maximum-likelihood approaches, and an algorithmic-analysis period from 2004 to 2015 . In Rao-Blackwellized grid mapping, each particle carries its own map . The survey treats MAP estimation, often over factor graphs, as the de facto standard but notes EKF systems with state-of-the-art performance. The gap shrinks when EKF linearization is accurate, sliding windows are used and inconsistency is addressed, and graphs still face unbounded growth and information loss under sparsification . The MSCKF sliding-window filter keeps 3D feature positions out of the state and is optimal up to linearization errors , while OKVIS argues that nonlinear optimization offers superior accuracy and stays tractable through sparsity . [Scene representation and mapping](/classical/scene-representation) covers what a robot keeps from the estimate. ## Where this meets the learned stack Learned components mostly enter classical estimators as measurements with uncertainty. TLIO regresses 3D displacement and its uncertainty from IMU data and fuses both into a stochastic cloning EKF , and MAC-VO learns a metrics-aware keypoint covariance and uses it to weight pose graph optimization . A September 2026 paper from Linus Kramer, William Talbot, Olga Vysotska and Marco Hutter is an example. For robots on construction sites, they replace the observation model of a Monte Carlo localization particle filter with a network that matches LiDAR scans against the building mesh, trained only on scans simulated inside that mesh. On real-world datasets it outperformed diffusion-based and ScanContext++ baselines at 18 ms per call . GAIT estimates legged-robot state without an explicit contact estimator and outperforms contact-aided model-based methods on a Unitree Go1 . Yuheng Qiu, Pieter Abbeel, Guanya Shi and colleagues at Amazon FAR, Carnegie Mellon and three other universities (October 2026) train inertial odometry from scratch without velocity or position labels: a teacher integrates the IMU over each short window, and a pose graph over many windows refines the targets . On six datasets from pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds and a humanoid, average velocity error came within 0.07 m/s of a supervised network of the same architecture, though its trajectory error on the EuRoC drone flights was 10.23 m against the supervised network's 3.72 m . The teacher used a reference attitude to remove gravity, and the IMU bias must be calibrated . Jiaxi Jiang, Marco Hutter, Christian Holz and colleagues at ETH Zurich (October 2026) estimate a humanoid's joint angles and world-space motion from ordinary video, training the pose decoder only on 128,000 synthetic images of sixteen humanoids . With no real pose labels, joint-angle error on three real humanoids was 18 to 32% below the best baseline on each . [Latent-dynamics world models](/world-models/latent-dynamics) act as learned belief states. PlaNet's latent dynamics model has deterministic and stochastic transition components trained with variational inference . DreamerV3 learns a model of the environment and improves its behaviour by imagining future scenarios . ## Timing is part of the state Fusing visual and inertial measurements requires each measurement's precise sampling time , and most consumer cameras use rolling shutters that capture each pixel row at a slightly different time . The camera-IMU offset can be a state variable, locally identifiable except in a few degenerate motions ; OpenVINS calibrates it in its sliding-window filter , and Kalibr estimates time offsets to a fraction of the smallest measurement period . Persistent directional residuals in per-sensor innovations point to calibration or timing bias instead of random noise. GrandTour, which its authors call the largest open-access legged-robotics dataset, supplies RTK-GNSS and total-station ground truth . The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers temporal residuals, and the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers timestamped interfaces.

[Scene representation and mapping](/classical/scene-representation) covers what a robot keeps from the estimate. ## Where this meets the learned stack Learned components mostly enter classical estimators as measurements with uncertainty. TLIO regresses 3D displacement and its uncertainty from IMU data and fuses both into a stochastic cloning EKF , and MAC-VO learns a metrics-aware keypoint covariance and uses it to weight pose graph optimization . Backprop KF makes the filter itself differentiable, representing its belief-parameter updates as a computation graph that can be trained from raw observations . AirIO preserves body-frame IMU measurements and encodes attitude, combining learned IMU correction with an uncertainty-aware EKF for aerial robots . A September 2026 paper from Linus Kramer, William Talbot, Olga Vysotska and Marco Hutter is an example. For robots on construction sites, they replace the observation model of a Monte Carlo localization particle filter with a network that matches LiDAR scans against the building mesh, trained only on scans simulated inside that mesh. On real-world datasets it outperformed diffusion-based and ScanContext++ baselines at 18 ms per call . GAIT estimates legged-robot state without an explicit contact estimator and outperforms contact-aided model-based methods on a Unitree Go1 . Yuheng Qiu, Pieter Abbeel, Guanya Shi and colleagues at Amazon FAR, Carnegie Mellon and three other universities (October 2026) train inertial odometry from scratch without velocity or position labels: a teacher integrates the IMU over each short window, and a pose graph over many windows refines the targets . On six datasets from pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds and a humanoid, average velocity error came within 0.07 m/s of a supervised network of the same architecture, though its trajectory error on the EuRoC drone flights was 10.23 m against the supervised network's 3.72 m . The teacher used a reference attitude to remove gravity, and the IMU bias must be calibrated . Jiaxi Jiang, Marco Hutter, Christian Holz and colleagues at ETH Zurich (October 2026) estimate a humanoid's joint angles and world-space motion from ordinary video, training the pose decoder only on 128,000 synthetic images of sixteen humanoids . With no real pose labels, joint-angle error on three real humanoids was 18 to 32% below the best baseline on each . [Latent-dynamics world models](/world-models/latent-dynamics) act as learned belief states. PlaNet's latent dynamics model has deterministic and stochastic transition components trained with variational inference . GrandTour, which its authors call the largest open-access legged-robotics dataset, supplies RTK-GNSS and total-station ground truth . The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers temporal residuals, and the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers timestamped interfaces.
