Feedback loops run beneath any learned policy, from motor drivers to whole-body torque control.
## PID: three ways to use an error For an error $e(t) = r(t) - y(t)$ between reference and measured output, a PID controller commands $$ u(t) = K_p\, e(t) + K_i \int_0^{t} e(\tau)\, d\tau + K_d\, \frac{de}{dt} $$ Ziegler and Nichols called the three actions proportional response, automatic reset and pre-act. Their 1942 tuning rules drive the loop into oscillation with proportional gain alone, then back off from the critical gain and period by fixed fractions . Integral action removes the steady-state offset that a constant disturbance leaves under proportional control, and it needs anti-windup when the actuator saturates. Åström and Murray quote a survey in which 97% of over eleven thousand regulatory controllers in refining, chemicals and pulp and paper used PID . A torque-driven inverted pendulum, the canonical underactuated plant, obeys $$ \ddot{\theta} = \frac{g}{\ell} \sin\theta + \frac{u + \tau_{bias}}{m \ell^2} $$ with $\theta$ measured from upright and $\tau_{bias}$ a constant torque from an off-center payload. Linearized about upright, the loop is stable only when $K_p > m g \ell$ . ## State space and LQR For a linear plant $\dot{x} = Ax + Bu$ under state feedback $u = -Kx$, the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) picks the gain that minimizes a quadratic cost trading state error against control effort : $$ J = \int_0^{\infty} \left( x^{\top} Q x + u^{\top} R u \right) dt $$ The optimal gain is $K = R^{-1} B^{\top} P$, where $P$ solves the algebraic Riccati equation : $$ A^{\top} P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^{\top} P + Q = 0 $$ A heavier angle penalty in $Q$ stiffens the controller and a heavier torque penalty in $R$ softens it; for the linearized pendulum, the LQR gain is a PD controller. The guarantee is local: swinging the pole up from hanging takes an energy-shaping controller, with LQR catching it at the top . ## MPC: re-solve the plan at every step Model-predictive control solves a short-horizon optimal control problem at every control step, from the measured state and subject to the constraints : $$ \min_{u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}} \; \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left( x_k^{\top} Q x_k + u_k^{\top} R u_k \right) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k), \; u_k \in \mathcal{U}, \; x_k \in \mathcal{X} $$ Only the first input is applied before the next solve, so feedback from the measured state absorbs part of the model error , and limits on states and inputs, from torque bounds to friction cones, enter the optimization directly . MPC grew out of 1970s and 1980s power-plant and refinery practice, where slow, constrained, multivariable plants defeated PID . On the MIT Cheetah 3, Di Carlo and colleagues' convex MPC solved each QP in under a millisecond at 20 to 30 Hz, and one gain set served every gait from standing to gallop . On legged hardware, DIAL-MPC optimizes full-order quadruped dynamics in real time without training and beats RL policies by 50% on climbing tasks . [Reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc) compares these controllers with learned policies. ## Whole-body QP: the bottom of the stack A legged or humanoid robot's whole-body controller turns desired accelerations and contact forces into joint torques. Khatib's 1987 operational-space formulation writes the dynamics in task space : $$ \Lambda(x)\, \ddot{x} + \mu(x, \dot{x}) + p(x) = F $$ with $\Lambda$ the task-space inertia and $\mu$, $p$ the Coriolis and gravity terms, mapped to joints through the [kinematic](/classical/kinematics) Jacobian. Sentis and Khatib extended it to a task hierarchy, with contact and joint-limit constraints first and posture in the remaining degrees of freedom , and hierarchical QP solves such priorities at control rate . Weighted controllers instead solve one quadratic program per tick: $$ \begin{aligned} \min_{\ddot{q},\, \tau,\, f} \quad & \sum_i w_i \, \lVert A_i \ddot{q} - b_i \rVert^2 \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & M(q)\, \ddot{q} + h(q, \dot{q}) = S^{\top} \tau + J_c(q)^{\top} f \\ & \tau_{min} \le \tau \le \tau_{max}, \qquad f \in \mathcal{F} \end{aligned} $$ Its variables are joint accelerations, torques and contact forces; the rigid-body dynamics are the equality constraint, $\mathcal{F}$ holds the friction cones, and each task is one weighted row of the objective . Learned and model-based whole-body control both ship. Figure reports that Helix 02's System 0 runs at 1 kHz and handles balance, contact and coordination across the whole body , while Boston Dynamics reports that the teleoperation system behind Atlas's large behavior models pairs Atlas's model-predictive controller with a VR interface . [Humanoid whole-body control](/rl-sim2real/humanoid-wbc) covers how learned policies relate to the QP. ## Impedance control: making contact a design variable A stiff position-controlled arm driven into a surface 2 mm nearer than modeled turns that error into stored collision energy. Hogan's 1985 impedance control instead commands the relationship between force and motion, so the arm presents a programmable mass-spring-damper: at a contact, a controller commands force or velocity, and the environment fixes the other . Admittance control is the dual: measure force with a wrist sensor and command motion. A backdrivable direct-drive arm realizes an impedance directly, while a stiff geared arm with a force-torque sensor runs admittance in software. Mason's and Raibert and Craig's hybrid force/position control builds a task frame from the contact geometry and controls force along the constrained axes and position along the free ones, never both on one axis . Polishing, for instance, controls force normal to the surface and position along it, which needs the contact geometry in advance. Learned policies now set impedance: Adaptive Compliance Policy learns spatially and temporally varying compliance from human demonstrations and reports over 50% improvement over state-of-the-art visuomotor policies . A diffusion-based impedance learner co-authored by Hogan adapts stiffness and damping online on a torque-controlled KUKA LBR iiwa . Intrinsic, which ran the 2026 AI for Industry Challenge, reports that 90% of the top teams in its real-workcell phase inserted the connector with rules-based routines, such as spiral searches, and force-torque feedback . ForceTwin, from Marco Hutter (ETH Zurich) and colleagues (September 2026), fits an articulated object's inertia, friction, damping and spring or door-closer forces from a person probing it with a handheld force-sensing gripper. As the feedforward model for impedance control on a Spot and a Franka FR3, it completed 87% of goals across nine object-robot pairs, against 60% with vision-language-model priors and 57% with kinematics-only twins . A non-backdrivable, position-controlled geared arm without a force sensor has no force channel: position error, gear ratio and the surface set the contact force, so a joint-position policy on it cannot regulate force in the contact-rich tasks of [dexterity](/frontier/dexterity). Series elastic actuation adds a deliberate spring for shock tolerance and more accurate, stable force control . Franka's interface exposes a 1 kHz torque-level layer with Cartesian impedance controllers , while Universal Robots' URScript force mode takes a task frame, compliant axes, target forces and position-deviation limits . Backdrivability is an actuator decision that fixes which of these schemes the hardware can attempt. The contact lab's transient force limit comes from published biomechanical measurements . ISO/TS 15066:2016 holds the original collaborative-robot tables . ISO republished ISO 10218-1 and ISO 10218-2 in February 2025, withdrawing the 2011 editions , and a 2026 comparison describes the 2025 series as fully absorbing ISO/TS 15066 . ## The policy-to-controller contract A learned action reaches the motors through a lower controller, so request type, rate, horizon, frame and saturation behavior belong to the interface. Peng and van de Panne showed that the action parameterization, from torques to target joint angles, affects learning, robustness and motion quality , and the same Cartesian delta behaves differently in contact under a position controller and under an impedance controller. Deployed stacks are multi-rate: Berkeley Humanoid runs its RL policy at 50 Hz, its state estimator at 1 kHz and its PD controller at 25 kHz . Model latency is part of the loop: a 3-billion-parameter VLA spends 46 ms on KV-cache prefill alone on an RTX 4090 . Deadline handling and hard bounds therefore sit outside the model, holding or stopping the robot when inference is late or an action is out of bounds. Data-driven controllers often lack well-understood guarantees, which motivates separate safety filters . The [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces) covers interface choice. ## Where this meets the learned stack MPC keeps a [sim-to-real](/rl-sim2real/sim2real-transfer) gap even when it re-solves against the [measured state](/classical/state-estimation) . That gap and the computational burden still limit whole-body MPC on real humanoids, and Ishihara and colleagues patch the model with a learned residual network . Boston Dynamics added reinforcement learning to Spot's existing MPC stack .

Its central test, force closure, asks whether the origin lies inside the convex hull of the contact wrenches ; the distance to that hull's boundary is the standard quality metric . ## The wrench space, live ## Contact models
A contact model says which forces a fingertip can transmit; Salisbury and Roth modeled several finger-contact types for three-fingered hands . A frictionless point contact pushes only along the surface normal. A point contact with friction obeys Coulomb's law: the tangential force can reach $\mu$ times the normal force before the contact slides . $$ \lVert f^t \rVert \le \mu \, f^n $$ The admissible forces form the friction cone around the inward normal, with half-angle $\alpha = \arctan \mu$. In the plane the cone is a wedge; in space it is a quadratic cone, and approximating it by a polyhedral one keeps the analysis linear . A soft-finger contact adds a torsional moment about the normal, bounded by a torsional coefficient times the normal load . Tilt the grip in the figure below and pick a surface to find where the pinch lets go. Cutkosky's taxonomy separates power grasps, which wrap the object for stability, from precision grasps, which hold it in the fingertips for dexterity . GraspQP reports that simplified force-closure analysis favors power grasps . ## The grasp wrench space [Perception](/classical/perception) supplies the object pose. A contact force both pushes and twists the object, so its wrench stacks the force over its moment about the object's reference frame : $$ w_i = \begin{bmatrix} f_i \\ r_i \times f_i \end{bmatrix} $$ In the plane this is $(f_x, f_y, \tau)$ with $\tau = r_x f_y - r_y f_x$ . The primitive wrenches lie along the cone edges at unit normal force. If each contact's force is limited separately, the grasp wrench space is the convex hull of the Minkowski sum of the contacts' primitive wrenches . If the total force is limited, it is the convex hull of their union : $$ \mathcal{W} = \operatorname{conv}\left\{ w_{ij} \right\}, \qquad w_{ij} = \begin{bmatrix} n_i \pm \mu \, t_i \\ r_i \times (n_i \pm \mu \, t_i) \end{bmatrix} $$ Testing whether the origin lies inside this polytope is a ray-shooting problem dual to a linear program . ## Force closure A grasp has force closure when the contacts can resist any external wrench, so the object's motion is fully constrained . That holds exactly when the hull contains a neighborhood of the origin : $$ \exists \, \varepsilon > 0 : \quad B_\varepsilon(0) \subset \mathcal{W} $$ An origin on the boundary leaves a disturbance the grasp cannot resist. Uncertainty in friction and contact position can be disastrous for closure . Without friction the cone collapses to the normal ray, and form closure, closure by geometry alone, needs at least four wrenches in the plane and seven in space, as Reuleaux noted in 1875 and Somoff in 1897 . Markenscoff, Ni and Papadimitriou showed that four fingers suffice for any planar object with a piecewise smooth boundary except a circle, twelve for any spatial object without rotational symmetry, and seven under very general conditions . With Coulomb friction, three fingers are necessary and sufficient to grasp any planar object, and four in space, under the most relaxed assumptions; a particular object can need fewer . Nguyen's antipodal grasp theorem settles the two-finger planar case: such a grasp with friction is force closure if and only if the line between the contacts lies inside both friction cones . A differentiable estimator later made force closure an optimization objective that tests closure within milliseconds for arbitrary hands . ## Grasp quality: the epsilon metric Ferrari and Canny turned the binary test into a number: the quality $\varepsilon$ is the radius of the largest origin-centered ball inside the grasp wrench space . $$ \varepsilon = \min_{F_k \in \partial \mathcal{W}} \; \operatorname{dist}\!\left( 0, F_k \right) $$ Because the hull is a polytope, $\varepsilon$ is the distance from the origin to its nearest facet , and with an $l$-edge polyhedral cone it is an approximation . With unit normal forces, $\varepsilon$ is the worst-case disturbance the grasp absorbs per unit of contact force, at the nominal friction. In FIRMGrasp's tests, 53% of nominally force-closed grasps lost closure in the adverse friction tail , and in a shake test the nominal margin ranked a successful grasp above a failed one with probability only 0.53 . In most cases the grasp most robust to pose error is not the one with the highest $\varepsilon$ . Predicting grasp stability well required a combination of metrics . Roa and Suárez review measures based on contact locations and hand configuration and show that the largest-minimum resisted wrench depends on the torque origin and on the force-torque metric. A grasp optimal under a shared total-force limit need not be optimal under per-finger limits, and most of their analysis is quasi-static . FRoGGeR's min-weight metric approximates $\varepsilon$ differentiably and synthesizes grasps in a median 0.834 s . ## Reading the hull The lab draws the object and each contact's friction cone beside the grasp wrench space projected from $(f_x, f_y, \tau)$, turns the origin ring green under force closure and reports $\varepsilon$. The default tripod of top, right and bottom contacts is force closure at $\mu = 0.7$. Without the bottom contact, the top-right pair's connecting line sits 45 degrees from each normal, outside cones of half-angle $\arctan 0.7 \approx 35$ degrees, so it fails Nguyen's test . Sliding contact 2 onto the bottom edge makes the pair antipodal and restores closure for any positive friction, and lowering $\mu$ lowers $\varepsilon$. ## Where this meets the learned stack Dex-Net 2.0 labels synthetic data with analytic metrics: 6.7 million datapoints from 1,500 object models, positive when expected $\varepsilon$ under object-pose, gripper-pose and friction uncertainty exceeds 0.002 and no collision is modeled. Its GQ-CNN takes a grasp-aligned depth crop and the gripper depth, and predicts robustness without regressing $\varepsilon$ . The planner samples antipodal parallel-jaw candidates from depth gradients and executes the most robust [reachable](/classical/kinematics), [collision-free](/classical/motion-planning) one. It assumes isolated rigid objects on a planar worksurface and one depth camera with known intrinsics. On an ABB YuMi with silicone fingertips and a Primesense Carmine 1.08, a success meant the object stayed held through lifting, transport and shaking . On eight 3D-printed adversarial objects, GQ-L-Adv, fine-tuned on synthetic examples of them, succeeded in 93% of 80 trials. A separate CEM-augmented run of 100 trials on 40 novel household objects, including articulated and deformable ones, reported 94% success and 99% precision: 68 of 69 grasps rated above 50% robustness succeeded. The two evaluations cannot be pooled, and missing depth on thin parts and object collisions remained failure modes . Dex-Net 4.0 cleared bins of up to 25 novel objects with over 95% reliability at more than 300 mean picks per hour . DexGraspNet 2.0 holds 427 million grasps , and GraspGen-X, a diffusion grasp generator trained on procedural grippers and 2 billion grasps, generalized zero-shot to novel real grippers . Learned [diffusion policies](/manipulation/diffusion-policy) take contacts from data, but dexterous data pipelines still solve contact mechanics: BODex synthesizes over 49 grasps per second on one RTX 3090 GPU , and DexEvolve's authors note that analytic synthesis rests on simplifying assumptions that yield infeasible grasps, which high-fidelity simulation must filter out . A 2026 [controller](/classical/control) enforces the quality margin during execution, keeping a median 94% of it at 0.09 ms per solve . [Sim-to-real transfer](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion) remained hard for dexterous grasping: Get a Grip found most multi-finger methods degrading on hardware . DexGraspNet 2.0 transferred zero-shot to real clutter at 90.7% success , and RobustDexGrasp, trained in simulation, reached 94.6% on 512 real objects . DexGraspVLA reports over 90% success in thousands of unseen cluttered scenes . Adding wrench and tactile feedback to vision raised one policy from 14 to 24 successes in 25 real trials . GENESIS-Handover, from Marco Hutter (ETH Zurich) and colleagues (October 2026), chooses how a robot presents an object by matching generated task-specific grips to the person's live hand . On a legged manipulator, handovers needing no adjustment rose from 6 to 16 of 60 against AFT-Handover .
